"a5359436-369e-5935-88c6-73a8053a9364" :question/math-academy-id "q-66526" :question/problem "$\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}})=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite $\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}=\frac{1}{{e}^{1/2}}={e}^{-1/2}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}})=\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-1/2})
$$

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-1/2})=-\frac{1}{2}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-6fd07e78-dd69-5881-8015-dd32bee64dd0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-6fd07e78-dd69-5881-8015-dd32bee64dd0" :answer-field/id #uuid "6fd07e78-dd69-5881-8015-dd32bee64dd0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6614a67a-a7fe-55e2-be74-7e1ab3c9e3c7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6042c78b-71af-5276-80cf-ccdcb9284bf0" "answer-6614a67a-a7fe-55e2-be74-7e1ab3c9e3c7" "answer-b10534f0-4c95-531e-94d6-ba5e4a60964c" "answer-f7b61c9c-6858-5b2e-a66c-1ae788e691c5" "answer-c6fff638-a832-599c-b20d-b7725b1e8582"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6042c78b-71af-5276-80cf-ccdcb9284bf0" :answer/id #uuid "6042c78b-71af-5276-80cf-ccdcb9284bf0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6614a67a-a7fe-55e2-be74-7e1ab3c9e3c7" :answer/id #uuid "6614a67a-a7fe-55e2-be74-7e1ab3c9e3c7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b10534f0-4c95-531e-94d6-ba5e4a60964c" :answer/id #uuid "b10534f0-4c95-531e-94d6-ba5e4a60964c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f7b61c9c-6858-5b2e-a66c-1ae788e691c5" :answer/id #uuid "f7b61c9c-6858-5b2e-a66c-1ae788e691c5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c6fff638-a832-599c-b20d-b7725b1e8582" :answer/id #uuid "c6fff638-a832-599c-b20d-b7725b1e8582" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233592 :question/problem "![](images/a6/a61a6232b2041bab3d455a7d765311ddfae25f674f8dbbf79696d2137355b159.png)

The Venn diagram shown above represents two events $A$ and $B$ and the number of outcomes in each region of the sample space.

Given that every outcome is equally likely, find $P({A}^{′}\cup {B}^{′}).$" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the probability of an event using a Venn diagram, we count the number of outcomes in the region that represents the event, and divide by the total number of outcomes of the sample space $S.$

In the Venn diagram, ${A}^{′}\cup {B}^{′}$ is represented by the area outside the circle $B$ or outside the circle $A$ (see the illustration below).

![](images/6a/6a3bb7b671e45aeb15d3239cae6fcedb7c36e52b15141d66b23e65066ab37edc.png)

We count up the outcomes:

- The number of outcomes in ${A}^{′}\cup {B}^{′}$ is 

$$
2+5+1=8
$$

- The total number of outcomes in $S$ is

$$
2+9+5+1=17.
$$

So, we have

$$
P({A}^{′}\cup {B}^{′})=\frac{8}{17}.
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3f94bd53-f137-5cf0-9547-b2c16a22c866"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-3f94bd53-f137-5cf0-9547-b2c16a22c866" :answer-field/id #uuid "3f94bd53-f137-5cf0-9547-b2c16a22c866" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-25d9c9bd-9d1a-5474-8d96-6dd5e36e339b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1537842d-13cc-58e0-a0d1-143d9983a915" "answer-fd4ece7b-d879-59f6-b3c7-36a00c82fb05" "answer-25d9c9bd-9d1a-5474-8d96-6dd5e36e339b" "answer-7dd7ce66-80c6-5c47-a014-bc47fefa20f4" "answer-48992171-11ab-56d9-b3bd-6dc0be5319e1"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1537842d-13cc-58e0-a0d1-143d9983a915" :answer/id #uuid "1537842d-13cc-58e0-a0d1-143d9983a915" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fd4ece7b-d879-59f6-b3c7-36a00c82fb05" :answer/id #uuid "fd4ece7b-d879-59f6-b3c7-36a00c82fb05" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{17}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-25d9c9bd-9d1a-5474-8d96-6dd5e36e339b" :answer/id #uuid "25d9c9bd-9d1a-5474-8d96-6dd5e36e339b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8}{17}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7dd7ce66-80c6-5c47-a014-bc47fefa20f4" :answer/id #uuid "7dd7ce66-80c6-5c47-a014-bc47fefa20f4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{9}{16}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-48992171-11ab-56d9-b3bd-6dc0be5319e1" :answer/id #uuid "48992171-11ab-56d9-b3bd-6dc0be5319e1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{9}{17}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233268 :question/problem "![](images/79/791a76ebbb34751b2ce345243c5de4baf95a32357ce48830e3ea43043011b5e1.png)

Each unit is $5\,\text{yd}$ long, $3\,\text{yd}$ wide, and $3\text{yd}$ high. If it costs $$2$ per cubic yard per day to rent a storage unit, how much does it cost the company each day to rent the storage units?" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the volume of one storage unit.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=5,\,w=3,\,h=3
$$

into the formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}V=5\cdot 3\cdot 3=45\,{\text{yd}}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The total volume of the ten units is

$$
45\cdot 10=450\,{\text{yd}}^{3}.
$$

Finally, to rent the storage units, each day the company must pay

$$
450\cdot $2=$900.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-45a670a5-6eca-551c-9bba-97922b332700"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "c7f9805c-ce96-515d-891a-332594997042" :question/math-academy-id "q-85920" :question/problem "A team of $5$ players is to be chosen at random from $7$ boys and $5$ girls.  What is the probability that $2$ boys and $3$ girls will be chosen? Round your answer to the nearest percent." :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ represent the event described in the question. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N},\end{aligned}
$$

where $N$ is the total number of ways to choose $5$ people out of a total of $12,$ and $n$ is the number of picks where $2$ are boys and $3$ are girls.

Since the order in which the players are chosen does not matter, we use combinations.

First, we compute $N.$ The number of ways to pick $5$ people from a total of $12$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}N={}_{12}{C}_{5} & =\frac{12!}{5!\cdot 7!}=792.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $n.$ The computation of $n$ can be divided into two steps: 

- the number of ways to choose $2$ (out of $7$) boys is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{7}{C}_{2}=\frac{7!}{2!\cdot 5!}=21\end{aligned}
$$

- the number of ways to choose $3$ (out of $5$) girls is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{5}{C}_{3} & =\frac{5!}{3!\cdot 2!}=10\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the results from the above steps, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n={}_{7}{C}_{2}\cdot {}_{5}{C}_{3}=21\cdot 10=210.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{210}{792}≈0.27=27%.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c3a0c2d2-5b3a-522b-a6d4-7655774ccad3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =6+5(t-2) \\  & =6+5t-10 \\  & =5t-4.\end{aligned}

"question-19e31d5d-5933-52fe-a699-d3240dcd05a2" :question/id #uuid "19e31d5d-5933-52fe-a699-d3240dcd05a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-288661" :question/problem "The equation

$$
(ax-8)(x+b)=4{x}^{2}-32x+48
$$

is true for all values of $x,$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants. What is the value of $a+b?$

$a+b=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Since the equation is true for all values of $x,$ the expressions on both sides must be exactly the same. That means the product on the left-hand side must expand to match the right-hand side.

First, let's expand the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(ax-8)(x+b) & =a{x}^{2}+abx-8x-8b \\  & =a{x}^{2}+(ab-8)x-8b.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we equate the expanded form to the right-hand side:

$$
a{x}^{2}+(ab-8)x-8b=4{x}^{2}-32x+48.
$$

Now, we compare the coefficients of corresponding terms.

- Equating the coefficients of ${x}^{2},$ we get

$$
a=4.
$$

- Equating the constant terms, we get

$$
-8\cdot b=48⇒b=-6.
$$

Let's verify that values $a=4$ and $b=-6$ produce the correct linear coefficient:

$$
\begin{aligned}ab-8 & =4\cdot (-6)-8 \\  & =-24-8 \\  & =-32\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

which matches the coefficient of $x$ on the right-hand side. So, our solution is valid.

Finally, we compute the value of $a+b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =4+(-6) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f" :answer-field/id #uuid "9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4" :answer/id #uuid "7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233432 :question/problem "![](images/ce/cec25c6ab182494771824bae8c2182bf38b57e2d1e81d913e3e49916c8cc3d60.png)

The residual plot above was constructed after fitting a linear regression model on a set of bivariate numerical data $(x,y).$
Which of the following statements are true?

I. When $x=8,$ the regression equation overestimates the value of $y.$

II. The residuals appear to be randomly scattered about the horizontal axis (there are no obvious trends).

III. This linear regression is probably a good fit for the data." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The residual equals the actual value minus the estimated value:

$$
\text{Residual}=\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated}
$$

 
From the plot, the residual at $x=8$ is negative. So, we have that $\text{Actual}<\text{Estimated},$ and therefore the model overestimates  this data point.

- Statement II is false. The plot shows the residuals tend to decrease as $x$ increases. So, there is a trend, as shown below.

![](images/0b/0bb186e7b1c1923e7e8b2776b202b1dcd9b930c56583199964e47530805d246d.png)

- Statement III is false. Since the residuals are *not* randomly scattered above and below the horizontal axis, our regression line is *not* a good fit for the given data.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a743042b-63eb-545c-bdc0-1aab409141d4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "0821d791-2798-561e-8237-7b4aabdd155c" :question/math-academy-id "q-35003" :question/problem "![](images/06/06e792c5b74eda036b55ac3728122737da22c9824f89f982b50657ab07391269.png)

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above? 

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=\text{DNE}$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=2$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)$" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. As $x$ approaches $0$ from the left and right we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x)=0,\,{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x)=1\,.
$$

 
Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x),$ and hence ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=\text{DNE}.$

- Statement II is false. As $x$ approaches $1$ from the left and right we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)=2,\,{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}\,.
$$

 
Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x),$ and hence ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=\text{DNE}.$

- Statement III is false. We see from the graph that 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=\text{DNE},\,{lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=\text{DNE}
$$

 We can't say that the limits are equal because we can't compare undefined values.

In conclusion, only statement I is true." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b5da9fec-9cf5-5ef3-8a64-44b81b106bd9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Given a frequency table containing continuous data split into $K$ classes, we can estimate the variance by treating all observations within each class as though they were equal to the midpoint of that class. This gives

$$
{\sigma }_{n}^{2}≈\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{K}{f}_{i}\cdot ({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},
$$

where

- ${f}_{i}$ is the frequency of the $i$th class,

- ${m}_{i}$ is the midpoint of the $i$th class,

- $n$ is the total number of observations, and

- $\overset{―}{x}$ is the estimated mean, calculated using the class midpoints.

To find the variance, we add columns to our table for the midpoints of each interval, the squared deviations of the midpoints from the mean, and the products of the squared deviations and frequencies.

| Range | ${f}_{i}$ | ${m}_{i}$ | ${({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ | ${f}_{i}{({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $8$ | $5$ | $72.25$ | $578$ |
| $10\le x<20$ | $7$ | $15$ | $2.25$ | $15.75$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $5$ | $25$ | $132.25$ | $661.25$ |

$$

$$

Then, we divide the sum of all the values in the last column by $20$ (the total number of observations):

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n}^{2} & ≈\frac{578+15.75+661.25}{20} \\  & =\frac{1255}{20} \\  & =62.75\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the estimated standard deviation is the square root of the estimated variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n} & ≈\sqrt{62.75}≈7.9\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186232372 :answer-field/correct "answer-50cba50f-0215-54ad-96b6-a3d381b47f01" :answer-field/choices ["answer-50cba50f-0215-54ad-96b6-a3d381b47f01"] 17592186234325 :question/problem "![](images/4c/4ce20d9d732816efda0a2fd3aebabc467f9f2c73d0b6037f4ad8f95d8e8ef1e7.png)

Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD?$" :question/worked-solution "The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $△ABD$ and $△BDC$ (see the illustration below).

![](images/6e/6e070d26915bcb11118f5a23f36b80038d5dd865e32a8517a12c10939ca02f0b.png)

First, we find the area of $△ABD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot 8\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{85}^{∘} \\  & =24\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{85}^{∘} \\  & ≈23.908\,7,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Now we find the area of $△BCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{BCD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 14\cdot 16\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{36.4}^{∘} \\  & =112\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{36.4}^{∘} \\  & ≈66.462\,9,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABD}+{A}_{BCD} \\  & ≈23.908\,7+66.462\,9 \\  & ≈90.371\,6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $90.$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a5f55799-fa35-55be-b5e7-23ed06c306d5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$

$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2f(x)}{3{x}^{2}}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted above." :question/worked-solution "Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2f(x)}{3{x}^{2}}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to 1}(-2f(x))}{{lim}_{x\to 1}3{x}^{2}}.
$$

We find from the graph that ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)=6.$ Calculating the limits of the numerator and denominator separately, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}(-2f(x))=-2(6)=-12
$$

and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}3{x}^{2}=3(1)^{2}=3.
$$

Taking the quotient of these limits, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2f(x)}{3{x}^{2}} & =\frac{{lim}_{x\to 1}(-2f(x))}{{lim}_{x\to 1}3{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-12}{3} \\  & =-4\,.\end{aligned}

has a factor of $(x-1)$ and has a remainder of $4$ when divided by $(x+2).$ Find the value of $a-b.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $(x-1)$ is a factor of $f(x)$, it must divide into $f(x)$ with no remainder. In other words, when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-1),$ the remainder is $0.$ It follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =f(1) \\  & =a(1)^{3}-2(1)^{2}+b(1)+1 \\  & =a-2+b+1 \\  & =a+b-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since we're told that the remainder is $4$ when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+2),$ it follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =f(-2) \\  & =a(-2)^{3}-2(-2)^{2}+b(-2)+1 \\  & =-8a-8-2b+1 \\  & =-8a-2b-7.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0=a+b-1 \\ 4=-8a-2b-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying each equation, we get

$$
\{\begin{aligned}a+b=1 \\ 8a+2b=-11.\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate $b,$ we multiply the first equation by $-2,$ and we add the resulting equation to the second equation. So we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & -2a-2b=-2 \\ +\,\,\, & \,8a+2b=-11 \\  & \,6a=-13.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get $a=-\frac{13}{6}.$ Finally, we substitute it into $a+b=1$ to find $b=\frac{19}{6}.$ 

Therefore, our final solution is $a-b=-\frac{16}{3}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-770121c3-2cf2-5300-81b4-eb965c9cabaa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-770121c3-2cf2-5300-81b4-eb965c9cabaa" :answer-field/id #uuid "770121c3-2cf2-5300-81b4-eb965c9cabaa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8bab351c-3d65-5fe3-9013-2a0e5d4247ea" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8bab351c-3d65-5fe3-9013-2a0e5d4247ea" "answer-9a53dd5a-69f1-5a67-8fc6-fee88e884332" "answer-8c0e57d9-947f-577b-9e25-695901eeae8d" "answer-52ccfcd0-dfef-547c-9767-ca8b5f2e8bad" "answer-3f4c8461-b983-5195-b309-a1fd4f447236"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8bab351c-3d65-5fe3-9013-2a0e5d4247ea" :answer/id #uuid "8bab351c-3d65-5fe3-9013-2a0e5d4247ea" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{16}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a53dd5a-69f1-5a67-8fc6-fee88e884332" :answer/id #uuid "9a53dd5a-69f1-5a67-8fc6-fee88e884332" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{5}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8c0e57d9-947f-577b-9e25-695901eeae8d" :answer/id #uuid "8c0e57d9-947f-577b-9e25-695901eeae8d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52ccfcd0-dfef-547c-9767-ca8b5f2e8bad" :answer/id #uuid "52ccfcd0-dfef-547c-9767-ca8b5f2e8bad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3f4c8461-b983-5195-b309-a1fd4f447236" :answer/id #uuid "3f4c8461-b983-5195-b309-a1fd4f447236" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233067 :question/worked-solution "*Method 1:*

By the definition, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(3)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h}.
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=10{x}^{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{10(3+h)^{2}-10(3)^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{90+60h+10{h}^{2}-90}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{60h+10{h}^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(60+10h) \\  & =60+(0) \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$

 

*Method 2:*

By the definition, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(3)={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{f(x)-f(3)}{x-3}.
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=10{x}^{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & ={lim}_{x\to 3}(\frac{10{x}^{2}-10(3)^{2}}{x-3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}(\frac{10({x}^{2}-{3}^{2})}{x-3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}(\frac{10(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}10(x+3) \\  & =10(3+3) \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1bf2afe7-a005-5071-84b9-bd40024ce506"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-1bf2afe7-a005-5071-84b9-bd40024ce506" :answer-field/id #uuid "1bf2afe7-a005-5071-84b9-bd40024ce506" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6db8fd27-a6bb-5d05-8c7a-556b2db63a39" :answer-field/choices ["answer-71a944ae-ff58-5447-8134-5585f04d64b8" "answer-b98cc99c-1897-5580-9a45-71a60760d8c5" "answer-10447d27-bbad-5243-827a-0ec88f52db0b" "answer-6db8fd27-a6bb-5d05-8c7a-556b2db63a39" "answer-d6da7332-d0ae-5c57-a840-c9de6058e7d8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-71a944ae-ff58-5447-8134-5585f04d64b8" :answer/id #uuid "71a944ae-ff58-5447-8134-5585f04d64b8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{f}^{′}(3)=30" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b98cc99c-1897-5580-9a45-71a60760d8c5" :answer/id #uuid "b98cc99c-1897-5580-9a45-71a60760d8c5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{f}^{′}(3)=40" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-10447d27-bbad-5243-827a-0ec88f52db0b" :answer/id #uuid "10447d27-bbad-5243-827a-0ec88f52db0b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{f}^{′}(3)=48" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6db8fd27-a6bb-5d05-8c7a-556b2db63a39" :answer/id #uuid "6db8fd27-a6bb-5d05-8c7a-556b2db63a39" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{f}^{′}(3)=60" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d6da7332-d0ae-5c57-a840-c9de6058e7d8" :answer/id #uuid "d6da7332-d0ae-5c57-a840-c9de6058e7d8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{f}^{′}(3)=72" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186234168 :question/problem "Express $\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{10})$ in terms of a reference angle." :question/worked-solution "To help us to visualize the angle, we first convert the measure of the angle into degrees. 

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by $\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi }.$ This gives

$$
(\frac{7\pi }{10})\cdot (\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi })={126}^{∘}.
$$

Therefore $\frac{7\pi }{10}$ is equivalent to ${126}^{∘},$ which lies in the $2\text{nd}$ quadrant.

![](images/89/89b5e2656378adb5d91c9f58c261e4beaae252b67819b904bf209f6ed8a5a25e.png)

To express $\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{10})$ in terms of $\operatorname{cot}⁡{\theta }_{R},$ we follow three steps:

1\. Find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}.$

2\. Calculate the value of the function for ${\theta }_{R}.$

3\. Determine whether the resulting value is positive or negative.

**Step 1**: Since $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{10}$ is in the $2$nd quadrant, the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\pi -\theta  \\  & =\pi -\frac{7\pi }{10} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is $\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{10})$, and therefore we're interested in $\operatorname{cot}⁡{\theta }_{R}=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{10}).$

**Step 3:** The ratio $\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{10})$ must be negative because tangent (and therefore cotangent) is always negative in the $2$nd quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{10})=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{10}).
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-427c3f91-22fc-5c34-bf37-633a78d7c0ba"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-427c3f91-22fc-5c34-bf37-633a78d7c0ba" :answer-field/id #uuid "Find the value of $\operatorname{sec}⁡0+\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "The angles $0$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](images/79/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

- Let's first consider the angle $0.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $0$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$  Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡0=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

- Now, let's consider the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$  Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡0+\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1+1=2.
$$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5809f205-7813-519f-9ba7-8f909067fdec"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5809f205-7813-519f-9ba7-8f909067fdec" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

Thus, ${N}^{′}(t)$ gives the rate at which the number of people inside the park changes $t$ minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the park at time $t$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $t.$ That is,

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\sqrt{x}+5x-13) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{1/2}+5x) \\  & =3{x}^{-1/2}+5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{-1/2}+5=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =8(x-1) \\ y & =8x-8-2 \\ y & =8x-10.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =8x-10 \\ x & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(\frac{5}{4},0).$" :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2f3486a1-cfa1-570d-be9b-887c8a18ac0b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "$\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt[4]{e})=$" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite $\sqrt[4]{e}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$
\sqrt[4]{e}={e}^{1/4}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt[4]{e})=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})
$$

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f1f049c7-00fd-5d21-8330-9fbecd737783"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f1f049c7-00fd-5d21-8330-9fbecd737783" :answer-field/id #uuid "f1f049c7-00fd-5d21-8330-9fbecd737783" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8511cc21-378c-5a60-9221-6fb771890a90" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b219a9cf-83fc-5cad-a42c-df24894c4cbe" "answer-4dc31748-131c-5761-b87b-12c70e2700fd" "answer-ffe0d590-58c4-5faf-8679-f3cf76a7cea1" "answer-f6bf7bc9-83ae-5185-89c3-ff3999355ed7" "answer-8511cc21-378c-5a60-9221-6fb771890a90"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b219a9cf-83fc-5cad-a42c-df24894c4cbe" :answer/id #uuid "b219a9cf-83fc-5cad-a42c-df24894c4cbe" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4dc31748-131c-5761-b87b-12c70e2700fd" :answer/id #uuid "4dc31748-131c-5761-b87b-12c70e2700fd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ffe0d590-58c4-5faf-8679-f3cf76a7cea1" :answer/id #uuid "ffe0d590-58c4-5faf-8679-f3cf76a7cea1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f6bf7bc9-83ae-5185-89c3-ff3999355ed7" :answer/id #uuid "f6bf7bc9-83ae-5185-89c3-ff3999355ed7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8511cc21-378c-5a60-9221-6fb771890a90" :answer/id #uuid "8511cc21-378c-5a60-9221-6fb771890a90" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-7e50efe9-568f-54f5-835e-03a6e09d3518" :question/id #uuid "7e50efe9-568f-54f5-835e-03a6e09d3518" :question/math-academy-id "q-34313" :question/problem "![](images/23/23f0dba237502bc7261fd8f28327beefd5872bb4b0f503930c488b2857fcef24.png)

Given that the point $A$ has coordinates $(-\sqrt{3},-1),$ calculate the angle $\theta .$" :question/worked-solution "We can form a triangle by creating a vertical line from $A$ to the $x$-axis. Let us call ${\theta }^{′}$ the acute angle that is formed with the $x$-axis such that ${\theta }^{′}+{180}^{∘}=\theta $

![](images/d1/d14f62179f831ebdc177eac7bd2899679864305d4104d4b61f304eb4fa9e133d.png)

Using the tangent ratio, we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡{\theta }^{′}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}.
$$

Finally, using the inverse tangent, we get

$$
{\theta }^{′}=\operatorname{arctan}⁡\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}={30}^{∘}.
$$

Finally, using $\theta ={\theta }^{′}+{180}^{∘},$ we get $\theta ={30}^{∘}+{180}^{∘}={210}^{∘}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields "1b5b5791-1037-533d-a2f0-5ffb4bac0dd8" :question/math-academy-id "q-140469" :question/problem "Find ${H}^{⊥}$ if $H=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -14\end{aligned}]\}.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors that span the subspace $H$ as ${h}_{1}$ and ${h}_{2}.$ 

A vector $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ belongs to ${H}^{⊥}$ if $x\cdot {h}_{1}=0$ and $x\cdot {h}_{2}=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x\cdot {h}_{1}=0 \\ x\cdot {h}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-4{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}=0 \\ 8{x}_{1}-14{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 7 & 0 \\ 8 & -14 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, we have $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one), so ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=\frac{7}{4}{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, our orthogonal complement is

$$
{H}^{⊥}=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]\,:\,{x}_{2}\in R\}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-356e4ab9-2091-593a-99dd-55afcb98c941"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $4{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the maximum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+y-2z
$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x+y+4z=4,\,h(x,y,z)=4{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=4 \\ h(x,y,z)=1\end{aligned}
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨1,1,-2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,4⟩+\mu ⟨8x,0,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda +8\mu x \\ 1=\lambda  \\ -2=4\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\mu x=0 \\ \lambda =1 \\ z=-\frac{3}{\mu }\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction. So, from the first equation above, we must have $x=0.$

Next, we substitute $x=0$  into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $z$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=0$ and $z=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+4z & =4 \\ 0+y+4(1) & =4 \\ y+4 & =4 \\ y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=0$ and $z=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+4z & =4 \\ 0+y+4(-1) & =4 \\ y-4 & =4 \\ y & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,0,1),\,(0,8,-1).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(0,0,1)$ | $(0,8,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $-2$ | $10$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(0,8,-1),$ and its  maximum value is $10.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n,$ we know that its variance, which we may denote as $\sigma_x^2,$ is given by

$$
\sigma_x^2 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline x)^2
$$

where $\overline x$ is the mean of $x.$ 

The summation term

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline x)^2
$$

is known as a **sum of squares** and is denoted $S_{xx}.$ As we'll see, this quantity often appears in statistical analysis, so giving it a separate notation is useful.

Similarly, if we have a data set $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n,$ then we define

$$
S_{yy} =  \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \overline y)^2.
$$

Now, suppose we have the bivariate data set

$$
(x_1, y_1), \qquad (x_2, y_2),\qquad \ldots, \qquad (x_n, y_n).
$$

Then, the covariance is given by

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) =  \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline x)(y_i - \overline y)
$$

and we may define $S_{xy}$ as

$$
S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y}).
$$

Finally, we can define the variance and covariance in terms of $S_{xx}, S_{yy},$ and $S_{xy}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{x}^{2} & =\frac{{S}_{xx}}{n},\,{\sigma }_{y}^{2}=\frac{{S}_{yy}}{n},\,\text{Cov}(x,y)=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186205126 :tutorial/content "Calculating $S_{xx}, S_{yy},$ and $S_{xy}$ using their definitions can be cumbersome. Thankfully, we have the following shortcut formulas:

One pallet contains $500$ bricks. The weight of a brick is normally distributed with a mean of $3\,\text{lb}$ and a standard deviation of $0.25\,\text{lb},$ while the weight of a pallet is normally distributed with a mean of $40\,\text{lb}$ and a standard deviation of $4\,\text{lb}.$ If one pallet with bricks is randomly selected, what is the probability that it weighs less than $1\,545\,\text{lb}?$ You may assume that the weights are independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7324\,$ | $\,0.7357\,$ | $\,0.7389\,$ | $\,0.7422\,$ |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ | $\,0.7704\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ | $\,0.7995\,$ | $\,0.8023\,$ |"] ["question-c6ec9582-211a-54f7-b78a-6175feef090c" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th brick, and let $Y$ denote the weight of a pallet. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(3,{0.25}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 500,
$$

and

$$
Y∼N(40,{4}^{2}).
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the weight of a randomly selected pallet with bricks. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{500}+Y,
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =500\cdot 3+40 \\  & =1\,540, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =500\cdot {0.25}^{2}+{4}^{2} \\  & =47.25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(1\,540,47.25).
$$

In order to find $P(W<1\,545),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<1\,545) & =P(Z<\frac{1\,545-1\,540}{\sqrt{47.25}}) \\  & ≈P(Z<0.73) \\  & =Φ(0.73)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.73)≈0.7673.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W<1\,545) & ≈Φ(0.73) \\  & ≈0.7673.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c6ec9582-211a-54f7-b78a-6175feef090c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-160c9e56-fbfc-5c34-9ac0-b74ec90271f9" :answer-field/id #uuid | $\,0.3\,$ | $\,0.6179\,$ | $\,0.6217\,$ | $\,0.6255\,$ | $\,0.6293\,$ |"] [17592186188560 :question/worked-solution "Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{20}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{20}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{20} & ∼N(20\cdot 1,\,20\cdot {2}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(20\cdot 1,\,20\cdot 4) \\  & =N(20,80).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(Y\le 21).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le 21) & =P(Z\le \frac{21-20}{\sqrt{80}}) \\  & =P(Z\le \frac{1}{\sqrt{80}}) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.11) \\  & =Φ(0.11)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
Φ(0.11)=0.5438.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(Y\le 21)=Φ(0.11)=0.5438.
$$"] [17592186188560 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186185640 :answer-field/correct 17592186185645] ["question-989181af-177e-5503-a508-c854844640ac" :question/id #uuid "989181af-177e-5503-a508-c854844640ac"] ["question-989181af-177e-5503-a508-c854844640ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-152019"] ["question-989181af-177e-5503-a508-c854844640ac" :question/problem "In a particular shop, cables are sold in coils. The length of the cable in a coil is normally distributed with a mean of $50\,\text{m}$ and a standard deviation of $0.7\,\text{m}.$ If John bought $5$ coils, what is the probability that the total length of the cables he bought is greater than $250\,\text{m}$ and less than $253\,m?$ You may assume that the lengths of the cable in the coils are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.7\,$ | $\,0.9554\,$ | $\,0.9564\,$ | $\,0.9573\,$ | $\,0.9582\,$ |
| $\,1.8\,$ | $\,0.9641\,$ | $\,0.9649\,$ | $\,0.9656\,$ | $\,0.9664\,$ |
| $\,1.9\,$ | $\,0.9713\,$ | $\,0.9719\,$ | $\,0.9726\,$ | $\,0.9732\,$ |"] ["question-989181af-177e-5503-a508-c854844640ac" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the length of cable in the $i$th coil. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(50,{0.7}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 5.
$$

Let the random variable $L$ denote the total length of the cables in $5$ randomly selected coils. Then, since

$$
L={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{5},
$$

we have that $L$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[L] & =5\cdot 50 \\  & =250, \\ \text{Var}[L] & =5\cdot {0.7}^{2} \\  & =2.45.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
L∼N(250,2.45).
$$

In order to find $P(250<L<253),$ we convert $L$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(250<L<253) & =P(\frac{250-250}{\sqrt{2.45}}<Z<\frac{253-250}{\sqrt{2.45}}) \\  & ≈P(0<Z<1.92) \\  & =Φ(1.92)-Φ(0) \\  & =Φ(1.92)-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.92)≈0.9726.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(250<L<253) & ≈Φ(0.95)-0.5 \\  & ≈0.4726.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-989181af-177e-5503-a508-c854844640ac" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-31e87839-a244-5651-ab20-8782a2fd6c04" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-141fc269-b2bd-5ee7-86fd-0b448fecc7f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-152022"] ["question-141fc269-b2bd-5ee7-86fd-0b448fecc7f6" :question/problem "Fred picked $10$ watermelons from his vegetable garden. The weight of watermelons he grows is normally distributed with a mean of $11\,\text{kg}$ and a standard deviation of $3\,\text{kg}.$ What is the probability that the total weight of the watermelons Fred picked is greater than $100\,\text{kg}$ and less than $110\,\text{kg}?$ You may assume that the weights of the watermelons are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.0\,$ | $\,0.8461\,$ | $\,0.8485\,$ | $\,0.8508\,$ | $\,0.8531\,$ |
| $\,1.1\,$ | $\,0.8686\,$ | $\,0.8708\,$ | $\,0.8729\,$ | $\,0.8749\,$ |
| $\,1.2\,$ | $\,0.8888\,$ | $\,0.8907\,$ | $\,0.8925\,$ | $\,0.8944\,$ |"] ["question-141fc269-b2bd-5ee7-86fd-0b448fecc7f6" :question/worked-solution "Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the weight of the $i$th watermelon. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(11,{3}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 10.
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denotes the total weight of the $10$ watermelons. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{10},
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =10\cdot 11 \\  & =110, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =10\cdot {3}^{2} \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(110,90).
$$

In order to find $P(100<W<110),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<W<110) & =P(\frac{100-110}{\sqrt{90}}<Z<\frac{110-110}{\sqrt{90}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.05<Z<0) \\  & =Φ(0)-Φ(-1.05) \\  & =Φ(0)-(1-Φ(1.05)) \\  & =0.5-(1-Φ(1.05)) \\  & =Φ(1.05)-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(1.05)≈0.8531.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(100<W<110) & ≈Φ(1.05)-0.5 \\  & ≈0.3531.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-141fc269-b2bd-5ee7-86fd-0b448fecc7f6" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-65f1e10a-d8c8-58e5-b10d-6e1e77a5ab90" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-dcde9f99-5a2a-52a5-a122-c3ef3631c507" :question/math-academy-id "q-335070"] ["question-dcde9f99-5a2a-52a5-a122-c3ef3631c507" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-y(t)+1,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].$*

<td align="center" width="80px">$1-{e}^{-t}-t{e}^{-t}$ </td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>"] ["question-dcde9f99-5a2a-52a5-a122-c3ef3631c507" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{-(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{-(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}(t-s){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}(-s+t+1){e}^{s-t} \\ {e}^{s-t}\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1-(t+1){e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-t}-t{e}^{-t} \\ 1-{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dcde9f99-5a2a-52a5-a122-c3ef3631c507" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-7d8ad94d-1b6b-50f4-917b-e60fcda59e4c" :answer-field/id #uuid "7d8ad94d-1b6b-50f4-917b-e60fcda59e4c"] ["answer-2ce80ed6-c2fb-573a-bcb7-17c24ee2cd02" :answer/id #uuid "2ce80ed6-c2fb-573a-bcb7-17c24ee2cd02"] ["answer-2ce80ed6-c2fb-573a-bcb7-17c24ee2cd02" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-2ce80ed6-c2fb-573a-bcb7-17c24ee2cd02" :answer/value "1-e^{-t}"] ["answer-field-7d8ad94d-1b6b-50f4-917b-e60fcda59e4c" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-7d8ad94d-1b6b-50f4-917b-e60fcda59e4c" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-7d8ad94d-1b6b-50f4-917b-e60fcda59e4c" :answer-field/correct "answer-2ce80ed6-c2fb-573a-bcb7-17c24ee2cd02"] ["answer-field-7d8ad94d-1b6b-50f4-917b-e60fcda59e4c" :answer-field/choices "answer-2ce80ed6-c2fb-573a-bcb7-17c24ee2cd02"] ["question-dcde9f99-5a2a-52a5-a122-c3ef3631c507" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-7d8ad94d-1b6b-50f4-917b-e60fcda59e4c"] [17592186229132 :knowledge-point/questions "question-dcde9f99-5a2a-52a5-a122-c3ef3631c507"] ["question-d29ce693-46aa-5cb5-a64c-988886b4e7a0" :question/id #uuid "d29ce693-46aa-5cb5-a64c-988886b4e7a0"] ["question-d29ce693-46aa-5cb5-a64c-988886b4e7a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-335072"] ["question-d29ce693-46aa-5cb5-a64c-988886b4e7a0" :question/problem "$$

</tr>
</tbody></table>"] ["question-d29ce693-46aa-5cb5-a64c-988886b4e7a0" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{2(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{2t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].$*

</tbody></table>"] ["question-8c12baec-9a09-54f7-8159-4ab5ea602070" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} & t{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8c12baec-9a09-54f7-8159-4ab5ea602070" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-083c749e-9d27-588e-b8bf-03bf5d6d7291" :answer-field/id #uuid ["activity-7fb4b445-0fd0-5c09-8ee7-7faef43b5ab2" :activity/first-step "step-cef7ab47-7ef6-5ce5-94ff-fd249257c533"] [17592186362342 :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the rectangular parallelepiped's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=4x+4y+4z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=125.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=125
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨4,4,4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4=\lambda yz \\ 4=\lambda xz \\ 4=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4x=\lambda xyz \\ 4y=\lambda xyz \\ 4z=\lambda xyz\end{aligned}
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =125 \\ x(x)(x) & =125 \\ {x}^{3} & =125 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(5,5,5),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(5,5,5)=4(5)+4(5)+4(5)=60\,\text{in}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(25,5,1) & =4(25)+4(5)+4(1) \\  & =121 \\  & >f(5,5,5).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186364648 :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the tank's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+2xz+2yz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=256.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=256
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨y+2z,x+2z,2x+2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y+2z=\lambda yz \\ x+2z=\lambda xz \\ 2x+2y=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x(y+2z)=\lambda xyz \\ y(x+2z)=\lambda xyz \\ z(2x+2y)=\lambda xyz\end{aligned}
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(y+2z) & =y(x+2z) \\ xy+2xz & =xy+2yz \\ 2xz & =2yz \\ 2z(x-y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =256 \\ (2z)(2z)z & =256 \\ 4{z}^{3} & =256 \\ {z}^{3} & =64 \\ z & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(8,8,4),$ and the minimum value is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(8,8,4)=8(8)+2(8)(4)+2(8)(4)=192\,{\text{ft}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(16,16,1) & =(16)(16)+2(16)(1)+2(16)(1) \\  & =320 \\  & >f(8,8,4).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186362346 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨-1,2⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-1,2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-1=4\lambda x \\ 2=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{1}{4\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=-\frac{1}{4}y\end{aligned}
$$

 

  Substituting $x=-\frac{1}{4}y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=4,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{8}+{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {y}^{2} & =\frac{32}{9} \\ y & =\pm \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=-\frac{1}{4}y=∓\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}),\,(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3})$ | $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3})$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $5+3\sqrt{2}$ | $5-3\sqrt{2}$ |

 

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3})\,,$ and its minimum value is $5-3\sqrt{2}.$"] [17592186362348 :question/worked-solution "We are given that the critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region's interior is $(0,0).$

**Step 1**: Find the critical points:

We see that ${f}^{′}(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x\in (-4,3),$ and ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at $x=-2.$ Therefore, the candidates are $x=-4,-2,3.$

**Step 2**: Compute the value of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-4) & =-1 \\ f(-2) & =f(-4)+{\int }_{-4}^{-2}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-1+6 \\  & =5 \\ f(3) & =f(-4)+{\int }_{-4}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-1+6-9 \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Select the smallest value of $f$ from our candidates.

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have

$$
{f}_{\text{min}}=min\{-1,5,-4\}=-4.
$$

**Step 1**: Find the critical points:

We see that ${f}^{′}(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x\in (0,5),$ and ${f}^{′}(x)=0$ at $x=2,4.$ Therefore, the candidates are $x=0,2,4,5.$

**Step 2**: Compute the values of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus:

The function is made up of three triangles. Let's add the areas bounded by these shapes to our diagram:

![](images/ea/ea837252a62313eae506ef3d101c0b70121f6380694a49c2f54e1a19702949a5.png)

Using the given information and the fundamental theorem of calculus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =4 \\ f(2) & =f(0)+{\int }_{0}^{2}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4+1 \\  & =5 \\ f(4) & =f(0)+{\int }_{0}^{4}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4+1+(-3) \\  & =2 \\ f(5) & =f(0)+{\int }_{0}^{5}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =4+1+(-3)+0.5 \\  & =2.5\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**:  Select the smallest value of $f$ from our candidates.

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have

$$
{f}_{\text{min}}=min\{4,5,2,2.5\}=2.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =1\cdot 0.4+4\cdot 0.6 \\  & =0.4+2.4 \\  & =2.8 \\ \text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =2\cdot 0.6+5\cdot 0.4 \\  & =1.2+2 \\  & =3.2\end{aligned}

| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.4$ | $0.6$ | $1$ |

$$

$$

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])(y-\text{E}[Y])f(x,y).
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=3$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.15$ | $0.25$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=2$ | $0.5$ | $0.1$ | $0.6$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.65$ | $0.35$ | $1$ |

$$

$$

Applying the formula for the covariance, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])(y-\text{E}[Y])f(x,y) \\  & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-1.2)(y-1.7)f(x,y) \\  & =(0-1.2)(1-1.7)f(0,1) \\  & +(0-1.2)(3-1.7)f(0,3) \\  & +(2-1.2)(1-1.7)f(2,1) \\  & +(2-1.2)(3-1.7)f(2,3) \\  & =(-1.2)(-0.7)(0.15) \\  & +(-1.2)(1.3)(0.25) \\  & +(0.8)(-0.7)(0.5) \\  & +(0.8)(1.3)(0.1) \\  & =-0.44.\end{aligned}

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |

Calculate the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$"] ["question-d4d126ea-cebf-548f-a0ce-ca7561957246" :question/worked-solution "The covariance of two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint support $S$ is defined as

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])(y-\text{E}[Y])f(x,y).
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=2$ | $0.3$ | $0.1$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.7$ | $0.3$ | $1$ |

We now compute $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{E}[Y],$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =2\cdot 0.4+3\cdot 0.6 \\  & =0.8+1.8 \\  & =2.6 \\ \text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =1\cdot 0.7+2\cdot 0.3 \\  & =0.7+0.6 \\  & =1.3\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for the covariance, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])(y-\text{E}[Y])f(x,y) \\  & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-2.6)(y-1.3)f(x,y) \\  & =(2-2.6)(1-1.3)f(2,1) \\  & +(2-2.6)(2-1.3)f(2,2) \\  & +(3-2.6)(1-1.3)f(3,1) \\  & +(3-2.6)(2-1.3)f(3,2) \\  & =(-0.6)(-0.3)(0.3) \\  & +(-0.6)(0.7)(0.1) \\  & +(0.4)(-0.3)(0.4) \\  & +(0.4)(0.7)(0.2) \\  & =0.02.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-d4d126ea-cebf-548f-a0ce-ca7561957246" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-811156d6-65a9-5f35-a8ae-1aca43ee3f12" :answer-field/id #uuid | $X=3$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ |

Calculate the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$"] ["question-a725de9b-9a65-5d96-80a3-b82e15275c01" :question/worked-solution "The covariance of two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint support $S$ is defined as

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])(y-\text{E}[Y])f(x,y).
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y.$ These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.5$ | $0$ | $0.5$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $0.5$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.7$ | $0.3$ | $1$ |

We now compute $\text{E}[X]$ and $\text{E}[Y],$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}x\cdot {f}_{X}(x) \\  & =1\cdot 0.5+3\cdot 0.5 \\  & =0.5+1.5 \\  & =2 \\ \text{E}[Y] & ={\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}y\cdot {f}_{Y}(y) \\  & =2\cdot 0.7+4\cdot 0.3 \\  & =1.4+1.2 \\  & =2.6\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for the covariance, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])(y-\text{E}[Y])f(x,y) \\  & ={\sum }_{(x,y)\in S}(x-2)(y-2.6)f(x,y) \\  & =(1-2)(2-2.6)f(1,2) \\  & +(1-2)(4-2.6)f(1,4) \\  & +(3-2)(2-2.6)f(3,2) \\  & +(3-2)(4-2.6)f(3,4) \\  & =(-1)(-0.6)(0.5) \\  & +(-1)(1.4)(0) \\  & +(1)(-0.6)(0.2) \\  & +(1)(1.4)(0.3) \\  & =0.6.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a725de9b-9a65-5d96-80a3-b82e15275c01" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-5afcdbc9-8272-5f52-8b74-ad215de0627c" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-d2d1682f-7eb6-5691-9d8f-0cd7e762540d"] [17592186162134 :knowledge-point/questions "question-cf31f09e-0f29-56f8-9f97-abccd7a0062d"] [17592186163290 :tutorial/content "We often want to measure the strength of the (linear) dependence between two random variables. One measure that we use for this purpose is covariance. 

The **covariance** between two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \textrm{E}\Big[\left(X - \textrm{E}[X]\right)\left(Y - \textrm{E}[Y]\right) \Big].
$$

Let's break this formula down a bit:

- $\left(X - \textrm{E}[X]\right)$ is the deviation of $X$ from its mean

- $\left(Y - \textrm{E}[Y]\right)$ is the deviation of $Y$ from its mean

Therefore, the covariance measures the expected value of the product of these deviations.

The covariance can also be expressed as

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] =\sum_{(x,y)\in S}(x − \textrm E[X])(y − \textrm E[Y])f(x,y)
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint PMF of $X$ and $Y,$ and $S$ is the joint support.

Let's sketch a few diagrams to get a feel for what the covariance tells us.

- A *positive* covariance means that if $X$ increases, then $Y$ is likely to increase. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **positively correlated**.

![](images/bb/bbfae3f0fb38bc8652cd26716e4b0b128cf1f2039350267034d97161d7f5dac4.png)

- A *negative* covariance means that if $X$ increases, then $Y$ is likely to decrease. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **negatively correlated**.

![](images/fd/fd45053fdc39f070e3438c3b8c61fe01613201595cfe00bd4cc6c6e481bf73ab.png)

Note the following:

- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then 

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] = 0.
$$

The reverse implication does not always hold! For example, two random variables can have zero covariance yet be dependent. This is because covariance measures *linear* dependence only.

- The covariance of a random variable with itself is its variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,X] & =\text{E}[(X-\text{E}[X])(X-\text{E}[X])] \\  & =\text{E}[{(X-\text{E}[X])}^{2}] \\  & =\text{Var}[X]\end{aligned}
$$

- Aside from indicating whether two random variables are positively or negatively correlated, the covariance *by itself* does not tell us very much. For example, if 

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X_1, Y_1] > \textrm{Cov}[X_2, Y_2] > 0
$$

this does not necessarily mean that the dependence between $X_1$ and $Y_1$ is somehow "stronger" than the dependence between $X_2$ and $Y_2.$ This is because the covariance does not take the variance of the individual random variables into account. 

In a future lesson, we'll use the covariance to define the so-called  **correlation coefficient,** which *does* consider the variance of the individual random variables and so *can* be used to compare the relative strength of the linear dependence between two pairs of random variables."] [17592186163343 :tutorial/content "You may have noticed that computing the covariance using the definition is quite a lot of work. Is there a formula that makes it easier?  

Indeed, there is. It can be shown that

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] =\textrm E [XY] − \textrm E [X]\cdot \textrm E [Y].
$$

We'll prove this formula at the end of the lesson. But for now, let's get some practice at applying it."] [17592186163293 :tutorial/content "If $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, the covariance between $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] =\iint_\limits{\mathbb R^2}(x − \textrm E[X])(y − \textrm E[Y])f(x,y) \, \textrm d x\textrm d y.
$$

As is the case with discrete random variables, it's often easier to compute the covariance using the following formula: 

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y]
=
\textrm{E} [XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y]
$$

Suppose we're given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

![](images/c5/c589b62f579cb5efe7c4a2b86aa9bebbbbec81517c8bd7872c3c6a0b019e08cc.svg)

To compute the covariance of this distribution, we first use the rule of the lazy statistician to find $\textrm{E}[XY]\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}xyf(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{1}{2}(x+\frac{y}{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}y{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}y{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{2}y]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}y[\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}y]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{6}y+\frac{1}{8}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{12}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{24}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\cdot {2}^{2}+\frac{1}{24}\cdot {2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}

["question-7658d4f4-3b1c-50cc-bb09-9642192fb8ae" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the sine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)
$$"] ["question-7658d4f4-3b1c-50cc-bb09-9642192fb8ae" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)-(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))=1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)=1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=1 \\ {a}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-1)=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {a}_{n}=\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+1)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x).
$$"] ["question-7658d4f4-3b1c-50cc-bb09-9642192fb8ae" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-58617cc3-c088-55aa-805f-3f4f74b88173" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-b98de4ab-a079-5d39-b165-ba7998caa236" :question/math-academy-id "q-343834"] ["question-b98de4ab-a079-5d39-b165-ba7998caa236" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{′}+5y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-1}}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{{field-2}}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})
$$"] ["question-b98de4ab-a079-5d39-b165-ba7998caa236" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & ∼0+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\cdot (-\frac{n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}))+{b}_{n}\cdot \frac{n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & ∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{′}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,+5(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+{b}_{n}sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})) \\  & \,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})\end{aligned}
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{5{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n})cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(-\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n})sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}) \\  & \,\,\,\,={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, equating the free terms and the cosine and sine coefficients, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5{a}_{0}}{2}=0 \\ \frac{{b}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n}=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi } \\ -\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{3}+5{b}_{n}=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

Next, from the third equation, 

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation gives

$$
(\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15})\frac{n\pi }{3}+5{a}_{n}=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi }\,⇒\,{a}_{n}=\frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}
$$

Therefore, for ${b}_{n}$ with $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{n}n\pi }{15} \\  & =\frac{n\pi }{15}\cdot \frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)} \\  & =\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{135(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot cos\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3})+\frac{9(-1)^{n}}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+225)}\cdot sin\,(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$"] ["question-b98de4ab-a079-5d39-b165-ba7998caa236" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-4e6a7300-844d-5db4-8005-d85823b210da" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-c1c1c9b0-94ce-5a76-9444-4ee707ea7768" :question/math-academy-id "q-138607"] ["question-c1c1c9b0-94ce-5a76-9444-4ee707ea7768" :question/problem "$$
X=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 5 & 6 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the observation matrix $X$ above, where the individual observations are given in columns. Find the mean-deviation form of $X.$"] ["question-c1c1c9b0-94ce-5a76-9444-4ee707ea7768" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the mean-deviation form of the observation matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & ⋯ & {x}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

is given by 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}| & | &  & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & ⋯ & {b}_{n} \\ | & | &  & |\end{aligned}]
$$

where ${b}_{i}={x}_{i}-m$ for $i=1,2,…,n,$ and $m$ is sample mean vector.

From the matrix, we have that  

$$
{x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}].
$$

As a result, the sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$"] ["question-c1c1c9b0-94ce-5a76-9444-4ee707ea7768" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-4e40b0a9-1361-5dd4-aab2-b04b18adc043" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}13 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -1\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}30 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}13 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{3-1}[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}18 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
C=\frac{1}{n-1}B{B}^{T},
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations.

So, we first need to compute the mean-deviation form of our observation matrix.

The sample mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{3}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}([\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the mean-deviation form is

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}4 & -7 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the sample covariance matrix is 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\frac{1}{3-1}[\begin{aligned}4 & -7 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -7 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}74 & -9 \\ -9 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186162355 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-585eb8e8-05fa-5f15-975e-62db16d4ca73" :answer/id #uuid "585eb8e8-05fa-5f15-975e-62db16d4ca73"]
