number of classes taken per semester and the average final grade in a sample of four college students.

| **Number of Courses** | $4$ | $3$ | $5$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Average Grade** | $80$ | $85$ | $75$ | $72$ |

We can collect this data in a matrix so that each column reports the number of courses and the average grade of a single student:

![](images/8a/8a489e90c10dbb65c2f5e005c32677696073cc63203116ed07d445a91d7f2d32.svg)

The matrix $X$ is called the **observation matrix.**

Suppose we want to determine the mean number of courses and the mean average grade of this sample. The **sample mean vector,** denoted $\mathbf m,$ is a vector containing these values. The sample mean vector is given by

$$
\mathbf{m} = \dfrac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{x}_i,
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_n$ are the individual observations (columns of $X$).

From our matrix above, we have that  

![](images/45/4549af29f9356865dc9f3edb67960da00a4007a71281778d4a273a1a6eb0dbf9.svg)

Therefore, the sample mean vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{1}{4}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}4 \\ 80\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 85\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 75\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 72\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}16 \\ 312\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the average number of courses is $4,$ and the average final grade is $78.$"] [17592186163321 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we studied data that reported the number of courses selected and the average grades of a sample of four college students. The observation matrix for this data was

![](images/9b/9bdfe848443d0014461cc51e2decfbed8dc151a72edb34825dd33ac964ed6b2f.svg)

The individual observations are

![](images/3f/3f935ba5f9adea7f75a63642837a3b993286f9535d5bf1842ce3a2267413c6bc.svg)

We also found the sample mean vector 

![](images/26/261e1d746aafa95ac2f7a6d1ff36a741ff5ae37ba738f75b451a542baed1c5fc.svg)

One thing we can do with this data is to check how much each observation differs from the mean values. To do that, we compute the difference between each observation and the sample mean vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={x}_{1}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 80\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{2} & ={x}_{2}-m=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 85\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{3} & ={x}_{3}-m=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 75\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ {b}_{4} & ={x}_{4}-m=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 72\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 78\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We collect these differences in a new matrix, as follows:

![](images/83/831e698a632d40ab447c75a3b169e29c6ae8ab10c6600d838bd699a38e837931.svg)

The matrix $B$ is the **mean-deviation form** of $X.$ It's often easier to work with the mean-deviation form, especially if the original data contains large numbers.

Notice that the mean of a mean-deviation form equals the zero vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}_{B} & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 7\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -6\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}([\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186163311 :tutorial/content "Let's consider again the mean-deviation matrix for the students' data we found previously:

![](images/1f/1f5440b7ae08ffd19bdae816854c236afe3ca254d5bd23e26f15e34cd9c9feb2.svg)

Calculating the product $B B^T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 7 & -3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & 7 \\ 1 & -3 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -10 \\ -10 & 98\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Let's analyze what we've obtained:

- The entry in the first row and first column (${\color{red}2}$) is the sum of the squares of the mean deviations of the number of courses.

- The entry in the second row and second column (${\color{blue}98}$) is the sum of the squares of the mean deviations of the final grades.

- The off-diagonal entries (${\color{purple}-10}$) are the sum of the products of the mean deviations.

Since there were $4$ observations in total, if we divide each entry by $4-1=3,$  we will get a matrix $C$ with the *sample variances* in the diagonal and the *sample covariance* in the off-diagonal positions:

![](images/7d/7d0216b462e1bf7dc34d638a7a0de30fcf063ce39d1865b45f85b526ba7bd0a8.svg)

This matrix is called the **covariance matrix** of the data.

In general, the sample covariance matrix is given by

$$
C = \dfrac{1}{n-1} B B^T,
$$

where $B$ is the observation matrix in the mean-deviation form, and $n$ is the number of observations."] [17592186162232 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] [17592186188679 :question/problem "A nationwide study found that $38%$ of families own a pet. If a town randomly samples $200$ families, find a normal approximation for the probability that more than $80$ of them are pet owners. You may assume that the population size is significantly larger than the sample size.

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*"] [17592186188679 :question/worked-solution "Given a population in which a proportion $p$ of the population has a particular characteristic, the sampling distribution of the sample proportion $\overset{^}{\,p}$ can be approximated as

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=200,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.38.$

Now, since

$$
np=200(0.38)=76>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=200(1-0.38)=124>5,
$$

and $n=200$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.38,\frac{0.38(1-0.38)}{200}) \\  & ∼N(0.38,0.0012).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $80$ families in the sample own a pet, then 

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}>\frac{80}{200}=0.4.
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.4).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.4) & =P(Z>\frac{0.4-0.38}{\sqrt{0.0012}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>0.58) \\  & =1-P(Z<0.58) \\  & =1-Φ(0.58).\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186188679 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-873cc424-c085-5723-b881-20ef7fecbd77" :answer/id #uuid "873cc424-c085-5723-b881-20ef7fecbd77"] $$
np=88(0.44)=38.72>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=88(1-0.44)=49.28>5,
$$

and $n=88$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.44,\frac{0.44(1-0.44)}{88}) \\  & ∼N(0.44,0.0028).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.52).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.52) & =P(Z>\frac{0.52-0.44}{\sqrt{0.0028}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.51) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.51) \\  & =1-Φ(1.51)\end{aligned}

$$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=96,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=0.72.$

Now, since

$$
np=96(0.72)=69.12>5
$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=96(1-0.72)=26.88>5,
$$

and $n=96$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

The sampling distribution of the sample proportion, in this case, can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,\frac{0.72(1-0.72)}{96}) \\  & ∼N(0.72,0.0021).\end{aligned}
$$

The probability we wish to find is
$P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}\le 0.8).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.8) & =P(\frac{0.7-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}<Z\le \frac{0.8-0.72}{\sqrt{0.0021}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.44<Z\le 1.75) \\  & =P(Z\le 1.75)-P(Z\le -0.44) \\  & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.75) & =0.9599 \\ Φ(-0.44) & =0.3300.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.7<\overset{^}{\,p}<0.8) & =Φ(1.75)-Φ(-0.44) \\  & =0.9599-0.3300 \\  & =0.6299.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-102d618f-6dbe-5b03-8427-52afbec9d15d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-42b08898-7743-5ffd-b5a7-2f858adb5713" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\overset{^}{\,p}∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}),
$$

where the sample size $n$ is much smaller than the population size, $np>5,$ and $n(1-p)>5.$

In our case

- the sample size is $n=60,$ and

- the population proportion is $p=\frac{480}{1600}=0.3.$

Now, since

$$

$$

and

$$
n(1-p)=60(1-0.3)=42>5,
$$

and the $n=60$ is much smaller than the population size, we can apply the above approximation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & ∼N(p,\frac{p(1-p)}{n}) \\  & ∼N(0.3,\frac{0.3(1-0.3)}{60}) \\  & ∼N(0.3,0.0035).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the probability we wish to find. If more than $24$ members in the sample play tennis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{^}{\,p} & >\frac{24}{60}=0.4\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the probability we wish to find is
$P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.4).$
So, we convert $\overset{^}{\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{^}{\,p}>0.4) & =P(Z>\frac{0.4-0.3}{\sqrt{0.0035}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.69) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.69) \\  & =1-Φ(1.69)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(1.69)=0.9545.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.4\le \overset{^}{\,p}) & =1-Φ(1.69) \\  & =0.0455.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-b7b25e27-3f05-5502-a400-9d84bc6b903e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-6f23f906-2914-521c-94e2-15d11518c774" :answer-field/id #uuid $$

$$
⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,\text{d}t.

$$

$$"] ["question-04de5946-03c2-52be-a91c-cc43fa9abf34" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-a756d2bc-643b-5bbc-b0e1-1d9618cee002" :answer-field/id #uuid "step-6ecbe002-c0f8-5d49-b600-f72c319b64d5"] [17592186157044 :question/problem "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x)=x^2 + e^{-2x}$ in the interval $[0,1].$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting at the point $x_0=0.5.$ Round your final answer to $3$ decimal places if needed."] [17592186157044 :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)},
$$

where $f'(x_n)$ and $f''(x_n)$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at $x_n,$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{2}+{e}^{-2x})^{′} \\  & =2x-2{e}^{-2x}, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(2x-2{e}^{-2x})^{′} \\  & =2+4{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Round your final answer to two decimal places."] ["question-afb3acd5-a2e1-5607-b3f9-fd70e360b05d" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{5}+3{x}^{2}-x)^{′}=5{x}^{4}+6x-1, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(5{x}^{4}+6x-1)^{′}=20{x}^{3}+6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{5{x}_{n}^{4}+6{x}_{n}-1}{20{x}_{n}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{n}(20{x}_{n}^{3}+6)-(5{x}_{n}^{4}+6{x}_{n}-1)}{20{x}_{n}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{15{x}_{n}^{4}+1}{20{x}_{n}^{3}+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=0.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{15{x}_{0}^{4}+1}{20{x}_{0}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{15(0.5)^{4}+1}{20(0.5)^{3}+6} \\  & =0.227\,941….\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{15{x}_{1}^{4}+1}{20{x}_{1}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{15(0.227\,941…)^{4}+1}{20(0.227\,941…)^{3}+6} \\  & =0.166\,829…, \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{15{x}_{2}^{4}+1}{20{x}_{2}^{3}+6} \\  & =\frac{15(0.166\,829…)^{4}+1}{20(0.166\,829…)^{3}+6} \\  & =0.166\,033….\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the last two approximations ${x}_{2}≈0.17$ and ${x}_{3}≈0.17$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is $x≈0.17,$ rounded to two decimal places."] ["question-afb3acd5-a2e1-5607-b3f9-fd70e360b05d" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] $$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)-3{x}^{2})^{′}=4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-6x=2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-3x), \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)-6x)^{′}=-16\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)-6=-2(8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)+3).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{x}_{n})-3{x}_{n})}{-2(8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4{x}_{n})+3)} \\  & ={x}_{n}+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{x}_{n})-3{x}_{n}}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4{x}_{n})+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=0.5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{x}_{0})-3{x}_{0}}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4{x}_{0})+3} \\  & =0.5+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot 0.5)-3\cdot 0.5}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0.5)+3} \\  & =0.272\,999….\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{x}_{1})-3{x}_{1}}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4{x}_{1})+3} \\  & =0.272\,999…+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot 0.272\,999…)-3\cdot 0.272\,999…}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0.272\,999…)+3} \\  & =0.283\,140…., \\ {x}_{3} & ={x}_{2}+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4{x}_{2})-3{x}_{2}}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4{x}_{2})+3} \\  & =0.283\,140…+\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot 0.283\,140…)-3\cdot 0.283\,140…}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0.283\,140…)+3} \\  & =0.283\,068….\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the last two approximations ${x}_{2}≈0.28$ and ${x}_{3}≈0.28$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is $x≈0.28,$ rounded to two decimal places."] ["question-c2a1716c-abcd-5c70-b5af-eb300c75e232" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] Round your final answer to two decimal places."] ["question-de551d86-8bf0-5d70-b4cf-bdf9b46a682a" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})},
$$

where ${f}^{′}({x}_{n})$ and ${f}^{″}({x}_{n})$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at ${x}_{n},$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =({x}^{6}-2{x}^{5}+{x}^{2})^{′}=6{x}^{5}-10{x}^{4}+2x, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =(6{x}^{5}-10{x}^{4}+2x)^{′}=30{x}^{4}-40{x}^{3}+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{6{x}_{n}^{5}-10{x}_{n}^{4}+2{x}_{n}}{30{x}_{n}^{4}-40{x}_{n}^{3}+2} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{n}(30{x}_{n}^{4}-40{x}_{n}^{3}+2)-(6{x}_{n}^{5}-10{x}_{n}^{4}+2{x}_{n})}{30{x}_{n}^{4}-40{x}_{n}^{3}+2} \\  & =\frac{24{x}_{n}^{5}-30{x}_{n}^{4}}{30{x}_{n}^{4}-40{x}_{n}^{3}+2} \\  & =\frac{12{x}_{n}^{5}-15{x}_{n}^{4}}{15{x}_{n}^{4}-20{x}_{n}^{3}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=1.8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{12{x}_{0}^{5}-15{x}_{0}^{4}}{15{x}_{0}^{4}-20{x}_{0}^{3}+1} \\  & =\frac{12(1.8)^{5}-15(1.8)^{4}}{15(1.8)^{4}-20(1.8)^{3}+1} \\  & =1.656\,564….\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =\frac{12{x}_{1}^{5}-15{x}_{1}^{4}}{15{x}_{1}^{4}-20{x}_{1}^{3}+1} \\  & =\frac{12(1.656\,564…)^{5}-15(1.656\,564…)^{4}}{15(1.656\,564…)^{4}-20(1.656\,564…)^{3}+1} \\  & =1.594\,573…, \\ {x}_{3} & =\frac{12{x}_{2}^{5}-15{x}_{2}^{4}}{15{x}_{2}^{4}-20{x}_{2}^{3}+1} \\  & =\frac{12(1.594\,573…)^{5}-15(1.594\,573…)^{4}}{15(1.594\,573…)^{4}-20(1.594\,573…)^{3}+1} \\  & =1.582\,950…, \\ {x}_{4} & =\frac{12{x}_{3}^{5}-15{x}_{3}^{4}}{15{x}_{3}^{4}-20{x}_{3}^{3}+1} \\  & =\frac{12(1.582\,950…)^{5}-15(1.582\,950…)^{4}}{15(1.582\,950…)^{4}-20(1.582\,950…)^{3}+1} \\  & =1.582\,567….\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the last two approximations ${x}_{3}≈1.58$ and ${x}_{4}≈1.58$ are the same when rounded to two decimal places.

Therefore, the critical point of the function is $x≈1.58,$ rounded to two decimal places."] ["question-de551d86-8bf0-5d70-b4cf-bdf9b46a682a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "answer-field-2e9f9e09-53f9-57a2-9d1e-832e556456f0"] [17592186157428 :knowledge-point/questions "question-de551d86-8bf0-5d70-b4cf-bdf9b46a682a"] [17592186158438 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to *find the roots* of a function using *Newton’s method*. That is, we solved equations of the form

$$
f(x) = 0,
$$

by starting with an initial guess and refining it step by step using the update rule

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.
$$

Now, we turn to a closely related problem of *finding a local minimum or maximum* of a function $f(x)$. Recall that these may occur at points where the derivative $f'(x)$ is equal to zero. In other words, we are looking for the roots of the function's derivative.

Earlier, we approximated the function by a straight line near our current guess. Here, instead of using a linear approximation, we assume that the function $f(x)$ behaves like a *parabola* near our current guess. That’s a reasonable assumption if $f$ is smooth. 

To make this idea precise, we use a second-order Taylor approximation, $F(x){:}$

$$
F(x) = f(x_n) + f'(x_n)(x - x_n) + \dfrac{1}{2} f''(x_n)(x - x_n)^2
$$

To find the minimum or maximum, we first need to take the derivative of this approximation, which is

$$
F'(x) = f'(x_n) + f''(x_n)(x - x_n).
$$

We then need to set $F'(x) =0$:

$$
f'(x_n) + f''(x_n)(x - x_n) = 0
$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$  as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}({x}_{n})(x-{x}_{n}) & =-{f}^{′}({x}_{n}) \\ x-{x}_{n} & =-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})} \\ x & ={x}_{n}-\frac{{f}^{′}({x}_{n})}{{f}^{″}({x}_{n})}\end{aligned}
$$

So, just like in root-finding, we start with an initial guess and improve it step by step. But this time, we apply Newton’s method to the derivative $f'(x)$ instead of the function $f(x)$ itself:

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)}
$$

**Note**: The second derivative $f''(x_n)$ must not be zero. If it is zero, or even very close to zero, the update step can become extremely large, leading us far away from the solution.

Just like in root-finding, Newton’s method works best when the function is smooth, and our initial guess is already close to the minimum or maximum."] [17592186158457 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function 

$$
f(x)= \ln(x+1)+\dfrac{2}{x+1}
$$

in the interval $[0,2].$ Let's calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization starting at the point $x_0=0.8.$ 

The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)},
$$

where $f'(x_n)$ and $f''(x_n)$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at $x_n,$ respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+\frac{2}{x+1})}^{′} \\  & =\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{x-1}{(x+1)^{2}}, \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={(\frac{1}{x+1}-\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}})}^{′} \\  & =-\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}+\frac{4}{(x+1)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3-x}{(x+1)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{n+1} & ={x}_{n}-\frac{\frac{{x}_{n}-1}{({x}_{n}+1)^{2}}}{\frac{3-{x}_{n}}{({x}_{n}+1)^{3}}} \\  & ={x}_{n}-\frac{{x}_{n}^{2}-1}{3-{x}_{n}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with $x_0=0.8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-\frac{{x}_{0}^{2}-1}{3-{x}_{0}} \\  & =0.8-\frac{(0.8)^{2}-1}{3-0.8} \\  & ≈0.964,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."] [17592186158355 :step/math-academy-id 688822] [17592186158356 :step/math-academy-id 688823] [17592186158357 :step/math-academy-id 688824] [17592186158358 :step/math-academy-id 688827] [17592186158359 :step/math-academy-id 688830] [17592186157519 :activity/expected-seconds 1500.0] ["question-c44a3fc0-0b84-5773-98c9-aa672df4ee82" :question/id #uuid "c44a3fc0-0b84-5773-98c9-aa672df4ee82"] ["question-c44a3fc0-0b84-5773-98c9-aa672df4ee82" :question/math-academy-id "q-164407"] ["question-c44a3fc0-0b84-5773-98c9-aa672df4ee82" :question/problem "Identify the following surface:

z=\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}},
$$

and an elliptic paraboloid centered at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is given by

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}},
$$

Thus, our equation is an elliptic paraboloid with the following parameters:

$$

["question-e1726d67-859b-50b6-a736-a3033ae62d0e" :question/math-academy-id "q-331948"] ["question-e1726d67-859b-50b6-a736-a3033ae62d0e" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t),\end{aligned}\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

${X}_{1}(s)=\frac{2(2s-9)}{(s-1)(s-4)},\,{X}_{2}(s)=$ {{field-1}}."] ["question-e1726d67-859b-50b6-a736-a3033ae62d0e" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{2{x}_{1}(t)-2{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-{x}_{1}(t)+3{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}\,\,
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-2L\{{x}_{2}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+3L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-4=2{X}_{1}(s)-2{X}_{2}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-3=-{X}_{1}(s)+3{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}.$

Rewriting the system in standard form, we get the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(s-2){X}_{1}(s)+2{X}_{2}(s)=4 \\ {X}_{1}(s)+(s-3){X}_{2}(s)=3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, from the second equation, we have 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=3-(s-3){X}_{2}(s).
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(s-2)[3-(s-3){X}_{2}(s)]+2{X}_{2}(s) & =4 \\ 3(s-2)-[(s-2)(s-3)-2]{X}_{2}(s) & =4 \\ -({s}^{2}-5s+4){X}_{2}(s) & =4-3(s-2) \\ -(s-1)(s-4){X}_{2}(s) & =-3s+10 \\ {X}_{2}(s) & =\frac{3s-10}{(s-1)(s-4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${X}_{1}(s):$

$$

bought sixteen more. If he now has $36$, how many comic books did he have at the start?"] ["question-671acf01-53e4-5ebe-ba29-cc75ccac1d67" :question/worked-solution "Let $x=$ the number of comic books Caden had at the start.

We note that:

- Half the number of comic books corresponds to $\frac{1}{2}x.$

- The number of comic books remaining after selling half of them corresponds to $x-\frac{1}{2}x.$

- The number of comic books remaining after selling half and buying sixteen more corresponds to $x-\frac{1}{2}x+16.$

The final number of comic books is $36,$ so we have the equation

$$
x-\frac{1}{2}x+16=36.
$$

We can solve this equation using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-\frac{1}{2}x+16 & =36 \\ (1-\frac{1}{2})x+16 & =36 \\ \frac{1}{2}x+16 & =36 \\ \frac{1}{2}x+16-16 & =36-16 \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =20 \\ 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x & =2\cdot 20 \\ x & =40\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, Caden had $40$ comic books at the start."] ["question-671acf01-53e4-5ebe-ba29-cc75ccac1d67" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-8b8bf0b2-6f55-5107-9e2d-cc11b6142890" :question/math-academy-id "q-112414"] ["question-8b8bf0b2-6f55-5107-9e2d-cc11b6142890" :question/problem "Find the solution $(a,b)$ to the following system of equations by eliminating the variable $a:$ 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5a+4b=7 \\ -2a+6b=20\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-8b8bf0b2-6f55-5107-9e2d-cc11b6142890" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the $a$-coefficient in the first equation is $5,$ while in the second equation it is $-2.$ 

If we multiply the first equation by $2$ and the second equation by $5,$ then the $a$-coefficient in the first and second equations will become $10$ and $-10,$ and these will cancel when we add the equations.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(\,5a+4b=7\,)\,\times (2) \\ (\,-2a+6b=20\,)\,\times (5)\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}10a+8b=14 \\ -10a+30b=100\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when we add the two equations, the variable $a$ will be eliminated:

$$
\begin{aligned}\cancel{10a}+8b & =14 \\ -\cancel{10a}+30b & =100 \\ (8b+30b) & =(14+100) \\ 38b & =114 \\ b & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $b=3.$ However, we still need to find $a.$ To do this, we substitute $b=3$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5a+4b & =7 \\ 5a+4(3) & =7 \\ 5a+12 & =7 \\ 5a & =-5 \\ a & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-1$ and $b=3,$ which can be written as $(-1,3).$"] ["question-8b8bf0b2-6f55-5107-9e2d-cc11b6142890" :question/difficulty $y=f(x),$ we apply the following transformations in the order given:

1\. Stretch it by a scale factor of $8$ parallel to the $y$-axis

2\. Stretch it by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $x$-axis

3\. Translate it to the left by $10$ units

What is the final function expression after applying all the transformations?"] [17592186233460 :question/worked-solution "To find the expression, let's apply each of the transformations in turn.

1\. Stretching the graph of $y=f(x)$ by a scale factor of $8$ parallel to the $y$-axis is equivalent to multiplying the function expression by $8.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

  $$
  y=8f(x).
  $$

2\. Stretching the graph of $y=8f(x)$ by a scale factor of $5$ parallel to the $x$-axis is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $\frac{1}{5}x.$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

  $$
  y=8f(\frac{1}{5}x)=8f(\frac{x}{5}).
  $$

3\. Translating the graph of $y=8f(\frac{x}{5})$ by $10$ units to the left is equivalent to replacing every instance of $x$ with $(x+10).$ Applying this transformation, we obtain 

  $$
  y=8f(\frac{1}{5}(x+10))=8f(\frac{x}{5}+2).
  $$

Therefore, the final function expression is $y=8f(\frac{x}{5}+2).$"] ["answer-field-ffa36a73-cb38-5a3e-b22f-94ae7972e4d0" :answer-field/id #uuid "ffa36a73-cb38-5a3e-b22f-94ae7972e4d0"] ["question-a5359436-369e-5935-88c6-73a8053a9364" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite $\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}=\frac{1}{{e}^{1/2}}={e}^{-1/2}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}})=\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-1/2})
$$

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=-\frac{1}{2}.$ Therefore:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-1/2})=-\frac{1}{2}
$$"] ["question-a5359436-369e-5935-88c6-73a8053a9364" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-6fd07e78-dd69-5881-8015-dd32bee64dd0" :answer-field/id #uuid The Venn diagram shown above represents two events $A$ and $B$ and the number of outcomes in each region of the sample space.

Given that every outcome is equally likely, find $P({A}^{′}\cup {B}^{′}).$"] [17592186233592 :question/worked-solution "To calculate the probability of an event using a Venn diagram, we count the number of outcomes in the region that represents the event, and divide by the total number of outcomes of the sample space $S.$

In the Venn diagram, ${A}^{′}\cup {B}^{′}$ is represented by the area outside the circle $B$ or outside the circle $A$ (see the illustration below).

![](images/6a/6a3bb7b671e45aeb15d3239cae6fcedb7c36e52b15141d66b23e65066ab37edc.png)

We count up the outcomes:

- The number of outcomes in ${A}^{′}\cup {B}^{′}$ is 

$$
2+5+1=8
$$

- The total number of outcomes in $S$ is

$$
2+9+5+1=17.
$$

So, we have

$$
P({A}^{′}\cup {B}^{′})=\frac{8}{17}.
$$"] ["answer-field-3f94bd53-f137-5cf0-9547-b2c16a22c866" :answer-field/id #uuid "3f94bd53-f137-5cf0-9547-b2c16a22c866"] ["answer-1537842d-13cc-58e0-a0d1-143d9983a915" :answer/id #uuid ["question-751e0aa2-a931-559b-9a2f-5250360d1346" :question/math-academy-id "q-118876"] ["question-751e0aa2-a931-559b-9a2f-5250360d1346" :question/problem "A company rents ten identical storage units in the form of a rectangular prism. Each unit is $5\,\text{yd}$ long, $3\,\text{yd}$ wide, and $3\text{yd}$ high. If it costs $$2$ per cubic yard per day to rent a storage unit, how much does it cost the company each day to rent the storage units?"] ["question-751e0aa2-a931-559b-9a2f-5250360d1346" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the volume of one storage unit.

We can find the volume $V$ of the rectangular prism using the formula

$$
V=lwh,
$$

where $l$ is the length, $w$ is the width, and $h$ is the height of the solid.

Substituting 

$$
l=5,\,w=3,\,h=3
$$

into the formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}V=5\cdot 3\cdot 3=45\,{\text{yd}}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

The total volume of the ten units is

$$
45\cdot 10=450\,{\text{yd}}^{3}.
$$

Finally, to rent the storage units, each day the company must pay

$$
450\cdot $2=$900.
$$"] ["question-751e0aa2-a931-559b-9a2f-5250360d1346" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-45a670a5-6eca-551c-9bba-97922b332700" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-751e0aa2-a931-559b-9a2f-5250360d1346"] ["question-c7f9805c-ce96-515d-891a-332594997042" :question/id #uuid "c7f9805c-ce96-515d-891a-332594997042"] ["question-c7f9805c-ce96-515d-891a-332594997042" :question/math-academy-id "q-85920"] ["question-c7f9805c-ce96-515d-891a-332594997042" :question/problem "A team of $5$ players is to be chosen at random from $7$ boys and $5$ girls.  What is the probability that $2$ boys and $3$ girls will be chosen? Round your answer to the nearest percent."] ["question-c7f9805c-ce96-515d-891a-332594997042" :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ represent the event described in the question. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N},\end{aligned}
$$

where $N$ is the total number of ways to choose $5$ people out of a total of $12,$ and $n$ is the number of picks where $2$ are boys and $3$ are girls.

Since the order in which the players are chosen does not matter, we use combinations.

First, we compute $N.$ The number of ways to pick $5$ people from a total of $12$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}N={}_{12}{C}_{5} & =\frac{12!}{5!\cdot 7!}=792.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $n.$ The computation of $n$ can be divided into two steps: 

- the number of ways to choose $2$ (out of $7$) boys is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{7}{C}_{2}=\frac{7!}{2!\cdot 5!}=21\end{aligned}
$$

- the number of ways to choose $3$ (out of $5$) girls is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{5}{C}_{3} & =\frac{5!}{3!\cdot 2!}=10\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the results from the above steps, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n={}_{7}{C}_{2}\cdot {}_{5}{C}_{3}=21\cdot 10=210.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{210}{792}≈0.27=27%.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c7f9805c-ce96-515d-891a-332594997042" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-c3a0c2d2-5b3a-522b-a6d4-7655774ccad3" :answer-field/id #uuid change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}⁡X=\frac{{log}_{b}⁡X}{{log}_{b}⁡a}
$$

In our case, $a=8,$ and $X=32.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ are powers of $2,$ we set $b=2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}⁡(32) & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡(32)}{{log}_{2}⁡(8)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{5})}{{log}_{2}⁡({2}^{3})} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["answer-field-f4740df2-7f5f-55f7-996f-1be23039010f" :answer-field/id #uuid "f4740df2-7f5f-55f7-996f-1be23039010f"] ["answer-29fbd695-065d-59f9-a978-64ab959589fe" :answer/id #uuid ["question-18899ab8-1919-5955-a40e-8e20033f8007" :question/math-academy-id "q-293604"] ["question-18899ab8-1919-5955-a40e-8e20033f8007" :question/problem "A generator consumes $3$ liters of fuel per hour for the first two hours of use and $5$ liters for each additional hour. Which function $F$ gives the total amount of fuel consumed after $t$ hours, where $t\ge 2?$"] ["question-18899ab8-1919-5955-a40e-8e20033f8007" :question/worked-solution "The total amount of fuel consumed consists of two parts.

- For the first $2$ hours, the generator consumes

$$
3\times 2=6\,\,\text{liters}.
$$

- For each additional hour beyond the first $2,$ the generator consumes

$$
5(t-2)\,\,\text{liters}.
$$

Therefore, the total amount of fuel $F$ consumed after $t$ hours, where $t\ge 2,$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =6+5(t-2) \\  & =6+5t-10 \\  & =5t-4.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-18899ab8-1919-5955-a40e-8e20033f8007" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-456409ce-9cbe-59f6-9c9f-5b1ca5269b70" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-19e31d5d-5933-52fe-a699-d3240dcd05a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-288661"] ["question-19e31d5d-5933-52fe-a699-d3240dcd05a2" :question/problem "The equation

$$
(ax-8)(x+b)=4{x}^{2}-32x+48
$$

is true for all values of $x,$ where $a$ and $b$ are constants. What is the value of $a+b?$

$a+b=$
{{field-1}}"] ["question-19e31d5d-5933-52fe-a699-d3240dcd05a2" :question/worked-solution "Since the equation is true for all values of $x,$ the expressions on both sides must be exactly the same. That means the product on the left-hand side must expand to match the right-hand side.

First, let's expand the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(ax-8)(x+b) & =a{x}^{2}+abx-8x-8b \\  & =a{x}^{2}+(ab-8)x-8b.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we equate the expanded form to the right-hand side:

$$
a{x}^{2}+(ab-8)x-8b=4{x}^{2}-32x+48.
$$

Now, we compare the coefficients of corresponding terms.

- Equating the coefficients of ${x}^{2},$ we get

$$
a=4.
$$

- Equating the constant terms, we get

$$
-8\cdot b=48⇒b=-6.
$$

Let's verify that values $a=4$ and $b=-6$ produce the correct linear coefficient:

$$
\begin{aligned}ab-8 & =4\cdot (-6)-8 \\  & =-24-8 \\  & =-32\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

which matches the coefficient of $x$ on the right-hand side. So, our solution is valid.

Finally, we compute the value of $a+b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =4+(-6) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-19e31d5d-5933-52fe-a699-d3240dcd05a2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f" :answer-field/id #uuid "9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f"] ["answer-7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4" :answer/id #uuid "7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4"] ["answer-7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4" :answer/value "-2"] ["answer-field-9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f" :answer-field/correct "answer-7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4"] ["answer-field-9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f" :answer-field/choices "answer-7e944915-2fc2-5b59-b074-8518099067d4"] ["question-19e31d5d-5933-52fe-a699-d3240dcd05a2" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-9df0f739-7e6e-51a0-aeca-cefca94dcd0f"] [17592186213005 :knowledge-point/questions "question-19e31d5d-5933-52fe-a699-d3240dcd05a2"] [17592186233432 :question/problem "![](images/ce/cec25c6ab182494771824bae8c2182bf38b57e2d1e81d913e3e49916c8cc3d60.png)

II. The residuals appear to be randomly scattered about the horizontal axis (there are no obvious trends).

III. This linear regression is probably a good fit for the data."] [17592186233432 :question/worked-solution "Let's examine the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. The residual equals the actual value minus the estimated value:

$$
\text{Residual}=\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated}
$$

 
From the plot, the residual at $x=8$ is negative. So, we have that $\text{Actual}<\text{Estimated},$ and therefore the model overestimates  this data point.

- Statement II is false. The plot shows the residuals tend to decrease as $x$ increases. So, there is a trend, as shown below.

![](images/0b/0bb186e7b1c1923e7e8b2776b202b1dcd9b930c56583199964e47530805d246d.png)

- Statement III is false. Since the residuals are *not* randomly scattered above and below the horizontal axis, our regression line is *not* a good fit for the given data.

["question-0821d791-2798-561e-8237-7b4aabdd155c" :question/math-academy-id "q-35003"] ["question-0821d791-2798-561e-8237-7b4aabdd155c" :question/problem "![](images/06/06e792c5b74eda036b55ac3728122737da22c9824f89f982b50657ab07391269.png)

Which of the following statements are true concerning the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown above? 

I. ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=\text{DNE}$

II. ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=2$

III. ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)={lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)$"] ["question-0821d791-2798-561e-8237-7b4aabdd155c" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. As $x$ approaches $0$ from the left and right we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x)=0,\,{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x)=1\,.
$$

 
Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x),$ and hence ${lim}_{x\to \,0}f(x)=\text{DNE}.$

- Statement II is false. As $x$ approaches $1$ from the left and right we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)=2,\,{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}\,.
$$

 
Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}f(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}f(x),$ and hence ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=\text{DNE}.$

- Statement III is false. We see from the graph that 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=\text{DNE},\,{lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=\text{DNE}
$$

 We can't say that the limits are equal because we can't compare undefined values.

In conclusion, only statement I is true."] ["question-0821d791-2798-561e-8237-7b4aabdd155c" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-b5da9fec-9cf5-5ef3-8a64-44b81b106bd9" {{field-1}}"] [17592186233682 :question/worked-solution "Given a frequency table containing continuous data split into $K$ classes, we can estimate the variance by treating all observations within each class as though they were equal to the midpoint of that class. This gives

$$
{\sigma }_{n}^{2}≈\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{K}{f}_{i}\cdot ({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},
$$

where

- ${f}_{i}$ is the frequency of the $i$th class,

- ${m}_{i}$ is the midpoint of the $i$th class,

- $n$ is the total number of observations, and

- $\overset{―}{x}$ is the estimated mean, calculated using the class midpoints.

To find the variance, we add columns to our table for the midpoints of each interval, the squared deviations of the midpoints from the mean, and the products of the squared deviations and frequencies.

| Range | ${f}_{i}$ | ${m}_{i}$ | ${({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ | ${f}_{i}{({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $8$ | $5$ | $72.25$ | $578$ |
| $10\le x<20$ | $7$ | $15$ | $2.25$ | $15.75$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $5$ | $25$ | $132.25$ | $661.25$ |

$$

$$

Then, we divide the sum of all the values in the last column by $20$ (the total number of observations):

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n}^{2} & ≈\frac{578+15.75+661.25}{20} \\  & =\frac{1255}{20} \\  & =62.75\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the estimated standard deviation is the square root of the estimated variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n} & ≈\sqrt{62.75}≈7.9\end{aligned}
$$"] ["answer-50cba50f-0215-54ad-96b6-a3d381b47f01" :answer/id #uuid "50cba50f-0215-54ad-96b6-a3d381b47f01"] ["answer-50cba50f-0215-54ad-96b6-a3d381b47f01" :answer/type :answer.type/math] Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD?$"] [17592186234325 :question/worked-solution "The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $△ABD$ and $△BDC$ (see the illustration below).

![](images/6e/6e070d26915bcb11118f5a23f36b80038d5dd865e32a8517a12c10939ca02f0b.png)

First, we find the area of $△ABD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot 8\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{85}^{∘} \\  & =24\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{85}^{∘} \\  & ≈23.908\,7,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Now we find the area of $△BCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{BCD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 14\cdot 16\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{36.4}^{∘} \\  & =112\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{36.4}^{∘} \\  & ≈66.462\,9,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABD}+{A}_{BCD} \\  & ≈23.908\,7+66.462\,9 \\  & ≈90.371\,6.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $90.$"] ["answer-field-a5f55799-fa35-55be-b5e7-23ed06c306d5" :answer-field/id #uuid "![](images/51/51b119021be889ff440ec31d901187c3ee9072a507336a8e1a1854f729f2734f.png)

Find ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2f(x)}{3{x}^{2}}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted above."] ["question-124cf999-fb4b-5e99-b208-917f67eaa2a5" :question/worked-solution "Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2f(x)}{3{x}^{2}}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to 1}(-2f(x))}{{lim}_{x\to 1}3{x}^{2}}.
$$

We find from the graph that ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)=6.$ Calculating the limits of the numerator and denominator separately, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}(-2f(x))=-2(6)=-12
$$

and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 1}3{x}^{2}=3(1)^{2}=3.
$$

Taking the quotient of these limits, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{-2f(x)}{3{x}^{2}} & =\frac{{lim}_{x\to 1}(-2f(x))}{{lim}_{x\to 1}3{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-12}{3} \\  & =-4\,.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-124cf999-fb4b-5e99-b208-917f67eaa2a5" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-2bbc0ee1-4baa-5173-b100-20018e22dddd" :answer-field/id #uuid factor of $(x-1)$ and has a remainder of $4$ when divided by $(x+2).$ Find the value of $a-b.$"] ["question-5db961df-fac4-59ee-a59e-6595583c0931" :question/worked-solution "Since $(x-1)$ is a factor of $f(x)$, it must divide into $f(x)$ with no remainder. In other words, when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x-1),$ the remainder is $0.$ It follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =f(1) \\  & =a(1)^{3}-2(1)^{2}+b(1)+1 \\  & =a-2+b+1 \\  & =a+b-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, since we're told that the remainder is $4$ when $f(x)$ is divided by $(x+2),$ it follows from the remainder theorem that

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =f(-2) \\  & =a(-2)^{3}-2(-2)^{2}+b(-2)+1 \\  & =-8a-8-2b+1 \\  & =-8a-2b-7.\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the system of equations

$$
\{\begin{aligned}0=a+b-1 \\ 4=-8a-2b-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying each equation, we get

$$
\{\begin{aligned}a+b=1 \\ 8a+2b=-11.\end{aligned}
$$

To eliminate $b,$ we multiply the first equation by $-2,$ and we add the resulting equation to the second equation. So we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & -2a-2b=-2 \\ +\,\,\, & \,8a+2b=-11 \\  & \,6a=-13.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get $a=-\frac{13}{6}.$ Finally, we substitute it into $a+b=1$ to find $b=\frac{19}{6}.$ 

Therefore, our final solution is $a-b=-\frac{16}{3}.$"] ["question-5db961df-fac4-59ee-a59e-6595583c0931" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] By the definition, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(3)={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h}.
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=10{x}^{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{10(3+h)^{2}-10(3)^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{90+60h+10{h}^{2}-90}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(\frac{60h+10{h}^{2}}{h}) \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(60+10h) \\  & =60+(0) \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$

 

*Method 2:*

By the definition, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(3)={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{f(x)-f(3)}{x-3}.
$$

Applying this to $f(x)=10{x}^{2}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & ={lim}_{x\to 3}(\frac{10{x}^{2}-10(3)^{2}}{x-3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}(\frac{10({x}^{2}-{3}^{2})}{x-3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}(\frac{10(x-3)(x+3)}{x-3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}10(x+3) \\  & =10(3+3) \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["answer-field-1bf2afe7-a005-5071-84b9-bd40024ce506" :answer-field/id #uuid "1bf2afe7-a005-5071-84b9-bd40024ce506"] ["answer-71a944ae-ff58-5447-8134-5585f04d64b8" :answer/id #uuid [17592186234168 :question/worked-solution "To help us to visualize the angle, we first convert the measure of the angle into degrees. 

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by $\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi }.$ This gives

$$
(\frac{7\pi }{10})\cdot (\frac{{180}^{∘}}{\pi })={126}^{∘}.
$$

Therefore $\frac{7\pi }{10}$ is equivalent to ${126}^{∘},$ which lies in the $2\text{nd}$ quadrant.

![](images/89/89b5e2656378adb5d91c9f58c261e4beaae252b67819b904bf209f6ed8a5a25e.png)

To express $\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{10})$ in terms of $\operatorname{cot}⁡{\theta }_{R},$ we follow three steps:

1\. Find its reference angle ${\theta }_{R}.$

2\. Calculate the value of the function for ${\theta }_{R}.$

3\. Determine whether the resulting value is positive or negative.

**Step 1**: Since $\theta =\frac{7\pi }{10}$ is in the $2$nd quadrant, the reference angle ${\theta }_{R}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\pi -\theta  \\  & =\pi -\frac{7\pi }{10} \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: The given ratio is $\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{10})$, and therefore we're interested in $\operatorname{cot}⁡{\theta }_{R}=\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{10}).$

**Step 3:** The ratio $\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{10})$ must be negative because tangent (and therefore cotangent) is always negative in the $2$nd quadrant. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{10})=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{10}).
$$"] ["answer-field-427c3f91-22fc-5c34-bf37-633a78d7c0ba" :answer-field/id #uuid "427c3f91-22fc-5c34-bf37-633a78d7c0ba"] ["answer-ecf7300d-5c9b-5c16-914a-b75e51c21227" :answer/id #uuid [17592186233306 :question/worked-solution "The angles $0$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](images/79/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

- Let's first consider the angle $0.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $0$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$  Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡0=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡0=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

- Now, let's consider the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$  Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{sec}⁡0+\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})=1+1=2.
$$"] ["answer-field-5809f205-7813-519f-9ba7-8f909067fdec" :answer-field/id #uuid "5809f205-7813-519f-9ba7-8f909067fdec"] ["answer-346c7c5f-30ec-593f-bea5-24e469b9441b" :answer/id #uuid "answer-field-3900d287-7003-527b-bb39-f80c78c2331d"] [17592186234105 :question/worked-solution "The function $N(t)$ gives the number of people inside the park $t$ minutes after opening. Then,

$$
{N}^{′}(t)=\frac{\text{d}N(t)}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{Change in }N}{\text{Change in }t}.
$$

Thus, ${N}^{′}(t)$ gives the rate at which the number of people inside the park changes $t$ minutes after opening.

In addition, we can compute the rate of change of the number of people inside the park at time $t$ by finding the difference between the entry and exit rates at time $t.$ That is,

$$
{N}^{′}(t)=E(t)-L(t).
$$"] ["answer-field-1ee88502-7069-5e01-a8d0-c684a215ef26" :answer-field/id #uuid "1ee88502-7069-5e01-a8d0-c684a215ef26"] ["answer-a912d151-5821-56b2-bfc3-6a30d519da07" :answer/id #uuid "answer-field-5749cf60-a3f1-5876-9c2b-03d5d66464f0"] [17592186234280 :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=6\sqrt{x}+5x-13.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\sqrt{x}+5x-13) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{1/2}+5x) \\  & =3{x}^{-1/2}+5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{-1/2}+5=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =8(x-1) \\ y & =8x-8-2 \\ y & =8x-10.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =8x-10 \\ x & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(\frac{5}{4},0).$"] ["answer-field-2f3486a1-cfa1-570d-be9b-887c8a18ac0b" :answer-field/id #uuid "2f3486a1-cfa1-570d-be9b-887c8a18ac0b"] "$\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt[4]{e})=$"] ["question-5f3a9a12-37bd-5534-bce9-24153ef1f5e3" :question/worked-solution "First, we rewrite $\sqrt[4]{e}$ as a power of $e$ (the base of the natural logarithm) as follows:

$$
\sqrt[4]{e}={e}^{1/4}
$$

Therefore, we have:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt[4]{e})=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})
$$

The natural logarithm reverses the action of the exponent. The principle is:

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x})=x
$$

In our case, we have $x=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{1/4})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{8}

:question/problem "Find ${H}^{⊥}$ if $H=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -14\end{aligned}]\}.$"] ["question-1b5b5791-1037-533d-a2f0-5ffb4bac0dd8" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote the vectors that span the subspace $H$ as ${h}_{1}$ and ${h}_{2}.$ 

A vector $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$ belongs to ${H}^{⊥}$ if $x\cdot {h}_{1}=0$ and $x\cdot {h}_{2}=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x\cdot {h}_{1}=0 \\ x\cdot {h}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-4{x}_{1}+7{x}_{2}=0 \\ 8{x}_{1}-14{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 7 & 0 \\ 8 & -14 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, we have $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one), so ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=\frac{7}{4}{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, our orthogonal complement is

$$
{H}^{⊥}=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]\,:\,{x}_{2}\in R\}.
$$"] ["question-1b5b5791-1037-533d-a2f0-5ffb4bac0dd8" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-356e4ab9-2091-593a-99dd-55afcb98c941" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=2 \\ h(x,y,z)=1\end{aligned}

$4{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.$"] ["question-3250257a-998e-56c2-b2b7-fdd8d8e6863b" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the maximum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+y-2z
$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x+y+4z=4,\,h(x,y,z)=4{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z)=4 \\ h(x,y,z)=1\end{aligned}
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨1,1,-2⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,1,4⟩+\mu ⟨8x,0,2z⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda +8\mu x \\ 1=\lambda  \\ -2=4\lambda +2\mu z\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\mu x=0 \\ \lambda =1 \\ z=-\frac{3}{\mu }\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction. So, from the first equation above, we must have $x=0.$

Next, we substitute $x=0$  into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =1 \\ {z}^{2} & =1 \\ z & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $z$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=0$ and $z=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+4z & =4 \\ 0+y+4(1) & =4 \\ y+4 & =4 \\ y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=0$ and $z=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y+4z & =4 \\ 0+y+4(-1) & =4 \\ y-4 & =4 \\ y & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,0,1),\,(0,8,-1).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(0,0,1)$ | $(0,8,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $-2$ | $10$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(0,8,-1),$ and its  maximum value is $10.$"] ["question-3250257a-998e-56c2-b2b7-fdd8d8e6863b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] is known as a **sum of squares** and is denoted $S_{xx}$. As we'll see, this quantity often appears in statistical analysis, so giving it a separate notation is useful.

$$

∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)2x_{i} \cdot x^(―) + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x^(―)^{2}

Next, we use the following results:

$$

$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4=\lambda yz \\ 4=\lambda xz \\ 4=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4x=\lambda xyz \\ 4y=\lambda xyz \\ 4z=\lambda xyz\end{aligned}
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =125 \\ x(x)(x) & =125 \\ {x}^{3} & =125 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(5,5,5),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(5,5,5)=4(5)+4(5)+4(5)=60\,\text{in}.

$$

$$"] [17592186364648 :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the tank's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to minimize the function

$$"] [17592186362346 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

Find the covariance of $X$ and $Y$."] [17592186159776 :answer-field/choices 17592186159780] [17592186163290 :tutorial/content "We often want to measure the strength of the (linear) dependence between two random variables. One measure that we use for this purpose is covariance.

The **covariance** between two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \textrm{E}\Big[\left(X - \textrm{E}[X]\right)\left(Y - \textrm{E}[Y]\right) \Big]
$$

Let's break this formula down a bit:

- $\left(X - \textrm{E}[X]\right)$ is the deviation of $X$ from its mean
- $\left(Y - \textrm{E}[Y]\right)$ is the deviation of $Y$ from its mean

Therefore, the covariance measures the expected value of the product of these deviations.

The covariance can also be expressed as

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] =\sum_{(x,y)\in S}(x - \textrm E[X])(y - \textrm E[Y])f(x,y)
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint PMF of $X$ and $Y$, and $S$ is the joint support.

Let's sketch a few diagrams to get a feel for what the covariance tells us.

- A *positive* covariance means that if $X$ increases, then $Y$ is likely to increase. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **positively correlated**.![](images/bb/bbfae3f0fb38bc8652cd26716e4b0b128cf1f2039350267034d97161d7f5dac4.png)
- A *negative* covariance means that if $X$ increases, then $Y$ is likely to decrease. We say that $X$ and $Y$ are **negatively correlated**.![](images/fd/fd45053fdc39f070e3438c3b8c61fe01613201595cfe00bd4cc6c6e481bf73ab.png)

Note the following:

- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then
$\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] = 0$.
The reverse implication does not always hold! For example, two random variables can have zero covariance yet be dependent. This is because covariance measures *linear* dependence only.
- The covariance of a random variable with itself is its variance:
$Cov[X, X]|= E[(X - E[X])(X - E[X])]; = E[(X - E[X])^{2}]; = Var[X]$

- Aside from indicating whether two random variables are positively or negatively correlated, the covariance *by itself* does not tell us very much. For example, if
$\textrm{Cov}[X_1, Y_1] > \textrm{Cov}[X_2, Y_2] > 0$
this does not necessarily mean that the dependence between $X_1$ and $Y_1$ is somehow "stronger" than the dependence between $X_2$ and $Y_2$. This is because the covariance does not take the variance of the individual random variables into account. In a future lesson, we'll use the covariance to define the so-called **correlation coefficient,** which *does* consider the variance of the individual random variables and so *can* be used to compare the relative strength of the linear dependence between two pairs of random variables."] [17592186163343 :tutorial/content "You may have noticed that computing the covariance using the definition is quite a lot of work. $$

As is the case with discrete random variables, it's often easier to compute the covariance using the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E} [XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y]

Suppose we're given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
{\frac{1}{2}(x + \frac{y}{2}),\begin{vmatrix}0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le 2, \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

To compute the covariance of this distribution, we first use the rule of the lazy statistician to find $\textrm{E}[XY]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[XY] &= \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{1}xyf(x, y)dxdy \\
&= \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{1}xy \cdot \frac{1}{2}(x + \frac{y}{2})dxdy \\
&= \int_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}y\int_{0}^{1}(x^{2} + \frac{1}{2}xy)dxdy \\

&= \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \\
&= \frac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}"] [17592186158438 :tutorial/content "In a previous lesson, we learned how to *find the roots* of a function using *Newton’s method*. That is, we solved equations of the form

$$
f(x) = 0
$$

by starting with an initial guess and refining it step by step using the update rule

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}
$$

Now, we turn to a closely related problem of *finding a local minimum or maximum* of a function $f(x)$. Recall that these may occur at points where the derivative $f'(x)$ is equal to zero. In other words, we are looking for the roots of the function's derivative.

Earlier, we approximated the function by a straight line near our current guess. Here, instead of using a linear approximation, we assume that the function $f(x)$ behaves like a *parabola* near our current guess. That’s a reasonable assumption if $f$ is smooth.

To make this idea precise, we use a second-order Taylor approximation, $F(x){:}$

$$
F(x) = f(x_n) + f'(x_n)(x - x_n) + \dfrac{1}{2} f''(x_n)(x - x_n)^2
$$

To find the minimum or maximum, we first need to take the derivative of this approximation, which is

$$
F'(x) = f'(x_n) + f''(x_n)(x - x_n)
$$

We then need to set $F'(x) =0$:

$$
f'(x_n) + f''(x_n)(x - x_n) = 0
$$

Finally, we solve for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{″}(x_{n})(x - x_{n}) &= -f^{′}(x_{n}) \\
x - x_{n} &= - (f^{′}(x_{n}))/(f^{″}(x_{n})) \\
x &= x_{n} - (f^{′}(x_{n}))/(f^{″}(x_{n}))
\end{aligned}
$$

So, just like in root-finding, we start with an initial guess and improve it step by step. But this time, we apply Newton’s method to the derivative $f'(x)$ instead of the function $f(x)$ itself:

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)}
$$

**Note**: The second derivative $f''(x_n)$ must not be zero. If it is zero, or even very close to zero, the update step can become extremely large, leading us far away from the solution.

Just like in root-finding, Newton’s method works best when the function is smooth, and our initial guess is already close to the minimum or maximum."] [17592186158457 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function

The Newton-Raphson process for optimization is

$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f'(x_n)}{f''(x_n)}
$$

where $f'(x_n)$ and $f''(x_n)$ are the first and second derivatives of $f(x)$ evaluated at $x_n$, respectively.

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{′}(x) &= (\ln (x + 1) + \frac{2}{x + 1})^{′} \\
&= \frac{1}{x + 1} - (2)/((x + 1)^{2}) \\
&= (x - 1)/((x + 1)^{2}), \\
f^{″}(x) &= (\frac{1}{x + 1} - (2)/((x + 1)^{2}))^{′} \\
&= - (1)/((x + 1)^{2}) + (4)/((x + 1)^{3}) \\
&= (3 - x)/((x + 1)^{3})
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{n + 1} &= x_{n} - ((x_{n} - 1)/((x_{n} + 1)^{2}))/((3 - x_{n})/((x_{n} + 1)^{3})) \\
&= x_{n} - \frac{x_{n}^{2} - 1}{3 - x_{n}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Starting with $x_0=0.8$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{1} &= x_{0} - \frac{x_{0}^{2} - 1}{3 - x_{0}} \\
&= 0.8 - ((0.8)^{2} - 1)/(3 - 0.8) \\
&\approx 0.964
\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."] [17592186158355 :step/math-academy-id 459710] [17592186158356 :step/math-academy-id 459711] [17592186158357 :step/math-academy-id 459712] [17592186158358 :step/math-academy-id 459715] [17592186158359 :step/math-academy-id 459718] [17592186233460 :question/problem "Given the graph of $y=f(x),$ we apply the following transformations in the order given:

:knowledge-point/title "Calculating Sums of Squares Given a Dataset or Summary Statistics"}] :question/problem "Consider the two sets of $5$ paired observations shown in the table below.

| **$\, x_i \,$** | $15$ | $12$ | $13$ | $16$ | $19$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **$\, y_i \,$** | $8$ | $13$ | $6$ | $15$ | $13$ |

Calculate $S_{xy}$." :question/worked-solution "Given a set of $n$ paired observations $x_{1}, x_2, \ldots, x_{n}$ and $y_{1}, y_2, \ldots, y_{n}$, $S_{xy}$ is the sum of products of the deviations of $x_i$ and $y_i$ from their respective means, that is

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xy} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))(y_{i} - y^(―))
\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the sample means $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}{:}$

$$
\overline{x} = \dfrac{15+12+13+16+19}{5} = 15
$$

$$
\overline{y} = \dfrac{8+13+6+15+13}{5} = 11
$$

Next, we calculate the differences between the $x_i$ and $\overline{x}$, $y_i$ and $\overline{y}$, and their product.

| **$\, x_i \,$** | $15$ | $12$ | $13$ | $16$ | $19$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **$\, y_i \,$** | $8$ | $13$ | $6$ | $15$ | $13$ |
| **$\, (x_i - \overline{x}) \,$** | $0$ | $-3$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $4$ |
| **$\, (y_i - \overline{y}) \,$** | $-3$ | $2$ | $-5$ | $4$ | $2$ |
| **$\, (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y}) \,$** | $0$ | $-6$ | $10$ | $4$ | $8$ |

Therefore, $S_{xy}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Cov(x, y) &= \frac{S_{xy}}{n}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $S_{xy}$ is the sum of products of the deviations of $x_i$ and $y_i$ from their means.

We are given that

$$
S_{xy} = 105
$$

Substituting the given statistic in the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
Cov(x, y) &= \frac{105}{35} \\
&= 3
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186204447 :question/id #uuid "afdb8bbd-524e-51f7-9c62-e82eb0471ab9" :question/math-academy-id "q-251494" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186204009 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "714000f9-caea-57a3-a8cb-6b8ec99960d1" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Variance and Covariance"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/id #uuid "c3a9827c-70b6-579a-935a-7abd7d1f3f4c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186202613}] :question/problem "Consider two sets of $25$ paired observations $x_{1}, x_{2}, …, x_{25}$, and $y_{1}, y_{2}, …, y_{25}$. $$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xx} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))^{2} \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{n}(∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

First, we calculate the sum of the $x_i$ data:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 10 + 9 + 8 + 8 + 5 = 40
$$

We are given that

$$
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^5 x_i^2 = 334
$$

Finally, by substituting into the above formula, we get

$$
S_{xx} =334 - \dfrac{1}{5}(40)^2 = 334- 320 = 14
$$"} {:db/id 17592186204442 :question/id #uuid "2e106c63-c0cc-5875-983c-f82c045e7559" :question/math-academy-id "q-251426"} {:db/id 17592186204455 :question/id #uuid "d73c45cf-d35a-5a29-81ab-7afc1b61c919" :question/math-academy-id "q-251897" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186204010 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1f0ed04b-f011-5818-952d-425a19e0cd5c" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Sums of Squares Using the Shortcut Formula"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d5544d61-e326-5e3f-bea4-a9593f319c11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "S_{yy} = 122" :db/id 17592186202724} {:answer/id #uuid "e5ea1675-2889-50cc-87bc-e2975c9701c0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "S_{yy} = 20" :db/id 17592186202725} {:answer/id #uuid "f75224cc-0a6c-51f7-ab71-7d74d64e6411" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "S_{yy} = 32" :db/id 17592186202726} {:answer/id #uuid "5e621d81-f488-505d-bab7-8c66bb6c7b75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "S_{yy} = 74.2" :db/id 17592186202727} {:answer/id #uuid "65c6c410-f6fd-58c6-a211-1416b4826272" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "S_{yy} = 16.5" :db/id 17592186202728}] :answer-field/id #uuid "f9735c4d-3772-5da2-be56-9a65ca5a65cd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186202723}] :question/problem "Consider the two sets of $5$ paired observations shown in the table below.

$$
\begin{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xy} &= 2964 - \frac{1}{30}(315)(278) \\

&= 45
\end{aligned}

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186204875 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205125 :tutorial/content "Given a data set $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$, we know that its variance, which we may denote as $\sigma_x^2$, is given by

$$
\sigma_x^2 = \dfrac1n \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline x)^2
$$

where $\overline x$ is the mean of $x$.

The summation term

$$
S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline x)^2
$$

is known as a **sum of squares** and is denoted $S_{xx}$. As we'll see, this quantity often appears in statistical analysis, so giving it a separate notation is useful.

Similarly, if we have a data set $y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_n$, then we define

$$
S_{yy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \overline y)^2
$$

Now, suppose we have the bivariate data set
$(x_1, y_1), \qquad (x_2, y_2),\qquad \ldots, \qquad (x_n, y_n)$.
Then, the covariance is given by

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = \dfrac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline x)(y_i - \overline y)
$$

and we may define $S_{xy}$ as

$$
S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \overline{x})(y_i - \overline{y})
$$

Finally, we can define the variance and covariance in terms of $S_{xx}, S_{yy}$, and $S_{xy}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
σ_{x}^{2} &= \frac{S_{xx}}{n}, σ_{y}^{2} = \frac{S_{yy}}{n}, Cov(x, y) = \frac{S_{xy}}{n}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f7e454c5-fb32-5adc-b4bd-0eb93ccd4ce7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10575 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "780a886e-f7ec-5134-8c19-6ef13b7e6958" :step/math-academy-id 226927 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204876}} {:db/id 17592186204876 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204008 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203803 :question/id #uuid "6f0e3d4b-943b-5710-a996-ac4d3c68778d" :question/math-academy-id "e-16399"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d0afa4d8-6d02-52c6-9836-12089de8f406" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048914} {:db/id 17592186049126}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204443} {:db/id 17592186204444}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Sums of Squares Given a Dataset or Summary Statistics"} :step/id #uuid "c4508f2d-5b01-5156-a636-efc40f9518ac" :step/math-academy-id 226928 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204877}} {:db/id 17592186204877 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204009 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203805 :question/id #uuid "7daa2313-4672-5624-aac2-e3b87b6ec366" :question/math-academy-id "e-16401"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "714000f9-caea-57a3-a8cb-6b8ec99960d1" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204447} {:db/id 17592186204448}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Variance and Covariance"} :step/id #uuid "b96fcd87-a442-5e10-907a-17ae7bf45eef" :step/math-academy-id 226931 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204878}} {:db/id 17592186204878 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205126 :tutorial/content "Calculating $S_{xx}, S_{yy}$, and $S_{xy}$ using their definitions can be cumbersome. Thankfully, we have the following shortcut formulas:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xx} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{n}(∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2} \\
S_{yy} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)y_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{n}(∑_(i = 1)^(n)y_{i})^{2} \\
S_{xy} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}y_{i} - \frac{1}{n}(∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})(∑_(i = 1)^(n)y_{i})
\end{aligned}
$$

We'll prove these at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "c497f58a-e56b-5fde-9a53-c8553e8dcbcf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10576 :tutorial/title "Shortcut Formulas"} :step/id #uuid "d1fb1eb8-ff7c-5cd3-b9e5-580d6a2360ac" :step/math-academy-id 226934 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204879}} {:db/id 17592186204879 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204010 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203806 :question/id #uuid "9804df95-f494-5d99-acbd-97c69344d401" :question/math-academy-id "e-16402"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1f0ed04b-f011-5818-952d-425a19e0cd5c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204442} {:db/id 17592186204455}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Sums of Squares Using the Shortcut Formula"} :step/id #uuid "88b4bb82-3260-512d-b14c-8e8a43f1aaa4" :step/math-academy-id 226935 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204880}} {:db/id 17592186204880 :step/content {:db/id 17592186204011 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186203804 :question/id #uuid "489e5ffd-9e78-567b-b009-25d0c004825a" :question/math-academy-id "e-16400"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "83df73fc-c0cc-5605-9b39-453de0c37cc7" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186204445} {:db/id 17592186204446} {:db/id 17592186233680}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating S(x,y) Using the Shortcut Formula"} :step/id #uuid "9f0e96ac-7d59-5c73-8d5d-f336df384031" :step/math-academy-id 226938 :step/next {:db/id 17592186204881}} {:db/id 17592186204881 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205148 :tutorial/content "We wish to prove that

$$
S_{xx} = ∑_(i)x_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{n}(∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2}
$$

We start with the definition of $S_{xx}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xx} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

First, we expand the binomial:

$$
∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i}^{2} - 2x_{i} \cdot x^(―) + x^(―)^{2})
$$

Distributing the summation, we have

$$
∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)2x_{i} \cdot x^(―) + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x^(―)^{2}
$$

Now, since $2, \overline x$, and $\overline{x}^2$ are constants, we can write this as

$$
∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - 2x^(―) \cdot ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + x^(―)^{2} \cdot ∑_(i = 1)^(n)1
$$

Next, we use the following results:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = n\overline x, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n 1 = n
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xx} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - 2x^(―) \cdot nx^(―) + x^(―)^{2} \cdot n \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - 2nx^(―)^{2} + nx^(―)^{2} \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - nx^(―)^{2} \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - n \cdot (\frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2} \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - n \cdot \frac{1}{n^{2}} \cdot (∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2} \\
&= ∑_(i)x_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{n}(∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

The proofs for $S_{yy}$ and $S_{xy}$ are similar." :tutorial/id #uuid "7dab2448-da48-5100-9373-89c074ae5326" :tutorial/math-academy-id 10852 :tutorial/title "Proving the Shortcut Formulas"} :step/id #uuid "ddc81863-5abf-5730-bfbc-1afae5ed8857" :step/math-academy-id 226941}] :activity/title "Sums of Squares" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186204149} {:db/id 17592186204875 :step/content {:db/id 17592186205125 :tutorial/content "Given a data set $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$, we know that its variance, which we may denote as $\sigma_x^2$, is given by

$$
S_{xx} = ∑_(i)x_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{n}(∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2}
$$

We start with the definition of $S_{xx}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xx} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

First, we expand the binomial:

$$
∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i}^{2} - 2x_{i} \cdot x^(―) + x^(―)^{2})
$$

Distributing the summation, we have

$$
∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - ∑_(i = 1)^(n)2x_{i} \cdot x^(―) + ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x^(―)^{2}
$$

Now, since $2, \overline x$, and $\overline{x}^2$ are constants, we can write this as

$$
∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - 2x^(―) \cdot ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i} + x^(―)^{2} \cdot ∑_(i = 1)^(n)1
$$

Next, we use the following results:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = n\overline x, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n 1 = n
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xx} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - 2x^(―) \cdot nx^(―) + x^(―)^{2} \cdot n \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - 2nx^(―)^{2} + nx^(―)^{2} \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - nx^(―)^{2} \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - n \cdot (\frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2} \\
&= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i}^{2} - n \cdot \frac{1}{n^{2}} \cdot (∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2} \\
&= ∑_(i)x_{i}^{2} - \frac{1}{n}(∑_(i = 1)^(n)x_{i})^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

as required.

17592186189373 :tutorial/content "A set of random variables is said to be **independent and identically distributed** (or **I.I.D.**) if the random variables are mutually independent and have the same probability distribution.

When we conduct a random sample of size $n$ from a population, the sample elements

$$
X_1,\quad X_2,\quad \ldots,\quad X_n
$$

are often considered to be I.I.D. random variables. This assumption often allows us to simplify the statistical analysis. 

Suppose that the random variables $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are I.I.D, where

$$
X_i\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i \leq n.
$$

Let's consider their sum

$$
Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots + X_n.
$$

Since each $X_i$ is normally distributed, it follows that $Y$ is normally distributed as well. Moreover, we can compute the mean and the variance of $Y$ as follows:

- Calculating the mean using the properties of expectation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+\text{E}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{E}[{X}_{n}] \\  & =\mu +\mu +⋯+\mu  \\  & =n\mu .\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, using the properties of variance, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\  & =\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{Var}[{X}_{n}] \\  & ={\sigma }^{2}+{\sigma }^{2}+⋯+{\sigma }^{2} \\  & =n{\sigma }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).
$$

We will soon use this important result to develop models of how random samples are distributed. But for now, let's practice working with I.I.D normal random variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "6bb107aa-ee09-57fa-9b9a-f4267b123dac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6260 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "791c1871-8fb1-51ca-a60a-df0bdf72b5f4" :step/math-academy-id 37959 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189101}}] :activity/title "I.I.D Normal Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186188454} {:db/id 17592186189102 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189373 :tutorial/content "A set of random variables is said to be **independent and identically distributed** (or **I.I.D.**) if the random variables are mutually independent and have the same probability distribution.

When we conduct a random sample of size $n$ from a population, the sample elements

$$
X_1,\quad X_2,\quad \ldots,\quad X_n
$$

are often considered to be I.I.D. random variables. This assumption often allows us to simplify the statistical analysis. 

Suppose that the random variables $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are I.I.D, where

$$
X_i\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i \leq n.
$$

Let's consider their sum

$$
Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots + X_n.
$$

Since each $X_i$ is normally distributed, it follows that $Y$ is normally distributed as well. Moreover, we can compute the mean and the variance of $Y$ as follows:

- Calculating the mean using the properties of expectation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+\text{E}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{E}[{X}_{n}] \\  & =\mu +\mu +⋯+\mu  \\  & =n\mu .\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).

:step/math-academy-id 37958 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189083}} {:db/id 17592186189373 :tutorial/content "A set of random variables is said to be **independent and identically distributed** (or **I.I.D.**) if the random variables are mutually independent and have the same probability distribution.

When we conduct a random sample of size $n$ from a population, the sample elements

$$
X_1,\quad X_2,\quad \ldots,\quad X_n
$$

are often considered to be I.I.D. random variables. This assumption often allows us to simplify the statistical analysis. 

Suppose that the random variables $X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n$ are I.I.D, where

$$
X_i\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad 1\leq i \leq n.
$$

Let's consider their sum

$$
Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots + X_n.
$$

Since each $X_i$ is normally distributed, it follows that $Y$ is normally distributed as well. Moreover, we can compute the mean and the variance of $Y$ as follows:

- Calculating the mean using the properties of expectation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y] & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}_{1}]+\text{E}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{E}[{X}_{n}] \\  & =\mu +\mu +⋯+\mu  \\  & =n\mu .\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, using the properties of variance, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[Y] & =\text{Var}[{X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}] \\  & =\text{Var}[{X}_{1}]+\text{Var}[{X}_{2}]+⋯+\text{Var}[{X}_{n}] \\  & ={\sigma }^{2}+{\sigma }^{2}+⋯+{\sigma }^{2} \\  & =n{\sigma }^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
Y = X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n\sim N(n\mu, n\sigma^2).
$$

We will soon use this important result to develop models of how random samples are distributed. But for now, let's practice working with I.I.D normal random variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "6bb107aa-ee09-57fa-9b9a-f4267b123dac" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6260 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186050707 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429566 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency.
