:question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)+3,\end{aligned}\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="180px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>

<td align="center">$\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector.

$$

$$

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$

$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$, $\text{L5}$, and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}.$"} {:db/id 17592186311584 :question/id #uuid "cebeb12c-43d2-5e26-85a3-7ca87fc81d5a" 17592186229982 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230191 :tutorial/content "Matrix exponentials can be used for solving *inhomogeneous systems* of ODEs as well. Consider the system

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t),
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix, and suppose we are given an initial condition $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$.

Our goal is to derive the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system.

First, we eliminate the *inhomogeneous term* by a change of variables. We define

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t)
$$

and differentiate it using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =\cancel{-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+\cancel{A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)}+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate both sides from $t_0$ to $t$ and get

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t_0)=\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Next, since $\mathbf{y}(t_0)=e^{-A(t_0-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(t_0),$ we have

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Finally, we convert back to the initial variable $\mathbf{x}(t).$ To do that we multiply both sides by $e^{A(t-t_0)}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\ x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to our IVP is

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where the first term represents the solution of the corresponding *homogeneous system*, and the second term gives a particular solution of our *inhomogeneous system*.

Let's see some concrete examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "ff1bfa7f-286f-5481-8170-effabae1aa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14524 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :question/math-academy-id "q-335166" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)+4,\end{aligned}\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">$\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr><tr>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "06d91f07-0fea-5beb-aa8a-cd77b3e6a896" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495188}} {:db/id 17592186495188 :step/content {:db/id 17592186396735 :question/answer-fields $\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$"} :step/id #uuid "2231ccca-1dd5-57de-b365-dbd0a5f43637" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495250}} {:db/id 17592186495193 :step/content {:db/id 17592186308718 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c139fc5d-402e-5c97-b048-caf60e14b36c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{sin}(2t)-\operatorname{cos}(2t)+3" :db/id 17592186306955} {:answer/id #uuid "6963f53e-90b3-59a4-b3ac-6bc885da9965" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\cos(2t)+2\sin(2t)" :db/id 17592186494533}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494533} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b933995-aeb2-5960-92c8-2edb1a0843a3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307958}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "03656a1f-f3fa-5cdf-b35f-3b5febfaad49" :question/math-academy-id "q-335054" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$

$$

$$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)+4,\end{aligned}\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ 4\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)-1 \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "06d91f07-0fea-5beb-aa8a-cd77b3e6a896" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495188}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6b596b99-7294-5ff0-b898-15ee8d9ff660" :answer/type {:db/id $\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$"} :step/id #uuid "2231ccca-1dd5-57de-b365-dbd0a5f43637" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495250}} "df39ea77-8f8f-5eba-a555-091c65f07d44" :question/math-academy-id "q-335404" :question/problem "Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-At}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$"} :step/id #uuid "c5aef665-a069-598d-9521-f09b9a91fe69"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c139fc5d-402e-5c97-b048-caf60e14b36c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{sin}(2t)-\operatorname{cos}(2t)+3" :db/id 17592186306955} {:answer/id #uuid "6963f53e-90b3-59a4-b3ac-6bc885da9965" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\cos(2t)+2\sin(2t)" :db/id 17592186494533}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494533} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b933995-aeb2-5960-92c8-2edb1a0843a3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307958} {:answer/id #uuid "c139fc5d-402e-5c97-b048-caf60e14b36c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{sin}(2t)-\operatorname{cos}(2t)+3" :db/id 17592186306955} {:answer/id #uuid "6963f53e-90b3-59a4-b3ac-6bc885da9965" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3-\cos(2t)+2\sin(2t)" :db/id 17592186494533} {:db/id 17592186495196 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495074 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c02e4fa5-edc3-5680-b383-eb861b94c2ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1" :db/id 17592186494771}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186494771} :answer-field/id #uuid "8e66a9d5-c3d1-5ab6-8270-3abb2df59cb7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186494982}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "30dbc074-1ece-5bdf-8ee0-957449e10161" :question/math-academy-id "q-335068" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=7y(t)+7 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-7x(t),\end{aligned}\,\begin{bmatrix}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix},$ where $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$*

<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $g(t)=\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 7 \\ -7 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\begin{bmatrix}7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -7\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}\text{d}s \\  & ={\begin{bmatrix}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(7(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡(7(t-s))\end{bmatrix}}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)-1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2fbeaf38-2336-5aee-bfc1-de7e502565a2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186495181}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c02e4fa5-edc3-5680-b383-eb861b94c2ae" :answer/type {:db/id :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281175}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-8{y}^{2}$ given that ${x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}\le 25.$ 

*Hint: The critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region ${x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}<25$ is $(0,0).$*" :question/worked-solution "We are given that the critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region's interior is $(0,0).$

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}=25.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=25
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-16y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,10y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=2\lambda x \\ -16y=10\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2x(1-\lambda )=0 \\ -2y(8+5\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,y=\pm \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,x=\pm 5,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(\pm 5,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),\,(5,0),\,(0,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm \sqrt{5})$ | $(\pm 5,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $-40$ | $25$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),$ and its minimum value is $-40.$"} {:db/id 17592186281544 :question/id #uuid "6c8aaf19-7032-5c17-8488-1228e55d6f6b" Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}8x & =2\lambda x \\ 20y & =2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}x(4-\lambda )=0 \\ y(10-\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,y=\pm 2,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(0,\pm 2).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,x=\pm 2,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm 2),\,(\pm 2,0),\,(0,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm 2)$ | $(\pm 2,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $40$ | $16$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(0,2)$ and $(0,-2),$ and its maximum value is $40.$"} {:db/id 17592186363465 :question/id #uuid "0965ed17-df89-5de8-b0cd-60d291248cdf" :db/id 17592186281055}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the minimum possible sum of three positive numbers whose product is $27.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the three numbers. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+y+z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=27.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=27
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda yz \\ 1=\lambda xz \\ 1=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $1=0.$ Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}yz & =xz \\ yz-xz & =0 \\ (y-x)z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =27 \\ x(x)(x) & =27 \\ {x}^{3} & =27 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(3,3,3),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(3,3,3)=3+3+3=9.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(9,3,1) & =9+3+1 \\  & =13 \\  & >f(3,3,3).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362342 :question/id #uuid "1ec51af1-dbfa-5fa9-8f74-3c330eb163be" :question/math-academy-id "q-99163" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198367 :knowledge-point/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "A rectangular parallelepiped has a volume of $125\,{\text{in}}^{3}.$ Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, determine the minimum sum of the lengths of its edges." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the rectangular parallelepiped's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=4x+4y+4z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=125.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=125
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨4,4,4⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4=\lambda yz \\ 4=\lambda xz \\ 4=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4x=\lambda xyz \\ 4y=\lambda xyz \\ 4z=\lambda xyz\end{aligned}
$$

This gives $x=y=z.$

Now, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =125 \\ x(x)(x) & =125 \\ {x}^{3} & =125 \\ x & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(5,5,5),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(5,5,5)=4(5)+4(5)+4(5)=60\,\text{in}.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(25,5,1) & =4(25)+4(5)+4(1) \\  & =121 \\  & >f(5,5,5).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364648 :question/id #uuid "9021d181-6a6e-589c-8096-c7ad92921266" :question/math-academy-id "q-99230" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198367 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "849449fb-bb08-54a3-b8ea-9f33ddd7a3e5" :knowledge-point/title "Solving Optimization Problems in Context"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f027768c-f196-5e3f-adf4-7554b2177b3b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "243\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364650} {:answer/id #uuid "f96459e6-4979-5896-b4e6-40cb50e3fdd2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "162\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364651} {:answer/id #uuid "5fe9f1a7-0904-5a92-b9f4-1e7ca2a2d4bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "128\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364652} {:answer/id #uuid "dc20d337-eb61-592e-aeed-865846e45bfb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "369\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364653} {:answer/id #uuid "42cfec62-7180-5eb9-8dbb-e33d7fe7ecf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "192\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364654}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "42cfec62-7180-5eb9-8dbb-e33d7fe7ecf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "192\,{\text{ft}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186364654} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ae58a56-6faf-52c9-9561-c87d35603ea0" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186364649}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "A rectangular metal tank without a lid should hold $256\,{\text{ft}}^{3}$ of liquid. Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the tank's minimum possible surface area." :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the tank's length, width, and height, respectively. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=xy+2xz+2yz,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=256.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=256
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨y+2z,x+2z,2x+2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y+2z=\lambda yz \\ x+2z=\lambda xz \\ 2x+2y=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the first, second, and third equations by $x,y,$ and $z$ respectively, we get the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x(y+2z)=\lambda xyz \\ y(x+2z)=\lambda xyz \\ z(2x+2y)=\lambda xyz\end{aligned}
$$

From the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x(y+2z) & =y(x+2z) \\ xy+2xz & =xy+2yz \\ 2xz & =2yz \\ 2z(x-y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $x=y=2z.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =256 \\ (2z)(2z)z & =256 \\ 4{z}^{3} & =256 \\ {z}^{3} & =64 \\ z & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(8,8,4),$ and the minimum value is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(8,8,4)=8(8)+2(8)(4)+2(8)(4)=192\,{\text{ft}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(16,16,1) & =(16)(16)+2(16)(1)+2(16)(1) \\  & =320 \\  & >f(8,8,4).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186395878 :question/id #uuid "b8d6d6ad-6f2f-560c-8794-1cc77ef79232" :question/math-academy-id "q-37959"} {:db/id 17592186399343 :question/id #uuid We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨1,-2y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=4
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨1,-2y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}1=2\lambda x \\ -2y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\lambda x=\frac{1}{2} \\ y(1+\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =4\,⇒\,x=\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(\pm 2,0).$

- Assuming $\lambda =-1$ in the second equation of the system, the first equation of the system gives 

$$
-x=\frac{1}{2}\,⇒\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
Then, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=4$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4\,⇒\,y=\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\pm 2,0),\,(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}).
$$

 

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(2,0)$ | $(-2,0)$ | $(-\frac{1}{2},\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $-2$ | $-\frac{17}{4}$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(2,0),$ and its maximum value is $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186281551 :question/id #uuid "172e1cdb-aee2-5490-b82d-56a90e36d5c9" :question/math-academy-id #uuid "b82b3836-2ed6-522e-8a6b-e9301766e38d" :step/math-academy-id 32293} {:db/id 17592186199326 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199484 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the minimum and maximum values of the function

$$
f(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2
$$

subject to constraint $g(x,y) = x^2+y^2 \leq 1.$ In other words, we wish to find the global extrema of $f(x,y)$ defined on the disc of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown below.

![](images/5a/5ac34145b3911b19eb3775a915e8f0462c78502be6d6292e7682265c86eafce7.png)

  

To find the extrema, we proceed as follows:

- First, we find the critical points of $f$ inside the domain $x^2+y^2 < 1.$

- Then, we find the extreme values of $f$ subject to the constraint $x^2+y^2=1$ using the method of Lagrange multipliers.

- Finally, we determine the maximum and minimum values by evaluating $f$ at the candidate points.

Recall that the critical points of a function $f(x,y)$ are the solutions to $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf 0^T.$ Now, since the derivative of $f$ is the transpose of its gradient $\nabla f,$ the critical points are also given by the solutions to $\nabla f = \mathbf 0.$

So, we can find the critical points by solving $\nabla f = \mathbf 0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=(0,0).$ Note that this point belongs to our domain.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)= x^2 + y^2  = 1.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4x=2\lambda x \\ 8y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(2-\lambda )=0 \\ y(4-\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,y=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(0,\pm 1 \right).$

- Assuming $\lambda =2$ in the first equation, the second equation of the system implies

$$
\begin{aligned}y(4-2)=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,x=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $\left(\pm 1, 0 \right).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\pm 1, 0), \qquad (0, \pm1), \qquad (0,0).
$$

Note that we add the critical point $(0,0)$ to the list of the candidates above.

Finally, we evaluate $f$ at these points: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(\pm 1,0)$ | $(0, \pm 1)$ | $(0, 0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $4$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum of $0$ at the point $(0, 0)$ and a maximum of $4$ at the points $(0, \pm 1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7cc22f9f-d1be-570d-acd7-d3f2e0af7a51" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7743 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7bbfb776-26d8-5be7-abb8-cae6bab3294c" :step/math-academy-id 44831 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199327}} {:db/id 17592186199327 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198405 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198047 :question/id #uuid "fb947756-3471-59c8-b3c4-9b21a1a91557" :question/math-academy-id "e-12457"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9bbc1e6a-c728-5c5a-84f8-06a92c30a023" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049390}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198946} {:db/id 17592186199016} {:db/id 17592186281548} {:db/id 17592186281551} {:db/id 17592186281552} {:db/id 17592186362346} {:db/id 17592186362354} {:db/id 17592186363472} {:db/id 17592186446811} {:db/id 17592186446813} {:db/id 17592186446817} {:db/id 17592186496295}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Extreme Values: Cases With No Inner Critical Points"} :step/id #uuid "0e5ab67d-1254-5853-868a-8e8a117b0032" :step/math-academy-id 44833 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199263}}] :activity/title "Optimizing Multivariable Functions Using Lagrange Multipliers" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198494} {:db/id 17592186199326 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199484 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the minimum and maximum values of the function

:step/math-academy-id 32293} {:db/id 17592186199484 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the minimum and maximum values of the function

$$
f(x,y) = 2x^2+4y^2
$$

subject to constraint $g(x,y) = x^2+y^2 \leq 1.$ In other words, we wish to find the global extrema of $f(x,y)$ defined on the disc of radius $1$ centered at the origin, as shown below.

![](images/5a/5ac34145b3911b19eb3775a915e8f0462c78502be6d6292e7682265c86eafce7.png)

  

To find the extrema, we proceed as follows:

- First, we find the critical points of $f$ inside the domain $x^2+y^2 < 1.$

- Then, we find the extreme values of $f$ subject to the constraint $x^2+y^2=1$ using the method of Lagrange multipliers.

- Finally, we determine the maximum and minimum values by evaluating $f$ at the candidate points.

Recall that the critical points of a function $f(x,y)$ are the solutions to $\boldsymbol f'(x,y) = \mathbf 0^T.$ Now, since the derivative of $f$ is the transpose of its gradient $\nabla f,$ the critical points are also given by the solutions to $\nabla f = \mathbf 0.$

So, we can find the critical points by solving $\nabla f = \mathbf 0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has the solution $(x,y)=(0,0).$ Note that this point belongs to our domain.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)= x^2 + y^2  = 1.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨4x,8y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}4x=2\lambda x \\ 8y=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x(2-\lambda )=0 \\ y(4-\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,y=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical points $\left(0,\pm 1 \right).$

- Assuming $\lambda =2$ in the first equation, the second equation of the system implies

$$
\begin{aligned}y(4-2)=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the constraint condition $x^2+y^2=1$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{0}^{2} & =1\,⇒\,x=\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $\left(\pm 1, 0 \right).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(\pm 1, 0), \qquad (0, \pm1), \qquad (0,0).
$$

Note that we add the critical point $(0,0)$ to the list of the candidates above.

Finally, we evaluate $f$ at these points: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(\pm 1,0)$ | $(0, \pm 1)$ | $(0, 0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $2$ | $4$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum of $0$ at the point $(0, 0)$ and a maximum of $4$ at the points $(0, \pm 1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7cc22f9f-d1be-570d-acd7-d3f2e0af7a51" :question/math-academy-id "q-162780" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum value of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-8{y}^{2}$ given that ${x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}\le 25.$ 

*Hint: The critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region ${x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}<25$ is $(0,0).$*" :question/worked-solution "We are given that the critical point of $f(x,y)$ in the region's interior is $(0,0).$

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}=25.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y),\,g(x,y)=25
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨2x,-16y⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,10y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x=2\lambda x \\ -16y=10\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2x(1-\lambda )=0 \\ -2y(8+5\lambda )=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this system, we break it up into several cases:

- Assuming $x=0$ in the first equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,y=\pm \sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}).$

- Assuming $y=0$ in the second equation of the system, the constraint condition $g(x,y)=25$ implies

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & =25\,⇒\,x=\pm 5,\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the critical point $(\pm 5,0).$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),\,(5,0),\,(0,0).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,\pm \sqrt{5})$ | $(\pm 5,0)$ | $(0,0)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,f(x,y)\,$ | $-40$ | $25$ | $0$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(0,\pm \sqrt{5}),$ and its minimum value is $-40.$"} :step/id #uuid "09e7c588-2af6-5084-a29b-554d52342a46" :step/next {:db/id 17592186496344}} {:db/id 17592186496344 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281547 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18f121e3-ccfa-57b8-b6ef-a2e2cd0f3b57" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186278810} {:answer/id #uuid "65b8a4fe-1d29-5ee2-ad9f-6c0583668e1c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186279516} {:answer/id #uuid "76c3a733-f198-5a7c-a7fb-0c39f1adc2a4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13" :db/id 17592186279650} {:answer/id #uuid "8bf6ea47-eaeb-5270-89ec-aea8d1830cbc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186279837} {:answer/id #uuid "944923f9-e97d-5493-8850-5c83f2a0ed3e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "29" :db/id 17592186279911}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279516} :answer-field/id #uuid "797a794d-3c44-5cfd-9959-01ae83cb5934" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281055}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b8c68071-089c-5bff-bc03-ba61a8eab03b" :question/math-academy-id "q-162788" :question/problem "Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the minimum possible sum of three positive numbers whose product is $27.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the three numbers. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+y+z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=27.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=27
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda yz \\ 1=\lambda xz \\ 1=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $1=0.$ Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}yz & =xz \\ yz-xz & =0 \\ (y-x)z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =27 \\ x(x)(x) & =27 \\ {x}^{3} & =27 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(3,3,3),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(3,3,3)=3+3+3=9.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(9,3,1) & =9+3+1 \\  & =13 \\  & >f(3,3,3).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4eb40113-e4c3-5ada-8661-3205e80bd911" :step/next {:db/id 17592186496379}} {:db/id 17592186496354 :step/content {:db/id 17592186496295 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2581670b-66e9-5d37-9926-806360eb8f15" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "50" :db/id 17592186495594} {:answer/id #uuid "280f9803-91c8-596b-9d69-7a1755e015d0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186495597} {:answer/id #uuid "4d7fc2e4-a9ae-57b1-a57d-6f3e9b58edf7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186495688} {:answer/id #uuid "5b25f91e-47c0-5de9-8785-cc22a420cdde" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "45" :db/id 17592186495717} {:answer/id #uuid "b0a20fa1-2478-557f-919f-c382ef996ee9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186495905}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186495594} :answer-field/id #uuid "bd28c84e-3672-589b-b259-7ab643cdcbfc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186496168}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a8d5ef6c-fa65-5bc9-a3b7-421525094db4" :question/math-academy-id "q-99271" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)=y-3x$ given that  ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 250.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩ \\ ⟨-3,1⟩ & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the maximum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=250.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=250
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨-3,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨2x,2y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-3=2\lambda x \\ 1=2\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{3}{2\lambda } \\ y=\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=-3y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-3y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =250 \\ 9{y}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =250 \\ {y}^{2} & =25 \\ y & =\pm 5\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=-3y=∓15.
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(-15,5),\,(15,-5).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y)$ | $(-15,5)$ | $(15,-5)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $50$ | $-50$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a maximum value at $(-15,5),$ and its maximum value is $50.$"} :step/id #uuid "698d6400-2972-5372-825e-a45e8f947672" :step/next {:db/id 17592186496355}} {:db/id 17592186496355 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362354 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5c47837c-91e7-575e-bb0e-eeba6e46e885" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186361251} {:answer/id #uuid "70afc2df-aa10-56b3-bc23-c23074c89c0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186361336} {:answer/id #uuid "8c0908b9-98ee-5adc-877d-81b2bba50711" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186361454} {:answer/id #uuid "9d6f809c-461e-5ba5-8943-29549871ecb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "35" :db/id 17592186361544} {:answer/id #uuid "b782daff-1cbf-5514-ba1c-f04c88f0cadf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{35}" :db/id 17592186361656}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186361544} :answer-field/id #uuid "69b59c33-2059-5031-b6c9-48e74e90a78e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186362072}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "7eb8a72b-0beb-5d49-b077-ac32cdeca74e" :question/math-academy-id "q-99274" :question/problem "Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum value of the function $f(x,y)=8x-3y$ given that $2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}\le 35.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the critical values of the function in the region's interior. We compute the critical points by solving $∇f=0,$ as follows:

$$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=35.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=35
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨8,-3⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,6y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}8=4\lambda x \\ -3=6\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{2}{\lambda } \\ y=-\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=-4y\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-4y$ into the condition $g(x,y)=35,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =35 \\ 32{y}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =35 \\ {y}^{2} & =1 \\ y & =\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=-4y=∓4.
$$

$$
(-4,1),\,(4,-1).

| $(x,y)$ | $(-4,1)$ | $(4,-1)$ |

:question/worked-solution "Let $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ be the three numbers. We wish to minimize the function

$$
f(x,y,z)=x+y+z,
$$

subject to the constraint 

$$
xyz=27.
$$

Note that we also have the constraints $x>0,y>0,z>0.$

Let $g(x,y,z)=xyz.$ Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z),\,g(x,y,z)=27
$$

We start by solving the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y,z),{f}_{y}(x,y,z),{f}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y,z),{g}_{y}(x,y,z),{g}_{z}(x,y,z)⟩ \\ ⟨1,1,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨yz,xz,xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1=\lambda yz \\ 1=\lambda xz \\ 1=\lambda xy\end{aligned}
$$

We cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this would give $1=0.$ Therefore, from the first and second equations above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}yz & =xz \\ yz-xz & =0 \\ (y-x)z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $z>0,$ we can conclude that $x=y.$

Similarly, from the second and third equations, we get that $z=y=x.$ So, using the constraint equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}xyz & =27 \\ x(x)(x) & =27 \\ {x}^{3} & =27 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is reached at the point $(3,3,3),$ and the minimum value is 

$$
f(3,3,3)=3+3+3=9.
$$

**Note:** It's easy to show that the obtained point is indeed the minimum (and not the maximum). To do that, we could compare the value of the function at this point with the value of the function at any other (arbitrary) point belonging to the domain. For example, 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(9,3,1) & =9+3+1 \\  & =13 \\  & >f(3,3,3).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4eb40113-e4c3-5ada-8661-3205e80bd911" :step/next {:db/id 17592186496379}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18f121e3-ccfa-57b8-b6ef-a2e2cd0f3b57" :answer/type {:db/id $$

Since the above equation has no solutions, we conclude that the function does not have critical values in the region's interior.

Next, we need to find the minimum value of $f(x,y)$ subject to the constraint $g(x,y)=2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=35.$ 

Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
∇f(x,y)=\lambda ∇g(x,y)\,g(x,y)=35
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,) \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(x,y),{f}_{y}(x,y)⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x}(x,y),{g}_{y}(x,y)⟩ \\ ⟨8,-3⟩ & =\lambda ⟨4x,6y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we cannot have $\lambda =0$ since this leads to a contradiction in the above equation. Therefore, assuming $\lambda \ne 0,$ we have the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}8=4\lambda x \\ -3=6\lambda y\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{2}{\lambda } \\ y=-\frac{1}{2\lambda }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,x=-4y\end{aligned}

x=-4y=∓4.

$$
(-4,1),\,(4,-1).

| $(x,y)$ | $(-4,1)$ | $(4,-1)$ |

:answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186271698}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find ${C}^{36},$ where

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $C:$

$$
C={{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $C=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${C}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{C}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{36} & =P{D}^{36}{P}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{bmatrix}}^{36}(\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}(\sqrt[18]{3})^{36} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[36]{3})^{36}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{3}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}27 & -3 \\ -27 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}15 & 6 \\ -12 & -3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186323922 :question/id #uuid "2975c4f9-6dee-5125-bb13-6ec3dea74ab8" :question/math-academy-id "q-37601"} {:db/id 17592186323925 :question/id #uuid "2c8cda82-c43a-5e00-b3a6-861564481ae4" :question/math-academy-id "q-37625"} {:db/id 17592186323927 :question/id #uuid "15dbc732-faa8-5570-a378-0344cccc0dac" :question/math-academy-id "q-37630"} {:db/id 17592186354492 :question/id #uuid "18c9e3a0-322a-5b85-8d72-26e41db87e30" :question/math-academy-id "q-86682" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0838f7e1-1e2a-5de4-899d-0534f10f1b2b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186351641} {:answer/id #uuid "4bdae80f-03b9-55c3-aadd-11684fd45d72" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186352262} {:answer/id #uuid "836126d0-86c5-54f1-8f69-77f8c1c3afc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186352716} {:answer/id #uuid "e3a16fcf-857f-5b60-adf6-cb3cf7586045" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186353550} {:answer/id #uuid "f648b42e-29eb-56ba-be95-7cf583a892a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186353717}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186351641} :answer-field/id #uuid "29f200b4-abd8-556b-96a6-d61eebe5f500" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186353886}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find ${A}^{71},$ where

$$

Therefore, $N$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $N$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$$

$$

$$

$$
C={{\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{\begin{bmatrix}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{\begin{bmatrix}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}(-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}10 & 15 \\ 20 & 5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ -2 & 11\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

:topic/math-academy-id 1969} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125419 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125790 :tutorial/content "One useful property of diagonalization is that it allows us to easily determine the power of a matrix.

As an example, we consider the $2\times 2$ matrix ![](images/53/53b7a9efd9f2ae1ef4adc7cee5f86f784722777b8c29f268dbd0e822ff1354f9.svg) with the diagonalization
![](images/e3/e3111a91b80d238cf5255eb9a9884dcd3f80e914039c5e789e32c07b55cf5b06.svg)

We will use the diagonalization of $A$ to compute $A^{55}.$

Let's start by computing $A^2.$ Using the properties of matrix multiplication, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =PD{P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\  & =PD\cancel{{P}^{-1}\cdot P}D{P}^{-1} \\  & =P(DD){P}^{-1} \\  & =P{D}^{2}{P}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $A^3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & ={A}^{2}\cdot A \\  & =P{D}^{2}{P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\  & =P{D}^{2}\cancel{{P}^{-1}\cdot P}D{P}^{-1} \\  & =P({D}^{2}D){P}^{-1} \\  & =P{D}^{3}{P}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that the matrix $P$ and its inverse $P^{-1}$ will always cancel each other out in the middle of the multiplication! So by induction, we have that

$$
A^{\color{blue}55}=P \cdot D^{\color{blue}55} \cdot P^{-1}.
$$

Now, we only need to find $D^{\color{blue}55}.$

Since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ {D}^{3} & ={D}^{2}D=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{3} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Following this pattern, we get

![](images/05/05e10fdc6944077a48b0214a41fae8d418a1b66c8d87a47d652158c84285c246.svg)

Therefore, we can conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{55} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{55}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given that $A = PDP^{-1},$ for any non-negative integer ${\color{blue}k},$ we obtain 

$$
A^{\color{blue}k} = P \cdot D^{\color{blue}k} \cdot P^{-1}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b7628bf0-02d4-514e-a564-669610253cd2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3576 :tutorial/title "Raising a Diagonalizable Matrix to a Power"} :step/id #uuid "934d1edd-bf1c-5c1f-8924-ede352d7d23b" :step/math-academy-id 20121 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125420}} {:db/id 17592186125420 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124530 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124339 :question/id #uuid "dfb93cc8-6bf0-59d4-8fbc-c94f5c0c1a69" :question/math-academy-id "e-5502"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "634729e9-7633-52d8-99fa-b00fc9cbe96a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049125} {:db/id 17592186050446}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125045} {:db/id 17592186125085} {:db/id 17592186272030} {:db/id 17592186323922} {:db/id 17592186323925} {:db/id 17592186323927} {:db/id 17592186354492} {:db/id 17592186354493} {:db/id 17592186379803} {:db/id 17592186388653} {:db/id 17592186392094} {:db/id 17592186394724}] :knowledge-point/title "Raising a Matrix to a Large Power Using the Properties of Diagonalization"} :step/id #uuid "d76255af-54d9-5dcb-9a9c-7b30b6c4a98a" :step/math-academy-id 20122 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125422}} {:db/id 17592186125421 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125791 :tutorial/content "Remember that the diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ and corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors $\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\mathbf{v_2}$ is
![](images/cd/cde63e04857414720bed0cb247e1e0c4bae76b69823f4aeb494cda13c139ac13.svg)

This idea also works in reverse. Given a diagonalization $A$ in the form 

$$
A=PDP^{-1},
$$

 

we can immediately deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are the diagonal entries of $D,$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of $P.$ This is because the diagonalization of a matrix is (almost) unique.

**Note:** The diagonalization is "almost" unique because the order of the eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs may vary, and the eigenvectors may be replaced with scalar multiples of themselves. However, none of these variations change the actual outcome regarding the eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs that we deduce." :tutorial/id #uuid "d23e5c1b-9483-574b-ab9f-f68b126993cd" :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124754} {:db/id 17592186125421 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125791 :tutorial/content "Remember that the diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ and corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors $\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\mathbf{v_2}$ is
![](images/cd/cde63e04857414720bed0cb247e1e0c4bae76b69823f4aeb494cda13c139ac13.svg)

This idea also works in reverse. Given a diagonalization $A$ in the form 

$$
A=PDP^{-1},
$$

 

we can immediately deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are the diagonal entries of $D,$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of $P.$ This is because the diagonalization of a matrix is (almost) unique.

**Note:** The diagonalization is "almost" unique because the order of the eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs may vary, and the eigenvectors may be replaced with scalar multiples of themselves. However, none of these variations change the actual outcome regarding the eigenvalue-eigenvector pairs that we deduce." :tutorial/id #uuid "d23e5c1b-9483-574b-ab9f-f68b126993cd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3577 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6ed440e4-0b21-56bd-92c6-0ef75f28a68c" :step/math-academy-id 20123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125492}} {:db/id 17592186125419 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125790 :tutorial/content "One useful property of diagonalization is that it allows us to easily determine the power of a matrix.

As an example, we consider the $2\times 2$ matrix ![](images/53/53b7a9efd9f2ae1ef4adc7cee5f86f784722777b8c29f268dbd0e822ff1354f9.svg) with the diagonalization
![](images/e3/e3111a91b80d238cf5255eb9a9884dcd3f80e914039c5e789e32c07b55cf5b06.svg)

We will use the diagonalization of $A$ to compute $A^{55}.$

Let's start by computing $A^2.$ Using the properties of matrix multiplication, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =PD{P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\  & =PD\cancel{{P}^{-1}\cdot P}D{P}^{-1} \\  & =P(DD){P}^{-1} \\  & =P{D}^{2}{P}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $A^3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & ={A}^{2}\cdot A \\  & =P{D}^{2}{P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\  & =P{D}^{2}\cancel{{P}^{-1}\cdot P}D{P}^{-1} \\  & =P({D}^{2}D){P}^{-1} \\  & =P{D}^{3}{P}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We see that the matrix $P$ and its inverse $P^{-1}$ will always cancel each other out in the middle of the multiplication! So by induction, we have that

$$
A^{\color{blue}55}=P \cdot D^{\color{blue}55} \cdot P^{-1}.
$$

Now, we only need to find $D^{\color{blue}55}.$

Since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\ {D}^{3} & ={D}^{2}D=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}{1}^{3} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Following this pattern, we get

![](images/05/05e10fdc6944077a48b0214a41fae8d418a1b66c8d87a47d652158c84285c246.svg)

Therefore, we can conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{55} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}}^{55}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, given that $A = PDP^{-1},$ for any non-negative integer ${\color{blue}k},$ we obtain 

$$
A^{\color{blue}k} = P \cdot D^{\color{blue}k} \cdot P^{-1}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b7628bf0-02d4-514e-a564-669610253cd2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3576 :tutorial/title "Raising a Diagonalizable Matrix to a Power"} :step/id #uuid "934d1edd-bf1c-5c1f-8924-ede352d7d23b" :step/math-academy-id 20121 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125420}} {:db/id 17592186125790 :tutorial/content "One useful property of diagonalization is that it allows us to easily determine the power of a matrix.

$$

Computing $A^3,$ we get

Since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we have the following:

$$

$$
