"q-86682" :question/problem "Find ${A}^{71},$ where

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $A:$

$$
A={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{71} & =P{D}^{71}{P}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{71}(\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}(-1)^{71} & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{71}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1ba7f498-1881-5ab1-ad8c-dead16debd6e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186492103}} {:db/id 17592186492090 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323905 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "75e25684-50a9-57d5-a453-f3280d5e984e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$" :db/id 17592186322066} {:answer/id #uuid "8f8f40aa-17fd-543a-b848-7fa918e8d3e6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$" :db/id 17592186322287} {:answer/id #uuid "b4b7aa57-385e-526d-af9f-e30495eb3d9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$" :db/id 17592186322558} {:answer/id #uuid "c02288ab-4da1-566a-bfba-eadf1b8d9b04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}$" :db/id 17592186322639} {:answer/id #uuid "e7df6b33-d577-517b-8051-21b8cf6af137" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$ and $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$" :db/id 17592186322963}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322066} :answer-field/id #uuid "3c700357-79a1-56bc-aa05-cd5a7a8ba8ef" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323288}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "55fe01d2-18d3-58de-b08f-22bbfece1371" :question/math-academy-id "q-37362" :question/problem "Find the eigenvectors of the $2\times 2$ matrix $N$ given that 

$$
N\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), right-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $N:$

$$
N={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $N$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $N$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P:$

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}$"} :step/id #uuid "3bdc3345-f3fe-56c7-9d48-45ed67552ad2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186492080}} {:db/id 17592186492095 :step/content {:db/id 17592186272030 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "02c36a09-640e-5f2f-bee6-5e3ec7470874" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}12 & 9 \\ -24 & -3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186269293} {:answer/id #uuid "3064e2aa-2353-5c23-8c5a-c90a2e00dae4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}15 & 9 \\ -21 & -6\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186269705} {:answer/id #uuid "47e19908-9201-5477-8a4f-5d2e1bcb5a23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ -12 & -9\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186269921} {:answer/id #uuid "6eb22d41-12a9-5433-9689-c05376bd7c15" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}15 & 6 \\ -12 & -3\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186270252} {:answer/id #uuid "918b8499-30b8-5523-aa6d-ee8503603d93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\begin{bmatrix}12 & 6 \\ -18 & -21\end{bmatrix}" :db/id 17592186270536}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186270252} :answer-field/id #uuid "68aed225-1b65-5210-aa67-e6df22bc4d41" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186271698}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a83d9fbf-2f37-5a9f-b9ba-27fe8d23afc4" :question/math-academy-id "q-140132" :question/problem "Find ${C}^{36},$ where

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $C:$

$$
C={{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $C=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${C}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{C}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{2}{3} & \frac{1}{3} \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So, we have been given the following diagonalization of $C:$

$$
C={{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Since $C=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${C}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{C}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{36} & =P{D}^{36}{P}^{-1} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt[18]{3} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[36]{3}\end{bmatrix}}^{36}(\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}(\sqrt[18]{3})^{36} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[36]{3})^{36}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{3}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}9 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}27 & -3 \\ -27 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}15 & 6 \\ -12 & -3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "702b377c-b5a4-541e-aae2-92f1f1c6521f"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "02c36a09-640e-5f2f-bee6-5e3ec7470874" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value 

$$
\begin{bmatrix}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}T=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ appears on both sides of the equation. Since this matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), left-multiplying the equation by the inverse gives the following expression for $T:$

$$
T={{{\begin{bmatrix}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{P}{{\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{D}{{\begin{bmatrix}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Therefore, $T$ is diagonalizable. The eigenvalues of $T$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4$ and the corresponding eigenvectors are the columns of the matrix $P.$ Computing $P,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}P={\begin{bmatrix}7 & 5 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2 & -5 \\ -3 & 7\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 5 \\ 3 & -7\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, the corresponding eigenvectors are: 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -7\end{bmatrix}$"} :step/id #uuid "74909bc5-d999-58f8-826a-ad660fd937ab" :step/next {:db/id 17592186492095}} :db/id 17592186280905}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/fd/fd18335a2034613658c65186c4fc6e3e74067e730183d3e66fbacf8ab3601928.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨0,\,z,\,-y⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=z=4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,R=-y.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-2x)-(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot (-2y)+(-y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(7y-2{x}^{2}y-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨0,z,-y⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(7y-2{x}^{2}y-2{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}8y-2{x}^{2}y-2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198619 :question/id #uuid "74d7a79e-d57c-5768-84fc-b3ae4dae67d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-161862"} {:db/id 17592186281374 :question/id #uuid "fca4156b-f8d5-50fa-a7b9-3894a3eed862" :question/math-academy-id "q-161895" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d747dec-4db3-5966-9a2d-772570a4c2a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}+6x" :db/id 17592186278717} {:answer/id #uuid "2b49f721-d34f-57b8-887a-a07af8acd027" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{x}^{3}-6x{y}^{2}-6x" :db/id 17592186278976} {:answer/id #uuid "3db364b4-51c0-5078-8edc-2aab3af9d03c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-6x" :db/id 17592186279134} {:answer/id #uuid "6a21fb2b-62f4-563c-8f2f-7175d9195a03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{x}^{3}-4x{y}^{2}+10x" :db/id 17592186279552} {:answer/id #uuid "7a5aa06e-86ef-5b2a-8470-8113b5d11a67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x" :db/id 17592186279682}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279682} :answer-field/id #uuid "99a942db-f0af-510b-bd6b-aeb36a731348" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281105}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/0e/0e374f18d8b87de2fddd9a2127ee84709746c7c1b75083441afcc7b6c79402fb.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨-z,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5,\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5)\cdot (-2x)-0\cdot (-2y)+x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x+x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-9x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨-z,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-9x)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281375 :question/id #uuid "a4e1f048-4c99-5435-999b-508c95c11d59" :question/math-academy-id "q-161899" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "46218ce4-ea58-5de1-86c0-d1c69e873ba0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{xy}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186279220} {:answer/id #uuid "4f46e641-3ee3-5376-98dd-a02b81e26818" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y-x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186279312} {:answer/id #uuid "7d9b5b14-4c9b-524f-9436-0ac569357f98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{xy-y}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186279717} {:answer/id #uuid "a8d59bc9-b571-564a-bff6-8c35092d9426" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186280086} {:answer/id #uuid "cc67d8e2-c014-5128-9067-69e0d0ab8a73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x+xy}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186280386}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280386} :answer-field/id #uuid "0ddaedb2-b68c-5509-aca4-917bce34c4eb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280859}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/8a/8a48be0b4c101babf157a05959e923576ad5614113b3eec9e93fe747d5dc3803.png)

$$

$$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-3)=2x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-3)=2y\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186405111 :question/id #uuid "883193fd-f5be-5d1c-8ffa-32b09d1431cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-161908" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d997b13e-de60-5563-841f-2fd5ee29d99e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{xy}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x" :db/id 17592186405113} {:answer/id #uuid "c47bf5a7-ddbb-55ea-94c5-903a6bd874ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+y" :db/id 17592186405114} {:answer/id #uuid "a933c2f8-9508-5563-b677-d1cf1467dfc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186405115} {:answer/id #uuid "9e7cafee-a688-51a7-b3d1-4d1daf466854" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186405116} {:answer/id #uuid "156642d0-8eb1-5036-896e-6fea2101a8de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186405117}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186405116} :answer-field/id #uuid "9854d104-9a4b-53d3-8285-a6f5f2377a4d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186405112}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/2f/2fff2eab1f5670dfcd3351dcbb9be1b3110e6ebdcd452cf4c5a273611d454c8b.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨1,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which expression belongs in the blank when the upper and lower surfaces are parametrized as graphs over $D$ and their outward flux integrands are added pointwise where defined, before integration?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨1,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower hemisphere ${S}_{2}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-1\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-0\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186434400 :question/id #uuid "93856fba-8ee0-5cd2-b018-66154e6d6da5" :question/math-academy-id "q-161909"} {:db/id 17592186198402 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F=⟨1,\,0,\,-x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=1+x.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=1+x$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+x)=1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=-x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 1-0\cdot 0+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower paraboloid ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=-x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 2x-0\cdot 2y+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-2x-x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-x)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x-1\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199468 :tutorial/content "Remember that when we measure the flux of a vector field through a *closed* surface, we always calculate with respect to an outward-pointing unit normal vector.

For example, suppose we have the vector field $\mathbf F,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{F} = \langle x, \,0, \, -y^2 \rangle
$$

and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the conical solid shown below. 

![](images/0b/0be83ceada68d0b56be4872f21652a7d18932ff059ea704576ca3cce892fa87b.png)

 

Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$ 

First, since $S$ is a closed surface, we have that

- the upper surface $S_1: z = g(x,y) = 2 - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ is oriented *upward*, and

- the lower surface $S_2: z = h(x,y) = 0$ is oriented *downward*.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- First, we consider the upper cone $S_1.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then

$$
P = x, \qquad
Q = 0, \qquad
R = -y^2.
$$

 
As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})-0\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})+(-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane.

- Next, we consider the lower plane $S_2.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n} = \langle 0,0,-1 \rangle.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨x,0,-{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across the entire surface is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "73467c61-810e-5e81-abcc-b5eb99d1e0ab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7651 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1bb12849-8513-5a29-9551-63f2f3815039" :step/math-academy-id \begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "73467c61-810e-5e81-abcc-b5eb99d1e0ab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7651 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1bb12849-8513-5a29-9551-63f2f3815039" :step/math-academy-id 44432 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199316}} {:db/id 17592186199468 :tutorial/content "Remember that when we measure the flux of a vector field through a *closed* surface, we always calculate with respect to an outward-pointing unit normal vector.

For example, suppose we have the vector field $\mathbf F,$ given by

$$
\mathbf{F} = \langle x, \,0, \, -y^2 \rangle
$$

and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the conical solid shown below. 

![](images/0b/0be83ceada68d0b56be4872f21652a7d18932ff059ea704576ca3cce892fa87b.png)

 

Let's calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$ 

First, since $S$ is a closed surface, we have that

- the upper surface $S_1: z = g(x,y) = 2 - \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ is oriented *upward*, and

- the lower surface $S_2: z = h(x,y) = 0$ is oriented *downward*.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- First, we consider the upper cone $S_1.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $\mathbf{F}=\langle P, \, Q, \, R \rangle,$ then

$$
P = x, \qquad
Q = 0, \qquad
R = -y^2.
$$

 
As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})-0\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})+(-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane.

- Next, we consider the lower plane $S_2.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $\mathbf{n} = \langle 0,0,-1 \rangle.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨x,0,-{y}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $\mathbf{F}$ across the entire surface is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "73467c61-810e-5e81-abcc-b5eb99d1e0ab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7651 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186199316 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198401 :question/math-academy-id "q-161899" :question/problem "![](images/8a/8a48be0b4c101babf157a05959e923576ad5614113b3eec9e93fe747d5dc3803.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨1,\,x,\,0⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper hemisphere ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=x,\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-1\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})-x\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})+0\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x+xy}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨1,x,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}0\,\text{d}A \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x+xy}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A+0 \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x+xy}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "4fb77fcc-508c-53c1-9504-71147177444b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481726}} {:db/id 17592186481703 :step/content {:db/id 17592186371981 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "69acc573-b0b8-5874-aab1-a28efcd81a93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "19x-2{x}^{3}+3{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186371983} {:answer/id #uuid "59cdcb69-6653-5e15-899a-5aa388d46281" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16x-x{y}^{2}+2{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186371984} {:answer/id #uuid "3bfc894d-49bf-586f-9c15-0545c41d8169" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186371985} {:answer/id #uuid "79846a78-79c8-5a37-ae61-84fe6a556fc5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20x+2y{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186371986} {:answer/id #uuid "c5c3b3f1-d211-5651-a1bd-4e92f6df7b3c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "20x+{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186371987}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186371985} :answer-field/id #uuid "106248c3-5a77-5d72-aed7-25c25eb96f2f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186371982}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "71368570-4ef4-5d96-b173-947fce0b9458" :question/math-academy-id "q-161898" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F=⟨z,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the paraboloid $z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=1.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. - the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=1$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot (-2x)-(0)\cdot (-2y)+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}19x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower plane ${S}_{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨z,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}19x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "619efe09-3031-5ed9-849a-5c2f5bf2ac5a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481697}} {:db/id 17592186481704 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198618 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1c3047a2-d5df-5a0c-ab0c-a0f194bdad31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}y+2{y}^{3}-6y" :db/id 17592186278851} {:answer/id #uuid "332e5ac0-126d-59e7-a343-89d3450f7bb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4y-2{x}^{2}y-2{y}^{3}" :db/id 17592186279037} {:answer/id #uuid "4371b2b7-1b47-5452-b1ab-806e3857aeef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8y-2{x}^{2}y-2{y}^{3}" :db/id 17592186279196} {:answer/id #uuid "ab87156c-d08c-577f-aff1-abc00dced344" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6y-2{x}^{2}y-2{y}^{3}" :db/id 17592186280110} {:answer/id #uuid "e2408eb1-f6f7-5772-bd58-8e40f81dd72f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}y+2{y}^{3}-8y" :db/id 17592186280591}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279196} :answer-field/id #uuid "27a2ccf4-8749-57d6-a76d-0242f177c147" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280905}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "ca709c99-e06d-5a3f-baf0-9520bf4a14bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-161830" :question/problem "![](images/fd/fd18335a2034613658c65186c4fc6e3e74067e730183d3e66fbacf8ab3601928.png)

Which expression belongs in the blank when the upper and lower surfaces are parametrized as graphs over $D$ and their outward flux integrands are added pointwise where defined, before integration?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. $$

$$

$$

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=1$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot (-2x)-(0)\cdot (-2y)+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}19x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨z,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}19x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

- Consider the upper cone ${S}_{1}.$

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-0\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})-(-x)\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨0,-x,-0⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}0\,\text{d}A \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A+0 \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1a630c08-382a-5c3a-8869-8aab867411d0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481734}} {:db/id 17592186481709 :step/content {:db/id 17592186405111 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d997b13e-de60-5563-841f-2fd5ee29d99e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{xy}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x" :db/id 17592186405113} {:answer/id #uuid "c47bf5a7-ddbb-55ea-94c5-903a6bd874ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+y" :db/id 17592186405114} {:answer/id #uuid "a933c2f8-9508-5563-b677-d1cf1467dfc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186405115} {:answer/id #uuid "9e7cafee-a688-51a7-b3d1-4d1daf466854" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186405116} {:answer/id #uuid "156642d0-8eb1-5036-896e-6fea2101a8de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186405117}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186405116} :answer-field/id #uuid "9854d104-9a4b-53d3-8285-a6f5f2377a4d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186405112}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "883193fd-f5be-5d1c-8ffa-32b09d1431cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-161908" :question/problem "![](images/2f/2fff2eab1f5670dfcd3351dcbb9be1b3110e6ebdcd452cf4c5a273611d454c8b.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨1,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which expression belongs in the blank when the upper and lower surfaces are parametrized as graphs over $D$ and their outward flux integrands are added pointwise where defined, before integration?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨1,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower hemisphere ${S}_{2}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-1\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-0\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6ae60978-ce20-5ee4-aae6-9abe617609aa" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481718}} {:db/id 17592186481718 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281379 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "34a8ff49-f833-5f3c-850a-8d217758437e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{3}+2{y}^{3}-12xy" :db/id 17592186279047} {:answer/id #uuid "63e9c76d-0951-5e6a-9281-3e125cd1d310" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2x+6y-1" :db/id 17592186279500} {:answer/id #uuid "9aac3735-e148-5a13-a799-508ff10d7ca3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-6x+2y" :db/id 17592186279963} {:answer/id #uuid "b48c9db8-b76f-57f1-9490-1c2b1d9bda32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}+2x-6y" :db/id 17592186280183} {:answer/id #uuid "e8f78e2b-f03d-51a5-a61b-fc3d2913a4bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2xy-1" :db/id 17592186280641}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279963} :answer-field/id #uuid "61b875c5-3db3-5698-aae1-ec503104d82f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281003}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2fe585d2-13a2-5e4d-ba70-80b8560f5587" :question/math-academy-id "q-161911" :question/problem "![](images/57/5709af87720dcb052d8ffc6cc600c5889e45849aee6bed69ec3646e43c3cefb1.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨z,\,1,\,0⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-3$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨z,1,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}0\,\text{d}A \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower paraboloid ${S}_{2}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-3)=2x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-3)=2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-3,\,Q=1,\,R=0.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-3)\cdot 2x-1\cdot 2y+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}+6x-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-6x+2y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & =0+{∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-6x+2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-6x+2y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8980b678-c09e-511b-8f7a-7cdc3940cc2c"} {:db/id 17592186481734 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198621 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b0db8ab-29d7-5fe3-9f20-8a503e358b7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-1" :db/id 17592186278839} {:answer/id #uuid "2b094c28-da56-5d15-a274-fa1ad40311ab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y-x" :db/id 17592186278971} {:answer/id #uuid "706d0a96-7dfe-5cc7-b55c-f78d8b793955" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-y" :db/id 17592186279612} {:answer/id #uuid "a892c1e1-5080-5e0f-8d79-ae3ae1774d7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2x-3" :db/id 17592186280080} {:answer/id #uuid "fc1bdc04-3a79-54f8-8b7e-e69a71a66f75" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3x-1" :db/id 17592186280799}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186278839} :answer-field/id #uuid "b28d0bd3-3943-5d91-91b9-a9ce611eece5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281148}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "5f651353-551c-55cb-9916-e19d1d757989" :question/math-academy-id "q-161907" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F=⟨1,\,0,\,-x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=1+x.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. $$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=1+x$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+x)=1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=-x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 1-0\cdot 0+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower paraboloid ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=-x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 2x-0\cdot 2y+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-2x-x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-x)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x-1\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cfabf4bc-f80d-55cf-ba91-6de33824c78e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481709}}] :activity/title "Calculating Flux Through Closed Surfaces" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186481578} {:db/id 17592186481676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281374 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0d747dec-4db3-5966-9a2d-772570a4c2a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}+6x" :db/id 17592186278717} {:answer/id #uuid "2b49f721-d34f-57b8-887a-a07af8acd027" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2{x}^{3}-6x{y}^{2}-6x" :db/id 17592186278976} {:answer/id #uuid "3db364b4-51c0-5078-8edc-2aab3af9d03c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-6x" :db/id 17592186279134} {:answer/id #uuid "6a21fb2b-62f4-563c-8f2f-7175d9195a03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{x}^{3}-4x{y}^{2}+10x" :db/id 17592186279552} {:answer/id #uuid "7a5aa06e-86ef-5b2a-8470-8113b5d11a67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x" :db/id 17592186279682}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279682} :answer-field/id #uuid "99a942db-f0af-510b-bd6b-aeb36a731348" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281105}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fca4156b-f8d5-50fa-a7b9-3894a3eed862" :question/math-academy-id "q-161895" :question/problem "![](images/0e/0e374f18d8b87de2fddd9a2127ee84709746c7c1b75083441afcc7b6c79402fb.png)

$$

Consider the vector field $F=⟨0,\,-x,\,-z⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which expression belongs in the blank when the upper and lower surfaces are parametrized as graphs over $D$ and their outward flux integrands are added pointwise where defined, before integration?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=3-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper cone ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=-x,\,R=-z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-0\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})-(-x)\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨0,-x,-0⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}0\,\text{d}A \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A+0 \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1a630c08-382a-5c3a-8869-8aab867411d0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481734}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b802cb74-ee56-571a-ba2b-74472252f1f3" :answer/type {:db/id "q-161907" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F=⟨1,\,0,\,-x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=1+x.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\bbox[3pt,border: 1pt solid black]{\phantom{AAAAAAA}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=1+x$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+x)=1 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=-x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 1-0\cdot 0+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower paraboloid ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=1,\,Q=0,\,R=-x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-1\cdot 2x-0\cdot 2y+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-2x-x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1-x)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x-1\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "cfabf4bc-f80d-55cf-ba91-6de33824c78e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481709}} {:db/id 17592186481709 :step/content {:db/id 17592186405111 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d997b13e-de60-5563-841f-2fd5ee29d99e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{xy}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x" :db/id 17592186405113} {:answer/id #uuid "c47bf5a7-ddbb-55ea-94c5-903a6bd874ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}+y" :db/id 17592186405114} {:answer/id #uuid "a933c2f8-9508-5563-b677-d1cf1467dfc4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186405115} {:answer/id #uuid "9e7cafee-a688-51a7-b3d1-4d1daf466854" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}" :db/id 17592186405116} {:answer/id #uuid "156642d0-8eb1-5036-896e-6fea2101a8de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}" :db/id 17592186405117}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186405116} :answer-field/id #uuid "9854d104-9a4b-53d3-8285-a6f5f2377a4d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186405112}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "883193fd-f5be-5d1c-8ffa-32b09d1431cb" :question/math-academy-id "q-161908" :question/problem "![](images/2f/2fff2eab1f5670dfcd3351dcbb9be1b3110e6ebdcd452cf4c5a273611d454c8b.png)

**Step 1**: Find the critical points.

We see that $f'(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x \in (1,9),$ and $f'(x) = 0$ at $x=3$ and $x=6.$ Therefore, the candidates are $x=1,3,6,9.$

**Step 2**: Compute the values of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =5 \\ f(3) & =f(1)+{\int }_{1}^{3}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5+3 \\  & =8 \\ f(6) & =f(1)+{\int }_{1}^{6}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5+3-5 \\  & =3 \\ f(9) & =f(1)+{\int }_{1}^{9}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5+3-5+4 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Select the smallest value of $f$ from our candidates.

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have 

$$
f_{\text{min}} = \min\{5, 8, 3, 7\} = 3.
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is $f_{\text{min}} = 3,$ and the value of $x$ that minimizes $f(x)$ is $x_{\text{min}} = 6.$"} {:db/id 17592186101211 :question/id #uuid function. Let's understand how this process works by studying a specific example.

The graph of $y = f'(x),$ the *derivative* of $f(x),$ is shown in the picture below. 

![](images/2e/2ee1721d439ee0234b0f8a99ed0e4a56c63041e36919b00978267cf361a5322c.png)

The areas of the shaded regions are indicated on the diagram. Additionally, it is known that $f(-2)=5.$ Our goal is find the *minimum* value of $f(x)$ on the interval $x\in [-2,2].$

To find the minimum value of $f(x),$ we use the candidates test.

According to the candidates test, the minimum value of $f(x)$ on $[-2,2]$ must occur at a critical point or an endpoint of the interval. Therefore, we proceed as follows.

**Step 1**: Find the critical points.

We see that $f'(x)$ is defined everywhere on $x\in (-2,2),$ so there are no non-stationary critical points. Additionally, we see that $f'(x)=0$ at $x=1.$ Therefore, the candidates are 

$$
x=-2,\quad x=1,\quad x=2.
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the value of $f$ for each candidate using the fundamental theorem of calculus.

- The value of $f(x)$ at the left endpoint is given:

$$
f(-2) = 5
$$

- To compute $f(1),$ we apply the fundamental theorem of calculus. Since the areas of the rectangle and middle triangle in our picture equal ${\color{red}{2}}$ and ${\color{red}{\dfrac12}},$ respectively, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =f(-2)+{\int }_{-2}^{1}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5-2-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we *subtracted* these areas since both lie *under* the $x$-axis.

- To compute $f(2),$ we apply the fundamental theorem of calculus once more. Using the fact that the area of the right triangle equals ${\color{blue}{\dfrac12}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & =f(-2)+{\int }_{-2}^{2}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5-2-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Select the smallest value of $f$ from our candidates. 

Comparing the values of $f$ found in step $2,$ we have

$$
f_{\text{min}} = \min\left\lbrace 5, \dfrac52, 3 \right\rbrace = \dfrac52.
$$

Therefore, the minimum value of $f$ is $f_{\text{min}}=\dfrac52,$ and the value of $x$ that minimizes $f(x)$ is $x_\text{min}=1.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a6d3aebd-5589-5160-b57f-ed0eb4f47691" section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186152743 :question/id #uuid "fda4f6af-c917-5961-9062-323f1cdf3aeb" :question/math-academy-id "q-76355" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c31779c1-61a9-5ddf-9ce4-388acac151e1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186393613} {:answer/id #uuid "b35b8c73-b6e1-55f6-a3a8-1f84f618409d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186393614} {:answer/id #uuid "d14288db-cd96-5f69-9f29-fa682d61a4a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186393615} {:answer/id #uuid "f83c51d2-6855-5059-8910-c179f8d7f6c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186393616} {:answer/id #uuid "865a2778-efa4-5860-8c94-4fab14e1e597" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta " :db/id 17592186393617}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186393614} :answer-field/id #uuid "8116cea9-3c1b-5e81-a58c-b2147c4e208d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186393612}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $y=\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$, where $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )=\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta | \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ because $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta >0.$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-0-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186364399 :question/id #uuid "3efc6eb6-1183-58cd-bd1a-3a29f39410eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-76614"} {:db/id 17592186364406 :question/id #uuid :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\operatorname{arcsin}⁡y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Let's use integration by parts. We denote

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\theta  & ⟹ & {u}^{′}=1, \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & ⟹ & v=\int {v}^{′}\,\text{d}\theta =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting into the formula for the integration by parts, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3}-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}-0)+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi }{6}+(\frac{1}{2}-1) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\pi -3}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186362989 :question/id #uuid "05fbe250-8eb4-5b81-83cc-08a815c1aec0" :question/math-academy-id "q-123510"} {:db/id 17592186363534 :question/id #uuid $$
\int\limits_Cf(x,y)\:\textrm{d}s
$$

for some function $f(x,y),$ where $C$ is a curve in the $xy$-plane defined using plane polar coordinates as

$$
r = r(\theta),\qquad \theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2.
$$

To calculate this line integral, we need to recall the following facts:

- A polar curve is just a special type of parametric curve in the parameter $\theta,$ where

$$
x = r(\theta)\cos\theta, \quad y = r(\theta)\sin\theta, \qquad \theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2.
$$

- The arc length element $\textrm d s$ in plane polar coordinates is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,.
$$

Substituting the above formulas into our line integral, we get the following result:

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}  f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,.
$$

the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta | \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ because $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta >0.$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-0-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0cb113d7-5c3c-54c0-89a9-97aef97d74cf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186483445}} {:db/id 17592186483445 :step/content {:db/id 17592186284545 :question/answer-fields $$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
