Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )=\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "167e09bf-7031-5c07-aef8-581424ee1431"} {:db/id 17592186497442 :step/content {:db/id 17592186345245 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3cee7c2d-32de-5ecb-b754-ad79568f9d67" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186342741} {:answer/id #uuid "5fee99df-a2f2-53ad-aa42-aeb2b8227900" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186343052} {:answer/id #uuid "7d9b8c0d-eb50-5a20-b648-4799432e59b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186343321} {:answer/id #uuid "817d31a5-4314-5a33-8e83-382ed5fd5388" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186343350} {:answer/id #uuid "8d7f6c1c-7a72-538c-9708-f7cf3bcb5c66" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186343475}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186343475} :answer-field/id #uuid "946d4e0c-fe04-5d7a-bb82-af9edb848223" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186344748}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "a681b3bc-0951-5b58-83e9-55d23d5a0373" :question/math-academy-id "q-76688" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$

\frac{\pi }{8}?$" :question/worked-solution "In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x(1-{y}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a773889b-d594-5730-87d3-566a19243567" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497450}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28f03a0e-89a7-5b16-bf01-1519355c07d9" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "e-10348" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186162132 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "130d80d7-d0f9-5979-b966-e6c0bf7a27e9" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Covariance Using the Definition"}] :question/problem "The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $X=1$ | $0.1$ | $0.5$ |
| $X=2$ | $0$ | $0.4$ |

Calculate the covariance of $X$ and $Y$." :question/worked-solution "The covariance of two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint support $S$ is defined as

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \sum_{(x,y)\in S}(x - \textrm E[X])(y - \textrm E[Y])f(x,y)
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y$. These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $f_X$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $X=1$ | $0.1$ | $0.5$ | $0.6$ |
| $X=2$ | $0$ | $0.4$ | $0.4$ |
| $f_Y$ | $0.1$ | $0.9$ | $1$ |

We now compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ and $\textrm{E}[Y]$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X] &= ∑_(x ∈ S_{X})x \cdot f_{X}(x) \\
&= 1 \cdot 0.6 + 2 \cdot 0.4 \\
&= 0.6 + 0.8 \\
&= 1.4 \\
E[Y] &= ∑_(y ∈ S_{Y})y \cdot f_{Y}(y) \\
&= 0 \cdot 0.1 + 1 \cdot 0.9 \\
&= 0 + 0.9 \\
&= 0.9
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for the covariance, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
Cov[X, Y] &= ∑_((x, y) ∈ S)(x - E[X])(y - E[Y])f(x, y) \\
&= ∑_((x, y) ∈ S)(x - 1.4)(y - 0.9)f(x, y) \\
&= (1 - 1.4)(0 - 0.9)f(1, 0) \\
&= + (1 - 1.4)(1 - 0.9)f(1, 1) \\
&= + (2 - 1.4)(0 - 0.9)f(2, 0) \\
&= + (2 - 1.4)(1 - 0.9)f(2, 1) \\
&= (-0.4)(-0.9)(0.1) \\
&= + (-0.4)(0.1)(0.5) \\
&= + (0.6)(-0.9)(0) \\
&= + (0.6)(0.1)(0.4) \\
&= 0.04
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050835} {:db/id 17592186162426 :question/id #uuid "93792b9c-cffc-5ec0-9d81-259a85223c4e" :question/math-academy-id "q-146170"} {:db/id 17592186162444 :question/id #uuid "7e2812ba-bf2f-5151-abd6-9825259d18ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-147416"} {:db/id 17592186162134 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161700 :question/id #uuid "ebf98f0c-765c-5cc4-bfa0-89ffefe450f4" :question/math-academy-id "e-10356"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fab3dcab-d386-5f54-bfba-f2e5951af9ba" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050368} {:db/id 17592186050682}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162429 :question/id #uuid "3f486e7e-5dfa-501f-90c2-497028f8a357" :question/math-academy-id "q-146266"} {:db/id 17592186162437 :question/id #uuid "4758a300-283b-5e89-b7ae-076ee4d5ef65" :question/math-academy-id "q-146387"} {:db/id 17592186411854 :question/id #uuid "1994bb13-7165-5891-a83f-5e7560b1da72" :question/math-academy-id "q-147946"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Covariance Given a Joint Probability Density Function"} {:db/id 17592186161700 :question/id #uuid "ebf98f0c-765c-5cc4-bfa0-89ffefe450f4" :question/math-academy-id "e-10356" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186162134 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fab3dcab-d386-5f54-bfba-f2e5951af9ba" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Covariance Given a Joint Probability Density Function"}] :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

Find the covariance of $X$ and $Y$." :question/worked-solution "The joint support of $X$ and $Y$ is given by the rectangle

$$
S = [0,1] \times [2,3]
$$

Moreover, we can write

$$
f(x,y) = g(x) \cdot h(y)
$$

where

$$
g(x) =\dfrac{3}{5} \sqrt{x}
$$

and $h(y) =y$.

Therefore, $X$ and $Y$ are independent, and consequently

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 0
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050368} {:db/id 17592186050682} {:db/id 17592186162429 :question/id #uuid "3f486e7e-5dfa-501f-90c2-497028f8a357" :question/math-academy-id "q-146266" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162134 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fab3dcab-d386-5f54-bfba-f2e5951af9ba" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Covariance Given a Joint Probability Density Function"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9808b13b-2fee-56b6-a014-1a93e20b5b91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186159777} {:answer/id #uuid "e0aa279a-fbf4-566c-a2e5-90c94f02f018" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186159778} {:answer/id #uuid "eadf298b-3043-50fd-acb0-90abef3abd34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{e}" :db/id 17592186159779} {:answer/id #uuid "0974ef81-d76c-5bb3-b890-13e356d506c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "e^{2}" :db/id 17592186159780} {:answer/id #uuid "4975ae33-06ab-5386-bc3d-6d44edc8ba9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186159781}] :answer-field/id #uuid "316d0a76-34fa-5862-a104-987d7995c329" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186159776}] :question/problem "The random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

Given that $\text{E}[X]=\frac{5}{4}$ and $\text{E}[Y]=\frac{9}{16},$ calculate the covariance of $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "The covariance of $X$ and $Y$ can be calculated using the formula

$$
\text{Cov}[X,Y]=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y].
$$

To find $\text{E}[XY],$ we use the rule of the lazy statistician:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}xyf(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}xy\cdot \frac{3}{8}(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{8}y{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{8}y{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{8}y[\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y+\frac{3}{4}{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{16}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{11}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the covariance formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{11}{16}-(\frac{5}{4})(\frac{9}{16}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{64}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162135 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161701 :question/id #uuid "5e69ba34-d7f9-512b-9d53-f00f8f556049" :question/math-academy-id "e-10357"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b4549d88-dfbd-57e0-a673-99e394563613" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048466} {:db/id 17592186049126}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162436 :question/id #uuid "e1aeae48-51d6-5217-b4c3-c57d2c601979" :question/math-academy-id "q-146384"} {:db/id 17592186162445 :question/id #uuid "30db451b-93c6-5bae-8115-d6afd25f7fca" :question/math-academy-id "q-147920"}] :knowledge-point/title "Stating the Covariance Using the Definition"} {:db/id 17592186161701 :question/id #uuid "5e69ba34-d7f9-512b-9d53-f00f8f556049" :question/math-academy-id "e-10357" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186162135 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b4549d88-dfbd-57e0-a673-99e394563613" :knowledge-point/title "Stating the Covariance Using the Definition"}] :question/problem "The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint support $S=S_X\times S_Y$ is given below.

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=5$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.45$ | $0.15$ |

Find an expression for the covariance in sigma notation." :question/worked-solution "The covariance of two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint support $S$ is defined as

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \sum_{(x,y)\in S}(x - \textrm E[X])(y - \textrm E[Y])f(x,y)
$$

First, let's find the marginal mass functions for $X$ and $Y$. These are given by the row and column totals, respectively.

| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=5$ | $f_X$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.25$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.45$ | $0.15$ | $0.6$ |
| $f_Y$ | $0.6$ | $0.4$ | $1$ |

We now compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ and $\textrm{E}[Y]$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[X] &= ∑_(x ∈ S_{X})x \cdot f_{X}(x) \\
&= 1 \cdot 0.4 + 4 \cdot 0.6 \\
&= 0.4 + 2.4 \\
&= 2.8 \\
E[Y] &= ∑_(y ∈ S_{Y})y \cdot f_{Y}(y) \\
&= 2 \cdot 0.6 + 5 \cdot 0.4 \\
&= 1.2 + 2 \\
&= 3.2
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for the covariance, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
Cov[X, Y] &= ∑_((x, y) ∈ S)(x - E[X])(y - E[Y])f(x, y) \\
&= ∑_((x, y) ∈ S)(x - 2.8)(y - 3.2)f(x, y)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048466} {:db/id 17592186162436 :question/id #uuid "e1aeae48-51d6-5217-b4c3-c57d2c601979" :question/math-academy-id "q-146384"} {:db/id 17592186162445 :question/id #uuid "30db451b-93c6-5bae-8115-d6afd25f7fca" :question/math-academy-id "q-147920" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162135 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b4549d88-dfbd-57e0-a673-99e394563613" :knowledge-point/title "Stating the Covariance Using the Definition"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "92816af4-0c70-5a6a-8b94-854320a1548d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_((x, y) ∈ S)(x - 3.8)(y - 1.96)f(x, y)" :db/id 17592186159873} {:answer/id #uuid "efe9ef9a-70ec-526c-b030-86dbeac05f5d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_((x, y) ∈ S)x(y - 1)f(x, y)" :db/id 17592186159874} {:answer/id #uuid "f6841ecd-0074-58fd-b57b-562f0dfbc325" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_((x, y) ∈ S)(x - 1.96)(y - 3.8)f(x, y)" :db/id 17592186159875} {:answer/id #uuid "f70f8b02-733d-54de-92f9-44d0a9305940" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_((x, y) ∈ S)(x - 1)(y - 2)f(x, y)" :db/id 17592186159876} {:answer/id #uuid "21019cb9-4a48-550a-99b7-893ad3830709" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "∑_((x, y) ∈ S)(xy - 1.96)f(x, y)" :db/id 17592186159877}] :answer-field/id #uuid "ee0ffc3c-5e92-543d-a922-72f19b24c70c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186159872}] :question/problem "The joint probability mass function $f(x, y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint support $S = S_{X} \cdot S_{Y}$ is given below.

If $\textrm{E} [X]=2.8$ and $\textrm{E}[Y] = 2.4$, calculate the covariance of $X$ and $Y$." :question/worked-solution "The covariance of $X$ and $Y$ can be calculated using the formula

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E} [XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y]
$$

We use the rule of the lazy statistician to find $\textrm{E}[XY]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[XY] &= ∑_((x, y) ∈ S)xy \cdot f(x, y) \\
&= (1)(2)(0.2) + (1)(3)(0.2) + (4)(2)(0.4) + (4)(3)(0.2) \\
&= 6.6
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the covariance formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
Cov[X, Y] &= E[XY] - E[X] \cdot E[Y] \\
&= 6.6 - (2.8)(2.4) \\
&=-0.12
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186162422 :question/id #uuid "e37b553f-54ac-5d84-b352-476c36a3f396" :question/math-academy-id "q-146149" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186162136 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "929a4b02-6c3d-59ce-b774-7ca6487077ff" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Covariance Using the Shortcut Formula"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "82b061aa-a562-5cec-b12f-b031e6b197d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2.4" :db/id 17592186159735} {:answer/id #uuid "9dc50379-a73f-56f1-a77e-1b9ac7f0f5e8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1.6" :db/id 17592186159736} {:answer/id #uuid "bf1e623d-3883-51ff-9be3-842a410c8835" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3.6" :db/id 17592186159737} {:answer/id #uuid "06809080-8efa-5670-a26b-998d5dc4f55a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "6.4" :db/id 17592186159738} {:answer/id #uuid "3b7115c8-ba08-5aac-b629-621bf83dee7c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4.8" :db/id 17592186159739}] :answer-field/id #uuid "b1eacff7-d507-52b8-80a6-7de096999f8b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186159734}] :question/problem "If $E[X] = 20$, $E[Y] = 2$, and $E[XY] = 44.8$ for two random variables $X$ and $Y$, calculate the covariance of $X$ and $Y$.

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186163006 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163290 :tutorial/content "We often want to measure the strength of the (linear) dependence between two random variables. One measure that we use for this purpose is covariance.

The **covariance** between two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] = \textrm{E}\Big[\left(X - \textrm{E}[X]\right)\left(Y - \textrm{E}[Y]\right) \Big]
$$

Let's break this formula down a bit:

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] =\textrm E [XY] - \textrm E[X]\cdot \textrm E[Y]
$$

We start with the definition of covariance, given by

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] =\textrm E\Big[\left(X- \textrm E[X]\right)\left(Y-\textrm E[Y]\right)\Big]
$$

Expanding the product in the brackets, we get

$$
Cov[X, Y] = E[XY - X \cdot E[Y] - E[X] \cdot Y + E[X] \cdot E[Y]]
$$

Now, recall that if $a$ and $b$ are constants, then

$$
\textrm E[a]=a, \qquad \textrm{E}[aX + bY] = a\cdot \textrm{E}[X] + b \cdot \textrm{E}[Y]
$$

Since $\textrm{E}[X]$ and are $\textrm{E}[Y]$ are both constants, the covariance formula simplifies as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Cov[X, Y] &= E[XY - X \cdot E[Y] - E[X] \cdot Y + E[X] \cdot E[Y]] \\
&= E[XY] - E[X \cdot E[Y]] - E[E[X] \cdot Y] + E[E[X] \cdot E[Y]] \\
&= E[XY] - E[X] \cdot E[Y] - E[X] \cdot E[Y] + E[X] \cdot E[Y] \\
&= E[XY] - E[X] \cdot E[Y]
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "57fd5059-dc1e-5473-9f12-db4e68dc88af" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5635 :tutorial/title "Proof of the Covariance Formula"} :step/id #uuid "7b510b48-c0dd-5ca6-a760-7383939e9b88" :step/math-academy-id 34611} {:db/id 17592186163009 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163293 :tutorial/content "If $X$ and $Y$ are continuous random variables, the covariance between $X$ and $Y$ is given by

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] =\iint_\limits{\mathbb R^2}(x - \textrm E[X])(y - \textrm E[Y])f(x,y) \, \textrm d x\textrm d y
$$

As is the case with discrete random variables, it's often easier to compute the covariance using the following formula:

$$
\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = \textrm{E} [XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y]
$$

Suppose we're given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability density function

$$
{\frac{1}{2}(x + \frac{y}{2}),\begin{vmatrix}0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le 2, \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

To compute the covariance of this distribution, we first use the rule of the lazy statistician to find $\textrm{E}[XY]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
E[XY] &= \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{1}xyf(x, y)dxdy \\
&= \int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{1}xy \cdot \frac{1}{2}(x + \frac{y}{2})dxdy \\
&= \int_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}y\int_{0}^{1}(x^{2} + \frac{1}{2}xy)dxdy \\
&= \int_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}y[\frac{1}{3}x^{3} + \frac{1}{4}x^{2}y]_{x = 0}^{x = 1}dy \\
&= \int_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}y[\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4}y]dy \\
&= \int_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{6}y + \frac{1}{8}y^{2})dy \\
&= [\frac{1}{12}y^{2} + \frac{1}{24}y^{3}]_{y = 0}^{y = 2} \\
&= \frac{1}{12} \cdot 2^{2} + \frac{1}{24} \cdot 2^{3} \\
&= \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \\
&= \frac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using methods discussed in previous lessons, we can compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ and $\textrm{E}[Y]{:}$

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{7}{12}, \qquad \textrm{E}[Y] = \dfrac76
$$

Finally, using the covariance formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
Cov[X, Y] &= E[XY] - E[X] \cdot E[Y] \\
&= \frac{2}{3} - (\frac{7}{12})(\frac{7}{6}) \\
&=-\frac{1}{72}
\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that if two random variables are independent then their covariance equals zero. - If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then

&= \int_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}y[\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{4}y]dy \\
&= \int_{0}^{2}(\frac{1}{6}y + \frac{1}{8}y^{2})dy \\
&= [\frac{1}{12}y^{2} + \frac{1}{24}y^{3}]_{y = 0}^{y = 2} \\
&= \frac{1}{12} \cdot 2^{2} + \frac{1}{24} \cdot 2^{3} \\
&= \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \\
&= \frac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using methods discussed in previous lessons, we can compute $\textrm{E}[X]$ and $\textrm{E}[Y]{:}$

$$
\textrm{E}[X] = \dfrac{7}{12}, \qquad \textrm{E}[Y] = \dfrac76
$$

Finally, using the covariance formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
Cov[X, Y] &= E[XY] - E[X] \cdot E[Y] \\
&= \frac{2}{3} - (\frac{7}{12})(\frac{7}{6}) \\
&=-\frac{1}{72}
\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that if two random variables are independent then their covariance equals zero. approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

- With step size $Δx=0.08,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.08)=0.13.$

- With step size $Δx=0.02,$ the observed local truncation error is $τ(0.02)=0.002.$

Estimate the order of the numerical method." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.08$ to $0.02.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.08}{0.02}=4.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={4}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.13$ to $0.002.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.13}{0.002}=65.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{p+1} & ≈65 \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{4}⁡(65) \\ p+1 & ≈3.011… \\ p & ≈2.011….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is $2.$"} {:db/id 17592186221987 :question/id #uuid "36473f35-3093-5439-832b-c821da150814" :question/math-academy-id :question/problem "The local truncation error (LTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}.
$$

Complete the following sentences.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Decreasing from $Δx=0.5$ to $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is reduced by a factor of $≈$
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ According to this data, the order of the method is approximately
{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =8(0.5)^{5}+2(0.5)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.031\,25+2\cdot 0.015\,625 \\  & =0.281\,25 \\  & ≈0.281.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =8(0.2)^{5}+2(0.2)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.000\,32+2\cdot 0.000\,064 \\  & =0.002\,688 \\  & ≈0.003.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.2}=2.5.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2.5}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\,25$ to $0.002\,688.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.281\,25}{0.002\,688}=104.631\,69…≈104.632.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2.5}^{p+1} & ≈104.631\,69… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2.5}⁡(104.631\,69…) \\ p+1 & ≈5.075… \\ p & ≈4.075….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$4.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{5})=O\,((Δx)^{4+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $4.$"} {:db/id 17592186443229 :question/id #uuid "1812d74c-f7ff-5b92-ad0c-d300745fe3f0" :question/math-academy-id "q-334643"} {:db/id 17592186443234 :question/id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Which of the following local truncation error expressions represent a first-order numerical method?
- **I.** $τ(Δx)=6(Δx)^{3}$
- **II.** $τ(Δx)=0.3(Δx)^{2}+2(Δx)^{3}$
- **III.** $τ(Δx)=9(Δx)^{3}+4(Δx)^{5}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

With that in mind, let's check each option in turn:

- For $τ(Δx)=6(Δx)^{3},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $6(Δx)^{3}=6(Δx)^{2+1}.$ So, statement I corresponds to an order $2$ method.

- For $τ(Δx)=0.3(Δx)^{2}+2(Δx)^{3},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $0.3(Δx)^{2}=0.3(Δx)^{1+1}.$ So, statement II corresponds to an order $1$ method.

- For $τ(Δx)=9(Δx)^{3}+4(Δx)^{5},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $9(Δx)^{3}=9(Δx)^{2+1}.$ So, statement III corresponds to an order $2$ method.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"."} {:db/id 17592186221982 :question/id #uuid "a3f43810-818f-5e05-945e-483e5e28efaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-333692"} {:db/id 17592186308493 :question/id {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.2$ to $0.1.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.2}{0.1}=2.
$$

Now, since the numerical method is of order $3,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$
{k}^{3}={2}^{3}=8.
$$

Therefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.1,$ the expected GTE is

$$
e(0.1)≈\frac{0.064}{8}=0.008.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308686 :question/id #uuid "5e9fb99c-0502-586a-b64c-76d5a0146e7d" :question/math-academy-id "q-334781"} {:db/id 17592186308687 :question/id #uuid "d047c5c7-9757-5ee5-9e01-a79118905089" :question/math-academy-id "q-334796"} {:db/id 17592186308689 :question/id #uuid "349cbec4-4185-5bf7-8486-3d5b581851b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334827"} {:db/id 17592186308699 :question/id #uuid "ce506036-afe4-59f4-88ca-ada7f672db57" :question/math-academy-id "q-334866"} {:db/id 17592186308709 :question/id #uuid "6a7b9303-06ef-5983-bd7d-577c4a789987" :question/math-academy-id "q-334946" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8d2823fe-ac2e-533e-b8ef-d3d1dec21d4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.05" :db/id 17592186306488}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306488} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf20e996-1ea4-5bae-aecf-b59e8d34708e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186308167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A numerical method for approximating a solution to an initial value problem is known to be order $1.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.5$ produces a local truncation error (LTE) of $τ(0.5)≈0.2.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.25,$ what LTE should we expect?

The **order** of a numerical method describes how fast these errors shrink as $\Delta x$ decreases.
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the *largest positive* integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^p\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}e(\frac{Δx}{k}) & ≈K{(\frac{Δx}{k})}^{p}=\frac{K(Δx)^{p}}{{k}^{p}}≈\frac{e(Δx)}{{k}^{p}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's demonstrate with an example. Suppose a numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.21,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.21) = 0.785.$

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.07,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.07) = 0.010.$

Using this data, we can estimate the order of the numerical method.

The step size decreases from $0.21$ to $0.07.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k = \dfrac{0.21}{0.07} = 3.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
k^p = 3^p.
$$

On the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.785$ to $0.010.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\dfrac{0.785}{0.010} = 78.5.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{p} & ≈78.5 \\ p & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(78.5) \\ p & ≈3.97….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the approximate order of the method is $4.$

But why is order important? Well, a higher order means that the error decreases faster as $\Delta x$ decreases. As a result, higher-order methods can achieve a target accuracy *with fewer steps*. In this way, order predicts the accuracy you gain when you make steps smaller." :tutorial/id #uuid "40e84a8b-32df-5566-99ff-2b37f338d69f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14500 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ec16a00b-18c7-517a-94d1-35859655f930" :step/math-academy-id 585132 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222295}} {:db/id 17592186222295 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221401 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221184 :question/id #uuid "fb9baafb-4eca-593f-ad3e-34744fdfd3f4" :question/math-academy-id "e-21684"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "48cd517d-be8a-5dc2-91af-fbd19231363c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049053} {:db/id 17592186049611} {:db/id 17592186049621}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221972} {:db/id 17592186221974} {:db/id 17592186308639} {:db/id 17592186308640} {:db/id 17592186308641} {:db/id 17592186308642} {:db/id 17592186391487} {:db/id 17592186443231} {:db/id 17592186443235} {:db/id 17592186443236} {:db/id 17592186443240}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Order of a Numerical Method By Comparing GTE for Different Step Sizes"} :step/id #uuid "8b58215f-a6df-5452-b05c-85bfbc0fd9f2" :step/math-academy-id 585133 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222296}} {:db/id 17592186222296 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222499 :tutorial/content "An alternative, but equivalent, definition for the **order** can be made in terms of the local truncation error.

A numerical method has **order** $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has **order** $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately $k^{p+1}.$

But why is the power $p+1$ for LTE but only $p$ for GTE?

Each local truncation error measures the error made in *one step* of the method. If a method has order $p,$ then the error made in a single step shrinks like

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right).
$$

However, on a fixed interval, using step size $\Delta x$ requires about

$$
N \approx \dfrac1{\Delta x}
$$

steps. The global truncation error results from *accumulating* these local errors over all steps.

Heuristically, adding up $N$ local errors of size $(\Delta x)^{p+1}$ gives

$$
e(\Delta x) \sim N \cdot (\Delta x)^{p+1} \sim \dfrac1{\Delta x} \cdot (\Delta x)^{p+1} = (\Delta x)^p.
$$

Thus, the local truncation error is one power of $\Delta x$ higher than the global truncation error.

Next, we will apply this definition to determine the order of a given numerical method." :tutorial/id #uuid "b5d4a6f3-fc92-557f-be1f-b14832313c21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14501 :tutorial/title :step/content {:db/id 17592186222512 :tutorial/content "We'll now show that the definition of order with respect to LTE is the same as with respect to GTE.

Indeed, suppose a numerical method with increment formula $\Delta y = \Phi(x, y, \Delta x) \cdot \Delta x$ satisfies the following:

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0
$$

On a fixed interval of length $L,$ the number of steps is $N \approx \dfrac{L}{\Delta x}.$ So,
$N = \mathcal O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\Delta x}\right)$ as $\Delta x \to 0.$

Now, recall the relationship between GTE and LTE, given by

$$
e(\Delta x) = e_N = e_{N-1} + \left[ \Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \Delta x) - \Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \Delta x) \right] \cdot \Delta x + \tau_N.
$$

Since $y(x_{N-1}) - y_{N-1} = e_{N-1},$ it is natural to say that changing the input $y$ by $e_{N-1}$ changes $\Phi$ by about a constant multiple of $e_{N-1}.$ So, heuristically,

$$
\Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \Delta x) - \Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \Delta x) \approx Ce_{N-1}
$$

for some $C$ that *doesn't* depend on $\Delta x$ (on a fixed interval). Hence, the GTE satisfies approximately

$$
e(\Delta x) = e_N \approx (1+C\Delta x)e_{N-1} + \tau_N.
$$

After $N$ steps, we get

$$
e(\Delta x) \approx (1+C\Delta x)^N e_0 + \sum_{n=1}^N(1+C\Delta x)^{N-n}\tau_n.
$$

Next, note that $(1+C\Delta x)^N \approx e^{CN\Delta x} \approx e^{CL},$ which is $\mathcal O(1)$ as $\Delta x \to 0.$ So, the weights $(1+C\Delta x)^{N-n}$ don't change the *power* of $\Delta x.$

So, we can treat the GTE as roughly the sum of the per-step local errors. Therefore,

$$
e(\Delta x) \approx \sum_{n=1}^N \tau_n
$$

With $\tau_n = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)$ for each $n=1,\ldots,N,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}e(Δx) & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{N}O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =N\cdot O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =O\,(\frac{1}{Δx})\cdot O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =O\,((Δx)^{p}).\end{aligned}
$$

Note that since $p$ is maximal in the LTE definition, this shows the GTE has order $p$ as well." :tutorial/id #uuid "380a28f7-f36f-50b0-982b-365f87b068bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14656 :tutorial/title "Connecting the Definitions of the Order of Numerical Methods"} :step/id #uuid "a05640d9-1389-5d1b-b299-1230e633c270" :step/math-academy-id 593404}] :activity/title "Order of Numerical Methods" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221478} {:db/id 17592186222294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222498 :tutorial/content "Each step of a numerical method produces a local truncation error $\tau,$ which, over multiple steps, accumulates into a global truncation error $e.$ Both LTE and GTE depend on step size $\Delta x.$

$$

In this way, order predicts the accuracy you gain when you make steps smaller." :tutorial/id #uuid "40e84a8b-32df-5566-99ff-2b37f338d69f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14500 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "ec16a00b-18c7-517a-94d1-35859655f930" :step/math-academy-id 585132 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222295}} {:db/id 17592186222498 :tutorial/content "Each step of a numerical method produces a local truncation error $\tau,$ which, over multiple steps, accumulates into a global truncation error $e.$ Both LTE and GTE depend on step size $\Delta x.$

The **order** of a numerical method describes how fast these errors shrink as $\Delta x$ decreases.
A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the *largest positive* integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^p\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately $k^p{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}e(\frac{Δx}{k}) & ≈K{(\frac{Δx}{k})}^{p}=\frac{K(Δx)^{p}}{{k}^{p}}≈\frac{e(Δx)}{{k}^{p}}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's demonstrate with an example. Suppose a numerical method is used to approximate the solution to an initial value problem.

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.21,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.21) = 0.785.$

- With step size $\Delta x = 0.07,$ the observed global truncation error is $e(0.07) = 0.010.$

Using this data, we can estimate the order of the numerical method.

The step size decreases from $0.21$ to $0.07.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k = \dfrac{0.21}{0.07} = 3.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the GTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
k^p = 3^p.
$$

On the other hand, the GTE actually decreases from $0.785$ to $0.010.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\dfrac{0.785}{0.010} = 78.5.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the GTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{p} & ≈78.5 \\ p & ≈{log}_{3}⁡(78.5) \\ p & ≈3.97….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the approximate order of the method is $4.$

But why is order important? Well, a higher order means that the error decreases faster as $\Delta x$ decreases. As a result, higher-order methods can achieve a target accuracy *with fewer steps*. In this way, order predicts the accuracy you gain when you make steps smaller." :tutorial/id #uuid "40e84a8b-32df-5566-99ff-2b37f338d69f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14500 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186222295 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221401 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221184 :question/id #uuid "fb9baafb-4eca-593f-ad3e-34744fdfd3f4" :question/math-academy-id "e-21684"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "48cd517d-be8a-5dc2-91af-fbd19231363c" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049053} {:db/id 17592186049611} {:db/id 17592186049621}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221972} {:db/id 17592186221974} {:db/id 17592186308639} {:db/id 17592186308640} {:db/id 17592186308641} {:db/id 17592186308642} {:db/id 17592186391487} {:db/id 17592186443231} {:db/id 17592186443235} {:db/id 17592186443236} {:db/id 17592186443240}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Order of a Numerical Method By Comparing GTE for Different Step Sizes"} :step/id #uuid "8b58215f-a6df-5452-b05c-85bfbc0fd9f2" :step/math-academy-id 585133 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222296}} {:db/id 17592186222296 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222499 :tutorial/content "An alternative, but equivalent, definition for the **order** can be made in terms of the local truncation error.

A numerical method has **order** $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0.
$$

In other words, a numerical method has **order** $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately $k^{p+1}.$

But why is the power $p+1$ for LTE but only $p$ for GTE?

Each local truncation error measures the error made in *one step* of the method. If a method has order $p,$ then the error made in a single step shrinks like

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right).
$$

However, on a fixed interval, using step size $\Delta x$ requires about

$$
N \approx \dfrac1{\Delta x}
$$

steps. The global truncation error results from *accumulating* these local errors over all steps.

Heuristically, adding up $N$ local errors of size $(\Delta x)^{p+1}$ gives

$$
e(\Delta x) \sim N \cdot (\Delta x)^{p+1} \sim \dfrac1{\Delta x} \cdot (\Delta x)^{p+1} = (\Delta x)^p.
$$

Thus, the local truncation error is one power of $\Delta x$ higher than the global truncation error.

Next, we will apply this definition to determine the order of a given numerical method." :tutorial/id #uuid "b5d4a6f3-fc92-557f-be1f-b14832313c21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14501 :tutorial/title "Order From Local Truncation Error"} :step/id #uuid "7d7d7ca0-178c-5ff6-b4a4-b9cd8fd8f8c0" :step/math-academy-id 585136 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222297}} {:db/id 17592186222499 :tutorial/content "An alternative, but equivalent, definition for the **order** can be made in terms of the local truncation error.

"76c4b12b-8383-5ed3-9f8c-d559ed16dcd4" :step/math-academy-id 585144 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222331}} {:db/id 17592186222331 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222512 :tutorial/content "We'll now show that the definition of order with respect to LTE is the same as with respect to GTE.

Indeed, suppose a numerical method with increment formula $\Delta y = \Phi(x, y, \Delta x) \cdot \Delta x$ satisfies the following:

$$
\tau(\Delta x) = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)\quad\textrm{as}\quad \Delta x \to 0
$$

On a fixed interval of length $L,$ the number of steps is $N \approx \dfrac{L}{\Delta x}.$ So,
$N = \mathcal O\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\Delta x}\right)$ as $\Delta x \to 0.$

Now, recall the relationship between GTE and LTE, given by

$$
e(\Delta x) = e_N = e_{N-1} + \left[ \Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \Delta x) - \Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \Delta x) \right] \cdot \Delta x + \tau_N.
$$

Since $y(x_{N-1}) - y_{N-1} = e_{N-1},$ it is natural to say that changing the input $y$ by $e_{N-1}$ changes $\Phi$ by about a constant multiple of $e_{N-1}.$ So, heuristically,

$$
\Phi(x_{N-1}, y(x_{N-1}), \Delta x) - \Phi(x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, \Delta x) \approx Ce_{N-1}
$$

for some $C$ that *doesn't* depend on $\Delta x$ (on a fixed interval). Hence, the GTE satisfies approximately

$$
e(\Delta x) = e_N \approx (1+C\Delta x)e_{N-1} + \tau_N.
$$

After $N$ steps, we get

$$
e(\Delta x) \approx (1+C\Delta x)^N e_0 + \sum_{n=1}^N(1+C\Delta x)^{N-n}\tau_n.
$$

Next, note that $(1+C\Delta x)^N \approx e^{CN\Delta x} \approx e^{CL},$ which is $\mathcal O(1)$ as $\Delta x \to 0.$ So, the weights $(1+C\Delta x)^{N-n}$ don't change the *power* of $\Delta x.$

So, we can treat the GTE as roughly the sum of the per-step local errors. Therefore,

$$
e(\Delta x) \approx \sum_{n=1}^N \tau_n
$$

With $\tau_n = \mathcal O\!\left((\Delta x)^{p+1}\right)$ for each $n=1,\ldots,N,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}e(Δx) & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{N}O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =N\cdot O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =O\,(\frac{1}{Δx})\cdot O\,((Δx)^{p+1}) \\  & =O\,((Δx)^{p}).\end{aligned}
$$

Note that since $p$ is maximal in the LTE definition, this shows the GTE has order $p$ as well." :tutorial/id #uuid "380a28f7-f36f-50b0-982b-365f87b068bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14656 :tutorial/title "Connecting the Definitions of the Order of Numerical Methods"} :step/id #uuid "a05640d9-1389-5d1b-b299-1230e633c270" :step/math-academy-id 593404} {:db/id 17592186222512 :tutorial/content "We'll now show that the definition of order with respect to LTE is the same as with respect to GTE.

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.25}=2.

$$
{k}^{1+1}={2}^{2}=4.

$$

$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-334724" :question/problem "The local truncation error (LTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}.
$$

Complete the following sentences.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Decreasing from $Δx=0.5$ to $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is reduced by a factor of $≈$
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ According to this data, the order of the method is approximately
{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =8(0.5)^{5}+2(0.5)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.031\,25+2\cdot 0.015\,625 \\  & =0.281\,25 \\  & ≈0.281.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =8(0.2)^{5}+2(0.2)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.000\,32+2\cdot 0.000\,064 \\  & =0.002\,688 \\  & ≈0.003.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.2}=2.5.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2.5}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\,25$ to $0.002\,688.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.281\,25}{0.002\,688}=104.631\,69…≈104.632.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2.5}^{p+1} & ≈104.631\,69… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2.5}⁡(104.631\,69…) \\ p+1 & ≈5.075… \\ p & ≈4.075….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$4.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{5})=O\,((Δx)^{4+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $4.$"} :step/id #uuid "d1344963-f111-577e-9b39-d9ba8d2a6219" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482618}}] :activity/title "Order of Numerical Methods" :activity/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-333576" :question/problem "Which of the following local truncation error expressions represent a first-order numerical method?
- **I.** $τ(Δx)=6(Δx)^{3}$
- **II.** $τ(Δx)=0.3(Δx)^{2}+2(Δx)^{3}$
- **III.** $τ(Δx)=9(Δx)^{3}+4(Δx)^{5}$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

With that in mind, let's check each option in turn:

- For $τ(Δx)=6(Δx)^{3},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $6(Δx)^{3}=6(Δx)^{2+1}.$ So, statement I corresponds to an order $2$ method.

- For $τ(Δx)=0.3(Δx)^{2}+2(Δx)^{3},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $0.3(Δx)^{2}=0.3(Δx)^{1+1}.$ So, statement II corresponds to an order $1$ method.

- For $τ(Δx)=9(Δx)^{3}+4(Δx)^{5},$ the dominant term as $Δx\to 0$ is $9(Δx)^{3}=9(Δx)^{2+1}.$ So, statement III corresponds to an order $2$ method.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"."} :step/id #uuid "054123fc-51ab-5f29-abe7-820e908c72d0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482628}} {:db/id 17592186482618 :step/content {:db/id 17592186482539 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2414084d-978d-5852-9a75-b14f36d5dc64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.008" :db/id 17592186481869}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481869} :answer-field/id #uuid "817219d2-4fac-5374-9c4a-6822ef9e7011" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186482448}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "4b679574-cdae-5555-900f-72dfd634fac3" :question/math-academy-id "q-334797" :question/problem "A numerical method for approximating a solution to an initial value problem is known to be order $3.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.25$ produces a global truncation error (GTE) of $e(0.25)≈0.125.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.10,$ what GTE should we expect?

$e(0.10)≈$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the global truncation error (GTE) satisfies

$$
e(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the GTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.25$ to $0.10.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.25}{0.10}=2.5.
$$

Now, since the numerical method is of order $3,$ the error is expected to decrease by a factor of

$$
{k}^{3}=(2.5)^{3}=15.625.
$$

Therefore, using a step size of $Δx=0.10,$ the expected GTE is

$$
e(0.10)≈\frac{0.125}{15.625}=0.008.
$$

So,

$$
e(0.10)≈0.008.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "017a4cef-d60d-58c4-aa28-d0d444164350" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482624}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2414084d-978d-5852-9a75-b14f36d5dc64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.008" :db/id 17592186481869}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186481869} :answer-field/id #uuid "817219d2-4fac-5374-9c4a-6822ef9e7011" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186482448} {:answer/id #uuid "2414084d-978d-5852-9a75-b14f36d5dc64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.008" :db/id 17592186481869} {:db/id 17592186482624 :step/content {:db/id 17592186308709 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8d2823fe-ac2e-533e-b8ef-d3d1dec21d4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.05" :db/id 17592186306488}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306488} :answer-field/id #uuid "cf20e996-1ea4-5bae-aecf-b59e8d34708e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186308167}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6a7b9303-06ef-5983-bd7d-577c4a789987" :question/math-academy-id "q-334946" :question/problem "A numerical method for approximating a solution to an initial value problem is known to be order $1.$  Suppose that using step size $Δx=0.5$ produces a local truncation error (LTE) of $τ(0.5)≈0.2.$  If we instead use a step size $Δx=0.25,$ what LTE should we expect?

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

In our case, the step size decreases from $0.08$ to $0.02.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.08}{0.02}=4.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={4}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.13$ to $0.002.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.13}{0.002}=65.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{p+1} & ≈65 \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{4}⁡(65) \\ p+1 & ≈3.011… \\ p & ≈2.011….\end{aligned}
$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-334724" :question/problem "The local truncation error (LTE) of a numerical method with step size $Δx$ is

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}.
$$

Complete the following sentences.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the local truncation error is $≈$
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Decreasing from $Δx=0.5$ to $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is reduced by a factor of $≈$
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ According to this data, the order of the method is approximately
{{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "A numerical method has order $p$ if $p$ is the largest positive integer such that the local truncation error (LTE) satisfies

$$
τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{p+1})\,\text{as}\,Δx\to 0.
$$

The order describes how fast errors shrink as $Δx$ decreases.

In other words, a numerical method has order $p$ if, for sufficiently small step sizes, reducing the step size by a factor of $k$ reduces the LTE by a factor of approximately ${k}^{p+1}.$

First, we compute the LTE for the given step sizes:

- With step size $Δx=0.5,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.5) & =8(0.5)^{5}+2(0.5)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.031\,25+2\cdot 0.015\,625 \\  & =0.281\,25 \\  & ≈0.281.\end{aligned}
$$

- With step size $Δx=0.2,$ the LTE is

$$
\begin{aligned}τ(0.2) & =8(0.2)^{5}+2(0.2)^{6} \\  & =8\cdot 0.000\,32+2\cdot 0.000\,064 \\  & =0.002\,688 \\  & ≈0.003.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we determine the order by comparing the errors. The step size decreases from $0.5$ to $0.2.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
k=\frac{0.5}{0.2}=2.5.
$$

As a result, for a numerical method of order $p,$ the LTE should decrease by a factor of approximately

$$
{k}^{p+1}={2.5}^{p+1}.
$$

On the other hand, the LTE actually decreases from $0.281\,25$ to $0.002\,688.$ So, it reduces by a factor of

$$
\frac{0.281\,25}{0.002\,688}=104.631\,69…≈104.632.
$$

Comparing the two scale factors for the LTE, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{2.5}^{p+1} & ≈104.631\,69… \\ p+1 & ≈{log}_{2.5}⁡(104.631\,69…) \\ p+1 & ≈5.075… \\ p & ≈4.075….\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, rounding to the nearest integer, the estimated order of the method is
$4.$

Indeed, this coincides with the definition of the order from the expression for the LTE:

$$
τ(Δx)=8(Δx)^{5}+2(Δx)^{6}\,⇒\,τ(Δx)=O\,((Δx)^{5})=O\,((Δx)^{4+1}),\,Δx\to 0.
$$

Hence, the order of the method is $4.$"} :step/id #uuid "d1344963-f111-577e-9b39-d9ba8d2a6219" :step/next {:db/id 17592186482618}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x)∼8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

*Hint: You may assume that all the cosine coefficients in the Fourier series of the particular solution are equal to zero.*

The Fourier series of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼{{field-1}}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,{{field-2}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)
$$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{b}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)-8(\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))=8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get 

$$
-8\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-8)\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x)=8+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the free terms and sine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8\cdot \frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=8 \\ {b}_{n}(-{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}-8)=\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{3}\pi }\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}_{0}}{2}=-1 \\ {b}_{n}=\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+8)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}∼-1+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\,\frac{3(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{3}\pi ({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+8)}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186368331 :question/id #uuid "fdf0a8e9-3b28-5328-8c13-b8779f952184" :question/math-academy-id "q-343876"} {:db/id 17592186368337 :question/id #uuid $4$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼-2+{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{6}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}}=\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=1$, we have ${\omega }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Since ${\omega }_{1}=\omega ,$ the $n=1$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=1$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{1}(x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{1}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))+x(-\frac{\pi }{2}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\frac{\pi }{2}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})) \\ {y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″} & =-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{1}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{1}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}y=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}):$

$$
[-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}]+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}{y}_{{p}_{1}}=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2})=6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-\pi A=0 \\ \pi B=6\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{6}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{1}}=\frac{6x}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi x}{2}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186317452 :question/id #uuid "de35c174-f52d-54b1-9320-5816b5069f2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-343905"} {:db/id 17592186317453 :question/id #uuid $$
{y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{{\pi }^{2}}=\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $4$-periodic function $(L=2)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{2}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))+x(-\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+{\pi }^{2}y=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x):$

$$
[-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)-{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-2\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+2\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2\pi A=1 \\ 2\pi B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=-\frac{1}{2\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{x}{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x).

{:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=f(x),$ where the $1$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2n\pi x).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{36{\pi }^{2}}=6\pi .
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $1$-periodic function $(L=\frac{1}{2})$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{(\frac{1}{2})}=2n\pi .
$$

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=6\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=3$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{3}(x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{{p}_{3}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x))+x(-6\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+6\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)) \\ {y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″} & =-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)-36{\pi }^{2}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{3}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{3}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+36{\pi }^{2}y=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x):$

$$
[-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)-36{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}]+36{\pi }^{2}{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-12\pi A\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x)+12\pi B\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x)=\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-12\pi A=0 \\ 12\pi B=\frac{1}{9}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=0 \\ B=\frac{1}{108\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{3}}=\frac{x}{108\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\pi x).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186397701 :question/id #uuid "dd94ef93-5daf-566f-92be-7aef938749ca" :question/math-academy-id "q-343899"} {:db/id 17592186397712 :question/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the differential equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x),$ where the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by 

$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{3(-1)^{n+1}}{{n}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{3}).
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below regarding the resonant component of a particular solution of the equation.

The natural frequency of the system matches the frequency of the {{field-1}} harmonic of the forcing function. 

Consequently, the particular solution contains a resonant term of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}={{field-2}}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation 

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=f(x)
$$

has a natural frequency of 

$$
\omega =\sqrt{\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

The frequencies of the forcing harmonics for a $6$-periodic function $(L=3)$ are 

$$
{\omega }_{n}=\frac{n\pi }{3}.
$$

For $n=2$, we have ${\omega }_{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.$ Since ${\omega }_{2}=\omega ,$ the $n=2$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

For the $n=2$ harmonic, the forcing term is 

$$
{f}_{2}(x)=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Because this frequency matches the natural frequency, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{′} & =(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))+x(-\frac{2\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{2\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})) \\ \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,{y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″} & =-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}x(A\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{{p}_{2}}^{″}$ and ${y}_{{p}_{2}}$ into the equation ${y}^{″}+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}y=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}):$

$$
\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,[-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})-\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}]+\frac{4{\pi }^{2}}{9}{y}_{{p}_{2}}=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})
$$

The resonant terms involving $x$ cancel out, leaving

$$
-\frac{4\pi }{3}A\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})+\frac{4\pi }{3}B\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3})=-\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$

Now, equating the sine and cosine coefficients, we obtain:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{4\pi }{3}A=-\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{4\pi }{3}B=0\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}A=\frac{9}{16\pi } \\ B=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the resonant component of a particular solution is

$$
{y}_{{p}_{2}}=\frac{9x}{16\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi x}{3}).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049479} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2077a0e4-25ea-549f-b18b-eeaee168ff0e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186222397} :activity/id #uuid "2774bc0e-42a3-5956-a4b7-a719151ea7c2" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049288 :topic/id #uuid "ea0735e9-7712-5a1c-a626-25cab33f54cb" :topic/math-academy-id 6386} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222397 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222522 :tutorial/content "Suppose a linear ODE has a periodic forcing term whose Fourier series is known, for example

$$
y' + ky = f(x),
\qquad\text{where}\qquad
f(x) \sim \frac{c_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(c_n\cos(\omega_n x) + d_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big).
$$

A standard strategy is to look for a *particular* solution with the *same Fourier frequencies*:

$$
y_p \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(a_n\cos(\omega_n x) + b_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big)
$$

Then, the method includes the following steps:

- **Step 1:** Differentiate term-by-term.

Using $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\cos(\omega_n x)=-\omega_n\sin(\omega_n x)$ and $\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\sin(\omega_n x)=\omega_n\cos(\omega_n x)$, we get

$$
y_p' \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(-a_n\omega_n\sin(\omega_n x) + b_n\omega_n\cos(\omega_n x)\Big).
$$

- **Step 2:** Substitute into the ODE and collect like terms

Then, we plug $y_p$ and $y_p'$ into the equation, and rewrite the left-hand side as

$$
\Big(\substack{\large\text{free} \[3pt] \large\text{term}}\Big) \;+\; 
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(\substack{\large\text{cosine} \[3pt] \large\text{coefficient}}\Big) \cos(\omega_n x) \;+\; 
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(\substack{\large\text{sine} \[3pt] \large\text{coefficient}}\Big) \sin(\omega_n x).
$$

- **Step 3:** Equate coefficients.

Because the Fourier series representation is unique (up to convergence issues we ignore here), we match:

- the free terms, and

- for each $n\ge 1$, the cosine coefficients and sine coefficients.

This produces:

- one equation for $a_0$ (from the constant term), and

- a $2\times 2$ linear system for $(a_n,b_n)$ for each $n\ge 1$.

- **Step 4:** Write the Fourier series of $y_p.$

After solving for $a_0$, $a_n$, and $b_n$, substitute them back into

$$
y_p \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \Big(a_n\cos(\omega_n x) + b_n\sin(\omega_n x)\Big).
$$

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "84328521-7170-5404-8ec2-a41475c2ad15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14711 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0521dca3-2fe6-50aa-8dc9-282e35ffe718" :step/math-academy-id 607546 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222398}} {:db/id 17592186222398 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221455 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221203 :question/id #uuid "03fbfe2c-b12f-5220-9fae-e0dfe210a505" :question/math-academy-id "e-21857"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4733fab7-18ca-5336-9aba-53212ddbf87b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049370} {:db/id 17592186050010}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186222031} {:db/id 17592186222032} {:db/id 17592186317443} {:db/id 17592186397662} {:db/id 17592186397676}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving First Order ODEs Given the Fourier Series of the Forcing Function"} :step/id #uuid "ab947003-2e2f-5620-996d-e8070699c2a1" :step/math-academy-id 607547 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222399}} {:db/id 17592186222399 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222523 :tutorial/content "For second-order linear ODEs, the overall algorithm is the same as for first-order equations: 

- we assume a Fourier series for $y_p$,

- substitute into the ODE, and

- match coefficients.

Before we start, we can use the forcing series properties to simplify our work. For a second-order equation of the form 

$$
y'' + \omega^2 y = f(x)
$$

with no $y'$ (damping) term, the particular solution can be simplified.

The key insight comes from the fact that the differential operator 

$$
L[y] = y'' + \omega^2 y
$$

maps cosines to cosines and sines to sines. This means we can match the form of our assumed solution $y_p$ to the form of the forcing function $f(x),$ which saves a great deal of work.

This leads to some powerful shortcuts:

- If $f(x)$ is a *pure cosine series* (an even function), we can assume $y_p$ is also a pure cosine series (all $b_n=0$).

- If $f(x)$ is a *pure sine series* (an odd function), we can assume $y_p$ is also a pure sine series (all $a_n=0$, including $a_0=0$).

- If the constant term in the series for $f(x)$ is zero, the constant term in $y_p$ will also be zero (so $a_0=0$).

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "12f51f58-a298-5fc1-9540-6d9f4611481b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14712 :tutorial/title "Second Order ODEs With Fourier Series"} :step/id #uuid "d1b21edf-14d7-5094-a313-f622ad12149b" :step/math-academy-id 607550 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222403}} {:db/id 17592186222400 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221456 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221204 :question/id #uuid "3944f6e4-a3a8-5bad-87c5-18227ce223bc" :question/math-academy-id "e-21858"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5e39d476-7dcb-5213-a461-df7bd1919b9f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050378}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186222035} {:db/id 17592186222037} {:db/id 17592186317447} {:db/id 17592186317448} {:db/id 17592186317449} {:db/id 17592186317450} {:db/id 17592186368331} {:db/id 17592186368337} {:db/id 17592186484247} {:db/id 17592186484267} {:db/id 17592186507450} {:db/id 17592186507482}] :knowledge-point/title "Solving Second Order ODEs Given the Fourier Series of the Forcing Function"} :step/id #uuid "2fb61d84-6e73-5592-aa15-0582c4b7b2f2" :step/math-academy-id 607551 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222401}} {:db/id 17592186222401 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222528 :tutorial/content "A forcing harmonic can cause *resonance* when its frequency matches the natural frequency of the homogeneous equation.

In cases like that, we proceed as follows:

- **Step 1:** Find the natural frequency.

For an equation of the form

$$
y''+\omega^2 y = f(x),
$$

the homogeneous solution oscillates with natural frequency $\omega$.

- **Step 2:** Find the forcing frequencies.

If $f$ is $2L$-periodic, then its Fourier series uses harmonics

$$
\cos\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right),\qquad \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right),
$$

whose frequencies are

$$
\omega_n=\frac{n\pi}{L}\qquad(n\ge 1).
$$

A harmonic is *resonant* exactly when $\omega_n=\omega$.

- **Step 3:** Form the particular solution ansatz for each harmonic.

- For a *non-resonant* harmonic ($\omega_n\ne \omega$), we use the standard ansatz:

$$
y_{p_n}=A\cos(\omega_n x)+B\sin(\omega_n x)
$$

- For a *resonant* harmonic ($\omega_n=\omega$), this form overlaps with the homogeneous solution. We must use the *modified ansatz* by multiplying by $x{:}$

$$
y_{p_n}=x\left(A\cos(\omega x)+B\sin(\omega x)\right)
$$

This extra factor of $x$ produces a new trial function that can match the forcing term.

When $f$ is given as a Fourier series, we check each harmonic:

- *non-resonant* harmonics contribute ordinary sine/cosine terms to $y_p,$ while

- *resonant* harmonics contribute terms multiplied by $x.$

In particular, the resonant harmonic is the one with index $n$ satisfying

$$
\frac{n\pi}{L}=\omega.
$$

Let's see how this works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "1aff3ba6-cd76-5ae7-bcd6-d05e9fb44694" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14776 :tutorial/title "Cases Where the Forcing Term Induces Resonance"} :step/id #uuid "6d7e21fe-4716-5031-8d15-1ac9a8196ed5" :step/math-academy-id 607555 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222402}} {:db/id 17592186222402 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221457 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221206 :question/id #uuid "926606c2-1e1a-5aab-8f2e-826163a204a2" :question/math-academy-id "e-21875"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9e42e65b-6e26-5a3f-9275-25a291e13138" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048966}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186222039} {:db/id 17592186222040} {:db/id 17592186317451} {:db/id 17592186317452} {:db/id 17592186317453} {:db/id 17592186368351} {:db/id 17592186368362} {:db/id 17592186397690} {:db/id 17592186397701} {:db/id 17592186397712} {:db/id 17592186507448} {:db/id 17592186507508}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Resonant Harmonics"} :step/id #uuid "ca55a627-e4f5-543f-96b1-6632f3610f35" :step/math-academy-id 607556} {:db/id 17592186222403 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222530 :tutorial/content "Consider the differential equation $y''-4y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $2$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$
f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{2}{n^2}\cos(n\pi x).
$$

Because $f$ has no free term and is a pure cosine series, we assume

$$
y_p \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x).
$$

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}n\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi x))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $y''_p$ and $y_p$ into the equation and have

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty -a_n n^2\pi^2\cos(n\pi x)
-
4\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\cos(n\pi x)\right)
=
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{2}{n^2}\cos(n\pi x).
$$

Rearranging the terms, we get

$$
\sum_{n=1}^\infty -a_n(n^2\pi^2+4)\cos(n\pi x)
=
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{2}{n^2}\cos(n\pi x).
$$

Now, equating the cosine coefficients, we obtain

$$
-a_n(n^2\pi^2+4)=\dfrac{2}{n^2}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
a_n=-\dfrac{2}{n^2(n^2\pi^2+4)}.
$$

Therefore, a Fourier series for a particular solution is

$$
y_p \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \: -\dfrac{2}{n^2(n^2\pi^2+4)} \cdot \cos(n\pi x).
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f2d6d8f9-00d1-552b-889a-e54ed8d22d21" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14873 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example of Solving a Second Order ODE"} :step/id #uuid "483f5b2d-f9cb-5272-a15f-759e449ff9c0" :step/math-academy-id 607559 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222400}}] :activity/title "Solving ODEs Using Fourier Series" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186221475} {:db/id 17592186222397 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222522 :tutorial/content "Suppose a linear ODE has a periodic forcing term whose Fourier series is known, for example
